Week 1: Big Data — The Big Picture

Study Guide | Ultimate Big Data Masters Program

1. Introduction to Big Data & Fundamentals

What is Big Data?

Big Data refers to data that is too large, complex, or fast-moving to be efficiently stored and processed using a single conventional computing system.

It is commonly described using the 5 V's of Big Data:

V

Meaning

Example

Volume

Massive quantities of data

Petabytes of social media or sensor data

Variety

Different types and formats of data

Structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data

Velocity

Speed at which data is generated and processed

Real-time transactions during an online sale

Veracity

Quality, accuracy, and reliability of data

Removing inaccurate or inconsistent records

Value

Business value extracted from data

Using customer data to improve business decisions

Types of Data

1. Structured Data

  • Has a fixed schema.
  • Organized into rows and columns.
  • Example: MySQL relational tables.

2. Semi-Structured Data

  • Has some organizational structure but does not follow a rigid tabular schema.
  • Examples: CSV, JSON, XML.

3. Unstructured Data

  • Does not follow a predefined schema.
  • Examples: images, videos, raw logs, documents.

2. Monolithic vs. Distributed Systems

Traditional monolithic systems struggle to handle Big Data because of limitations in scalability and hardware capacity.

Feature

Monolithic System

Distributed System

Architecture

Single large system containing the required hardware resources

Cluster of interconnected machines (nodes) working together

Scaling

Vertical scaling

Horizontal scaling

Approach

Add CPU/RAM to an existing machine

Add more machines/nodes to the cluster

Scalability

Limited by the capacity of a single machine

Can scale by adding additional nodes

Vertical Scaling

Increasing the capacity of a single machine by adding resources such as:

  • CPU
  • RAM
  • Storage

Horizontal Scaling

Increasing capacity by adding more machines to the cluster.

Core Requirements of Big Data Systems

  1. Distributed Storage — Store data across multiple physical machines.
  2. Distributed Processing — Process data concurrently across multiple nodes.
  3. Scalability — Allow the system to expand horizontally as data volume increases.

3. Hadoop Ecosystem

Hadoop is an open-source framework designed primarily for distributed storage and distributed processing of large datasets.

Core Components

HDFS — Hadoop Distributed File System

Provides distributed storage by spreading data across multiple nodes.

MapReduce

A distributed processing framework used to process large datasets.

Note: MapReduce is now less commonly used for modern Big Data processing because of its relatively slower execution model and complexity compared with Spark.

YARN — Yet Another Resource Negotiator

Manages and allocates computing resources across the Hadoop cluster.

Hadoop Ecosystem Tools

4. Introduction to Apache Spark

Apache Spark was developed to address several limitations of MapReduce, particularly its execution speed and programming complexity.

Key Characteristics

  • General-purpose distributed compute engine
  • In-memory processing capabilities
  • High performance
  • Supports batch and streaming workloads
  • Supports multiple programming languages

Spark vs. MapReduce

A key concept to remember:

Spark replaces MapReduce as a processing engine; it does not replace Hadoop's entire ecosystem.

Spark can work with independent storage systems and resource managers.

Supported Languages

  • Python → PySpark
  • Scala
  • Java
  • R

Spark Stack

Storage + Compute + Resource Management

Storage
→ HDFS / Amazon S3 / ADLS

Compute
→ Apache Spark

Resource Manager
→ YARN / Kubernetes

7. HDFS Architecture Deep Dive

HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) is Hadoop's distributed storage system.

It follows a Master–Worker architecture.

Key Components

NameNode — Master

The NameNode manages filesystem metadata.

It maintains:

  • Directory structure
  • File metadata
  • File-to-block mapping
  • Block location information

When a client wants to access a file, it first communicates with the NameNode to determine where the required blocks are located.

DataNode — Worker

DataNodes store the actual physical data blocks.

They are responsible for:

  • Storing data blocks
  • Serving data to clients
  • Replicating blocks
  • Reporting their status to the NameNode

HDFS Defaults

Property

Default

Block Size

128 MB

Replication Factor

3

Heartbeat Mechanism

DataNodes periodically send heartbeat signals to the NameNode to indicate that they are operational.

If a DataNode stops responding, the NameNode can identify it as unavailable and initiate recovery/re-replication of the affected blocks.

Data Locality

Data Locality means moving computation closer to where the data physically resides.

Instead of moving large volumes of data across the network:

Move computation to the data.

This reduces:

  • Network traffic
  • Data transfer overhead
  • Processing latency

and improves overall cluster performance.

Quick Revision

Big Data → 5 V's

Volume + Variety + Velocity + Veracity + Value

Big Data Architecture

Distributed Storage + Distributed Processing + Scalability

Hadoop

HDFS → Storage
MapReduce → Processing
YARN → Resource Management

Spark

Modern distributed compute engine that can replace MapReduce

Data Architecture

Database → Transactions → OLTP

Data Warehouse → Analytics → OLAP

Data Lake → Raw Big Data → Schema on Read

Data Engineering

Source → Ingestion → Data Lake → Processing → Serving → BI

HDFS

NameNode → Metadata

DataNode → Actual Data

Data Locality → Compute near the data

Important Concepts to Remember

1. Big Data is not simply "a lot of data."
It involves challenges related to volume, variety, velocity, veracity, and value.

2. Horizontal scaling is fundamental to Big Data.
Instead of continuously buying a bigger machine, distributed systems add more machines.

3. Spark is a compute engine.
It does not inherently replace distributed storage such as HDFS or S3.

4. Data Lake ≠ Data Warehouse.
A Data Lake is designed to store raw data at scale, while a Data Warehouse is optimized for structured analytical workloads.

5. HDFS separates metadata from actual data.
NameNode manages metadata; DataNodes store the actual blocks.

Week 2: Distributed Storage & Data Lake

Study Guide | Ultimate Big Data Masters Program

1. HDFS Fundamentals & Architecture Deep Dive

HDFS Architecture

HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) follows a Master–Worker architecture.

Component

Role

Responsibility

NameNode

Master

Stores filesystem metadata, directory structure, file-to-block mappings, and block locations

DataNode

Worker

Stores the actual physical data blocks

Simple Analogy

Think of the NameNode as the index of a book.

  • The NameNode tells you where the information is located.
  • The DataNodes contain the actual information.

HDFS Read Architecture

Client → NameNode → DataNode(s)

The NameNode is involved in metadata lookup, but the actual data is read directly from the DataNodes.

HDFS Read Process

Step 1 — Client requests file information

The client sends a request to the NameNode asking where the required file blocks are located.

Step 2 — NameNode provides block locations

The NameNode checks its metadata and returns the locations/IP addresses of the relevant DataNodes.

Step 3 — Client reads data directly

The client connects directly to the respective DataNodes and streams the required blocks.

Key Point

NameNode provides metadata; DataNodes provide data.

The actual file data does not pass through the NameNode.

2. HDFS Block Size

The default HDFS block size in modern Hadoop is typically 128 MB.

Block size has a direct impact on:

  • Number of blocks
  • NameNode metadata
  • Parallelism
  • Processing performance

Smaller Block Size

Example: 32 MB or 64 MB

Advantages

  • Creates more blocks.
  • Provides more potential units of parallel processing.

Disadvantages

  • Increases the total number of blocks.
  • Increases metadata maintained by the NameNode.
  • Can increase NameNode memory requirements.

Larger Block Size

Example: 256 MB or 512 MB

Advantages

  • Reduces the total number of blocks.
  • Reduces NameNode metadata overhead.

Disadvantages

  • Fewer blocks mean fewer parallel processing units.
  • May reduce processing parallelism for certain workloads.

Quick Comparison

Block Size

Main Advantage

Main Disadvantage

Smaller

More parallelism

More metadata

Larger

Less metadata

Less parallelism

128 MB

Common default

Balance between the two

Remember: Block size is a trade-off between parallelism and metadata overhead.

3. HDFS High Availability, Scalability & Fault Tolerance

NameNode Federation

NameNode Federation allows multiple independent NameNodes/namespaces to operate within the same HDFS cluster.

It helps:

  • Scale metadata management
  • Reduce the memory limitations of a single NameNode
  • Improve namespace scalability

Fault Tolerance

HDFS achieves fault tolerance primarily through data replication.

The typical default replication factor is:

Replication Factor = 3

This means each block can have multiple copies distributed across DataNodes.

If one DataNode fails, another replica can serve the data.

Secondary NameNode

The Secondary NameNode periodically combines:

  • FsImage
  • Edit Logs

This helps keep metadata checkpoints manageable and makes recovery faster.

Important: The Secondary NameNode is not a backup NameNode and does not automatically take over when the primary NameNode fails.

Rack Awareness

HDFS uses Rack Awareness to distribute block replicas across different physical racks.

This protects against failures such as:

  • Rack failure
  • Network switch failure
  • Power failure affecting an entire rack

Key Concept

Replication protects data from node failures, while rack awareness protects data from larger infrastructure failures.

6. HDFS vs. Cloud Data Lakes

One of the most important changes introduced by cloud data platforms is the separation of compute and storage.

Traditional HDFS

Compute + Storage → Same Cluster

HDFS typically operates as part of a Hadoop cluster where compute and storage infrastructure are closely coupled.

Cloud Data Lake

Compute ↔ Independent Cloud Storage

Cloud object storage such as Amazon S3 and Azure ADLS Gen2 allows storage to exist independently from compute clusters.

This enables multiple compute engines or clusters to access the same underlying data.

Storage Architecture Comparison

7. Distributed Processing: MapReduce

MapReduce is a distributed processing programming model designed to process large datasets across multiple machines.

The basic flow is:

Input → Map → Shuffle & Sort → Reduce → Output

MapReduce Data Flow

Input Data

    ↓

Record Reader

    ↓

Mapper

    ↓

Shuffle & Sort

    ↓

Reducer

    ↓

Output

8. MapReduce Execution Phases

Phase 1 — Record Reader & Mapper

The Record Reader reads the input data and converts it into key-value pairs.

The Mapper processes the input and produces intermediate key-value pairs.

Conceptually:

Input (K₁, V₁)

↓

Mapper

↓

Intermediate (K₂, V₂)

Data Locality

Map tasks generally run as close as possible to the DataNode containing the required data.

This follows the principle:

Move computation to the data rather than moving large amounts of data across the network.

Phase 2 — Shuffle

The Shuffle phase transfers intermediate Mapper output across the network.

Its primary purpose is to ensure that values belonging to the same key are sent to the same Reducer.

For example:

Mapper 1 → (Apple, 2)

Mapper 2 → (Apple, 4)

Mapper 3 → (Apple, 3)

After Shuffle:

Reducer → Apple → [2, 4, 3]

Phase 3 — Sort

The intermediate data is organized and grouped by key before being passed to the Reducer.

Conceptually:

Apple → [2, 4, 3]

Banana → [5, 1]

Orange → [7, 2]

Phase 4 — Reducer

The Reducer processes grouped values and performs the required aggregation or business logic.

For example:

Apple → [2, 4, 3]

Reducer:

2 + 4 + 3 = 9

Output:

Apple → 9

9. MapReduce Architecture

Overall Flow

Input File Blocks

↓

Multiple Mappers

↓

Shuffle & Sort

↓

Reducers

↓

Final Output

Key Characteristics

  • Multiple Mappers can execute in parallel.
  • Shuffle involves network transfer.
  • Sort groups intermediate data by key.
  • Reducers process grouped values.
  • Data locality minimizes unnecessary data movement during the Map phase.

Quick Revision

HDFS

NameNode → Metadata

DataNode → Actual Data

Replication → Fault Tolerance

Rack Awareness → Protection against rack-level failures

Federation → Namespace scalability

HDFS Read

Client → NameNode → Block Locations → DataNodes → Data

NameNode does not serve the actual file data.

HDFS Block Size

Smaller blocks → More parallelism + More metadata

Larger blocks → Less metadata + Less parallelism

Cloud Data Lake

HDFS → Tightly coupled compute + storage

Cloud Data Lake → Decoupled compute + storage

MapReduce

Input → Map → Shuffle → Sort → Reduce → Output

Important Concepts to Remember

1. NameNode stores metadata, not actual file data.

2. DataNodes store the actual HDFS blocks.

3. The client reads data directly from DataNodes after obtaining block locations from the NameNode.

4. Replication provides fault tolerance; Rack Awareness provides additional protection against rack-level failures.

5. Secondary NameNode is not a standby NameNode.

6. Cloud object storage separates storage from compute, allowing both to scale independently.

7. Shuffle is one of the most network-intensive stages of MapReduce.

8. Data locality reduces network traffic by bringing computation closer to the data.

Week 3: Distributed Processing Fundamentals & Apache Spark

Study Guide | Ultimate Big Data Masters Program

1. MapReduce Deep-Dive & Optimizations

In a MapReduce job, processing large amounts of distributed data relies primarily on two phases:

Mapper

The Mapper provides parallelism.

It:

  • Reads input blocks.
  • Processes the input records.
  • Generates intermediate key-value pairs.

Reducer

The Reducer provides aggregation.

It:

  • Receives Mapper output.
  • Groups data by key.
  • Performs aggregation or other reduction logic.
  • Produces the final result.

Optimization Rule of Thumb

Push as much computation as possible toward the Mapper and minimize the work performed by the Reducer.

Doing more work earlier in the pipeline can reduce the amount of data that needs to be transferred and processed later.

Configuring the Number of Reducers

By default, a MapReduce job runs with 1 Reducer.

The number of Reducers can be configured based on workload requirements.

Number of Reducers

When to Use

Effect

1 Reducer

Small or simple workloads

Simple execution but may become a bottleneck

Multiple Reducers (>1)

Large aggregations

Allows parallel reduction and avoids a single Reducer bottleneck

0 Reducers

Jobs requiring no aggregation

Mapper output becomes the final output; Shuffle & Sort can be skipped

When to Increase Reducers

Use multiple Reducers when a single Reducer takes too long to process a large aggregation.

Example:

Mapper 1 ──┐

Mapper 2 ──┼──→ Shuffle & Sort ──→ Reducer 1

Mapper 3 ──┘                    ├──→ Reducer 2

                                └──→ Reducer 3

This allows the reduction workload to be distributed across multiple machines.

When to Set Reducers to 0

If the job does not require aggregation—for example, a simple filtering operation—the number of Reducers can be set to 0.

In this case:

Mapper → Final Output

The expensive Shuffle and Sort phases can be skipped.

2. Shuffle, Sort & Partition

When multiple Reducers are used, the MapReduce framework needs a mechanism to determine which Reducer should receive each intermediate key-value pair.

This is where Partitioning, Shuffle, and Sort come into play.

Partitioning

Partitioning determines which key-value pair is sent to which Reducer.

Important Rule

Number of partitions = Number of Reducers

For example:

3 Reducers → 3 Partitions

Default Partitioner

The default system partitioner generally uses a hash-based partitioning mechanism.

A simplified example is:

Partition = hash(key) % number_of_reducers

This ensures that the same key is consistently sent to the same Reducer.

Custom Partitioner

Developers can implement custom logic to control how data is distributed.

For example:

Word length < 4  → Reducer 1

Word length ≥ 4  → Reducer 2

Shuffle

Shuffle is the physical transfer of intermediate Mapper output across the network to the appropriate Reducer.

Key Idea

Shuffle = Network movement of Mapper output to Reducers.

Because Shuffle involves network communication, it can become an expensive stage of a distributed job.

Sort

The Sort phase groups data by key on the Reducer side so that all values belonging to the same key can be processed together.

Example:

Before Sort:

Apple   → 1

Orange  → 1

Apple   → 1

Banana  → 1

Orange  → 1

After Sort:

Apple   → [1, 1]

Banana  → [1]

Orange  → [1, 1]

This grouped structure is then provided to the Reducer.

3. Combiners — Local Aggregation

A Combiner is essentially a mini-reducer that performs local aggregation on the Mapper output before the data is transferred across the network.

Without a Combiner

Mapper → Shuffle → Reducer

Large amounts of intermediate data may need to travel across the network.

With a Combiner

Mapper → Combiner → Shuffle → Reducer

The Combiner reduces the amount of data that needs to be transferred.

Advantages

  • Reduces network traffic.
  • Improves performance.
  • Performs local aggregation.
  • Reduces the amount of intermediate data sent to Reducers.

Example

Suppose a Mapper produces:

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

A Combiner can locally convert this to:

Apple → 4

Instead of sending four records over the network, only one aggregated record needs to be transferred.

Important Caution

Combiners are safe for operations such as:

  • Sum
  • Min
  • Max

However, they cannot be directly used for calculating an Average.

Why?

Because averaging already-averaged subsets can produce an incorrect final average unless the computation is designed to retain the required count and sum information.

Remember: A Combiner should only be used when the operation is safe for local partial aggregation.

4. The Transition to Apache Spark

Challenges of MapReduce

MapReduce was revolutionary for distributed processing, but it has several limitations.

1. Poor Performance

MapReduce relies heavily on disk I/O.

When multiple MapReduce jobs are chained together, intermediate results are repeatedly:

Written to Disk → Read from Disk → Processed → Written to Disk

This creates significant overhead.

2. High Code Complexity

Simple data-processing operations can require large amounts of complex Java code.

This makes development:

  • More time-consuming
  • Harder to maintain
  • More difficult to debug

3. Batch Only

Traditional MapReduce is primarily designed for batch processing.

It is not designed for:

  • Real-time streaming
  • Interactive querying
  • Low-latency processing

5. What is Apache Spark?

Apache Spark is an open-source, multi-language, general-purpose distributed compute engine.

One of its major advantages is its ability to keep intermediate data in memory (RAM) when appropriate, reducing repeated disk I/O.

Key Characteristics

  • Open-source
  • Distributed
  • General-purpose
  • Multi-language
  • In-memory processing capabilities
  • High performance
  • Supports batch and streaming workloads

Why is Spark Faster?

A simplified comparison:

MapReduce

Process

   ↓

Write to Disk

   ↓

Read from Disk

   ↓

Process

   ↓

Write to Disk

Spark

Process

   ↓

Keep Intermediate Data in Memory

   ↓

Continue Processing

This reduction in disk I/O can significantly improve performance for workloads involving multiple processing stages.

Plug-and-Play Architecture

Spark does not provide its own distributed storage system.

It can work with external storage systems such as:

  • HDFS
  • Amazon S3
  • Azure ADLS Gen2

Spark can also run with external resource managers such as:

  • YARN
  • Kubernetes
  • Mesos

Spark Stack

Storage

HDFS / S3 / ADLS

        ↓

Compute

Apache Spark

        ↓

Resource Management

YARN / Kubernetes / Mesos

Key Concept

Spark is primarily a compute engine, not a storage system.

7. Spark Architecture & Core Concepts

Spark APIs

Spark provides different levels of APIs for processing data.

Layer 1 — Core APIs

The foundational API is based on RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets).

RDDs provide:

  • Low-level control
  • Flexibility
  • Fine-grained transformations

However, they generally require more code and are more difficult to work with than higher-level APIs.

Layer 2 — Higher-Level APIs

Spark provides higher-level abstractions such as:

  • DataFrames
  • Spark SQL
  • Structured Streaming
  • MLlib

These APIs provide simpler syntax and allow Spark to apply additional optimizations.

API Hierarchy

               Apache Spark

                     │

          ┌──────────┴──────────┐

          │                     │

      Core APIs           Higher-Level APIs

          │                     │

         RDD        DataFrame / Spark SQL

                             │

                    Structured Streaming

                             │

                           MLlib

8. Resilient Distributed Dataset — RDD

An RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset) is a fundamental distributed data abstraction in Apache Spark.

RDD Characteristics

1. Resilient

RDDs are fault tolerant.

If a partition is lost because a worker node fails, Spark can use Lineage to recompute the lost partition.

2. Distributed

RDD data is divided into partitions and distributed across worker nodes.

3. Dataset

An RDD represents a distributed collection of data.

RDD Immutability

RDDs are immutable.

Once an RDD has been created, it cannot be modified.

Instead, transformations create a new RDD from an existing RDD.

For example:

RDD 1

  ↓ map()

RDD 2

  ↓ filter()

RDD 3

The original RDDs remain unchanged.

9. RDD Fault Tolerance & Lineage

One of Spark's key strengths is its ability to recover lost data without necessarily requiring a complete copy of every intermediate dataset.

Suppose:

RDD 1 → RDD 2 → RDD 3 → RDD 4

If a partition of RDD 4 is lost because a worker fails, Spark can use the transformation history—called Lineage—to recompute that partition.

Key Concept

Lineage = The history of transformations used to build an RDD.

This is one of the reasons RDDs are considered resilient.

10. Transformations vs. Actions

Spark operations are broadly divided into two categories:

Type

Description

Evaluation

Examples

Transformation

Creates a new RDD/DataFrame from an existing dataset

Lazy

map(), filter()

Action

Triggers execution and returns or writes a result

Triggers execution

collect(), saveAsTextFile()

Transformations

A transformation creates a new dataset based on an existing dataset.

Examples:

map()

filter()

flatMap()

reduceByKey()

Transformations are lazy.

When a transformation is called, Spark does not immediately execute it.

Instead, Spark records the required operation.

Actions

An Action triggers actual execution of the accumulated transformations.

Examples:

collect()

saveAsTextFile()

count()

When an Action is encountered, Spark evaluates the required execution plan.

Simple Rule

Transformation = What should Spark do?

Action = Now actually do it.

11. Lazy Evaluation & DAG

What is Lazy Evaluation?

Spark uses Lazy Evaluation for transformations.

For example:

rdd1 = ...

rdd2 = rdd1.map(...)

rdd3 = rdd2.filter(...)

Spark does not immediately execute map() or filter().

Instead, it builds an execution plan.

Only when an Action is called does Spark execute the required operations.

Directed Acyclic Graph — DAG

The execution plan created by Spark is represented as a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph).

Example:

Load Data

    ↓

map()

    ↓

filter()

    ↓

reduceByKey()

    ↓

collect()

    ↓

Execution

Why is Lazy Evaluation Important?

Because Spark waits until it sees the complete execution plan, it can optimize the processing.

For example:

1 Billion Records

        ↓

     Filter

        ↓

   5 Records

Instead of unnecessarily processing all 1 billion records through every possible operation, Spark can optimize the execution plan so that filtering happens as early as possible.

Lazy Evaluation allows Spark to understand the complete DAG before execution and optimize the execution plan.

12. Spark Execution: Word Count Example

To write code using PySpark, an entry point to the Spark environment is required.

SparkSession

SparkSession is the modern entry point for Spark applications.

It provides access to Spark functionality and consolidates functionality that historically existed across:

  • SparkContext
  • SQLContext
  • HiveContext

When working directly with RDDs, the SparkContext is still accessible through the SparkSession.

PySpark RDD Word Count Workflow

Step 1 — Load Data

rdd1 = spark.sparkContext.textFile(

    "/user/itv005857/data/inputfile.txt"

)

This loads the input file into an RDD.

Step 2 — Split Lines into Words

rdd2 = rdd1.flatMap(

    lambda x: x.split(" ")

)

flatMap() splits each line into individual words.

Example:

Input:

"hello world"

Output:

hello

world

Step 3 — Assign Count of 1

rdd3 = rdd2.map(

    lambda word: (word, 1)

)

Each word is converted into a key-value pair:

hello → (hello, 1)

world → (world, 1)

hello → (hello, 1)

Step 4 — Aggregate by Key

rdd4 = rdd3.reduceByKey(

    lambda x, y: x + y

)

reduceByKey() combines values belonging to the same key.

Example:

hello → [1, 1, 1]

becomes:

hello → 3

Step 5 — Trigger Execution & Save Output

rdd4.saveAsTextFile(

    "/user/itv005857/data/newoutput"

)

This is an Action, so Spark executes the accumulated DAG.

Alternatively:

rdd4.collect()

can be used to bring the result back to the driver for display.

Caution: Avoid using collect() on very large datasets because it brings the entire result into the driver's memory and can cause an Out Of Memory (OOM) error.

13. Complete PySpark Word Count Example

# 1. Load data into an RDD

rdd1 = spark.sparkContext.textFile(

    "/user/itv005857/data/inputfile.txt"

)

# 2. Transformations (Lazy)

rdd2 = rdd1.flatMap(

    lambda x: x.split(" ")

)

rdd3 = rdd2.map(

    lambda word: (word, 1)

)

rdd4 = rdd3.reduceByKey(

    lambda x, y: x + y

)

# 3. Action (Triggers execution of the DAG)

rdd4.saveAsTextFile(

    "/user/itv005857/data/newoutput"

)

# Alternative: use collect() to print results

# Use with caution on large datasets

# rdd4.collect()

Quick Revision

Concept

Remember

Mapper

Provides parallel processing and generates intermediate key-value pairs

Reducer

Aggregates values by key

Partitioner

Determines which Reducer receives each key

Shuffle

Transfers Mapper output across the network

Sort

Groups data by key before reduction

Combiner

Performs local aggregation before Shuffle

Spark

Distributed compute engine designed to overcome several MapReduce limitations

RDD

Immutable, distributed, fault-tolerant data abstraction

Lineage

Transformation history used to recompute lost RDD partitions

Transformation

Lazy operation that creates a new dataset

Action

Triggers execution

DAG

Logical execution plan representing dependencies between operations

Lazy Evaluation

Allows Spark to optimize the execution plan before running it

SparkSession

Modern entry point for Spark applications

collect()

Brings results to the driver; risky for large datasets

saveAsTextFile()

Writes RDD output to storage

Important Concepts to Remember

1. Mapper = Parallelism; Reducer = Aggregation.

2. Try to perform as much computation as possible before the Shuffle stage.

3. Number of partitions generally equals the number of Reducers.

4. Shuffle is expensive because it involves network data transfer.

5. A Combiner reduces the amount of data transferred during Shuffle by performing local aggregation.

6. Spark is a compute engine, not a storage system.

7. RDDs are immutable and fault tolerant through Lineage.

8. Transformations are lazy; Actions trigger execution.

9. Lazy Evaluation allows Spark to build and optimize the DAG before execution.

10. collect() should be used carefully because it brings the complete result to the Driver.

One-line mental model for Week 3

MapReduce:
Map → Partition → Shuffle → Sort → Reduce

Spark:
Load → Transform → Build DAG → Action → Execute

RDD:
Immutable + Distributed + Fault Tolerant + Lineage

Week 4: Apache Spark Core APIs (RDD)

Study Guide | Ultimate Big Data Masters Program

1. Python Foundations for PySpark

Normal Functions vs. Lambda Functions

Normal Function

A normal function is defined using def, has an explicit name, and can be reused throughout a program.

def my_sum(x, y):

    return x + y

Lambda Function

A lambda function is an anonymous, inline function generally used for short, single-use logic.

lambda x, y: x + y

Comparison

Feature

Normal Function

Lambda Function

Definition

Uses def

Uses lambda

Name

Explicitly named

Usually anonymous

Use Case

Reusable / complex logic

Short, inline operations

Example

def my_sum(x, y):

lambda x, y: x + y

Python map() / reduce() vs. Spark map() / reduce()

The names are similar, but the execution model is different.

Python

Python map() and reduce() are higher-order functions that generally operate locally on the machine running the Python program.

Spark

Spark map() and reduce() are distributed operations that can execute across multiple cluster worker nodes.

Key Difference: Python operations are primarily local, while Spark operations are designed for distributed processing.

2. End-to-End PySpark Practice Use Cases

Dataset Schema

order_id, date, customer_id, order_status

Sample Input

1,2013-07-25 00:00:00.0,11599,CLOSED

Spark Session Initialization

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

import getpass

username = getpass.getuser()

spark = SparkSession.builder \

    .config('spark.ui.port', '0') \

    .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", f"/user/{username}/warehouse") \

    .enableHiveSupport() \

    .master('yarn') \

    .getOrCreate()

Load Data into an RDD

orders_rdd = spark.sparkContext.textFile(

    "/public/trendytech/retail_db/orders/*"

)

Use Case 1 — Count Orders by Category

Requirement: Count orders in each category and sort the result by count in descending order.

mapped_orders = orders_rdd.map(

    lambda x: (x.split(",")[3], 1)

)

category_counts = mapped_orders.reduceByKey(

    lambda x, y: x + y

)

sorted_category_counts = category_counts.sortBy(

    lambda x: x[1],

    False

)

Execution Logic

Orders

   ↓

Extract order_status

   ↓

(status, 1)

   ↓

reduceByKey()

   ↓

Count by category

   ↓

sortBy(count, descending)

Use Case 2 — Top 10 Premium Customers

Requirement: Find the top 10 customers based on the number of orders placed.

customer_orders = orders_rdd.map(

    lambda x: (x.split(",")[2], 1)

)

top_10_customers = customer_orders \

    .reduceByKey(lambda x, y: x + y) \

    .sortBy(lambda x: x[1], False) \

    .take(10)

Execution Logic

Orders

   ↓

Extract customer_id

   ↓

(customer_id, 1)

   ↓

reduceByKey()

   ↓

Count orders per customer

   ↓

sortBy(count, descending)

   ↓

take(10)

Use Case 3 — Count Distinct Customers

Requirement: Count the number of unique customers who placed at least one order.

distinct_customers_count = orders_rdd \

    .map(lambda x: x.split(",")[2]) \

    .distinct() \

    .count()

Execution Logic

Orders

   ↓

Extract customer_id

   ↓

distinct()

   ↓

count()

Use Case 4 — Customers with Maximum CLOSED Orders

Requirement: Find customers with the highest number of CLOSED orders.

closed_orders = orders_rdd.filter(

    lambda x: x.split(",")[3] == 'CLOSED'

)

top_closed_customers = closed_orders \

    .map(lambda x: (x.split(",")[2], 1)) \

    .reduceByKey(lambda x, y: x + y) \

    .sortBy(lambda x: x[1], False)

Execution Logic

Orders

   ↓

filter(status == CLOSED)

   ↓

(customer_id, 1)

   ↓

reduceByKey()

   ↓

Count CLOSED orders

   ↓

sortBy(count, descending)

3. RDD Transformations & Actions Reference

Operation

Type

Behavior / Output Shape

map(func)

Transformation

Narrow: One input record produces one output record.

filter(func)

Transformation

Narrow: Filters records based on a condition; output size ≤ input size.

flatMap(func)

Transformation

Narrow: One input can produce multiple outputs; collections are flattened.

reduceByKey(func)

Transformation

Wide: Performs aggregation by key and involves Shuffle.

sortBy(func) / sortByKey()

Transformation

Wide: Requires data redistribution for global sorting.

distinct()

Transformation

Wide: Removes duplicate records across partitions.

join()

Transformation

Wide: Performs a key-based join across distributed partitions.

reduce(func)

Action

Aggregates all elements into a single final value.

count()

Action

Returns the total number of records.

countByValue()

Action

Returns the frequency of each unique value.

4. Partitioning & Development Workflow

Developing Locally with parallelize()

When developing Spark logic, loading a multi-terabyte dataset just to test a transformation is inefficient.

Instead, developers can use parallelize() to create an RDD from a small local collection.

Example

words = [

    "big", "Data", "Is", "SUPER", "Interesting",

    "BIG", "data", "IS", "A", "Trending", "technology"

]

result = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(words) \

    .map(lambda x: x.lower()) \

    .map(lambda x: (x, 1)) \

    .reduceByKey(lambda x, y: x + y) \

    .collect()

Development Flow

Small Local Collection

        ↓

parallelize()

        ↓

RDD

        ↓

map()

        ↓

map()

        ↓

reduceByKey()

        ↓

collect()

Best Practice: Use small sample datasets during development and testing before running logic against large production datasets.

5. RDD Partitioning

Partitioning determines how data is divided into smaller logical pieces that can be processed in parallel.

Key Rule

A commonly taught relationship is:

Number of RDD partitions is influenced by the number of underlying input splits/blocks and the configuration of the Spark application.

For example, a 1 GB file with 128 MB HDFS blocks may result in approximately:

1 GB ÷ 128 MB = 8 input blocks

which can provide approximately 8 input partitions, subject to Spark's input-splitting behavior and configuration.

getNumPartitions()

Returns the number of partitions in an RDD.

rdd.getNumPartitions()

defaultMinPartitions

Defines a minimum baseline for the number of partitions used by certain Spark operations.

The default is commonly 2, depending on Spark configuration.

defaultParallelism

Defines the default level of parallelism used by certain Spark operations.

It represents the number of tasks that can generally execute concurrently based on the available cluster configuration.

6. DAG Execution Engine: Jobs, Stages & Tasks

Spark breaks execution into Jobs → Stages → Tasks.

Overall Flow

                 ACTION

                     ↓

                  JOB

                     ↓

             ┌───────┴───────┐

             ↓               ↓

          STAGE 1       SHUFFLE BOUNDARY

             │               │

      map(), filter()        ↓

             │             STAGE 2

             │          reduceByKey()

             ↓               │

          TASKS            TASKS

Job

A Job is created when an Action is invoked on an RDD.

Examples:

count()

collect()

saveAsTextFile()

Each Action can trigger a separate Spark Job.

Stage

A Stage is a subdivision of a Job.

Stages are separated by Wide Transformations / Shuffle boundaries.

For example:

map()

   ↓

filter()

   ↓

reduceByKey()

   ↓

sortBy()

   ↓

collect()

The Shuffle caused by reduceByKey() creates a stage boundary.

Simplified Formula

For a straightforward linear DAG:

Number of Stages ≈ Number of Shuffle Boundaries + 1

Task

A Task is the smallest unit of execution sent to a worker for processing a partition.

Key Relationship

For a given stage:

Number of Tasks ≈ Number of Partitions processed by that stage

Example:

Stage 1

 ├── Task 1 → Partition 1

 ├── Task 2 → Partition 2

 ├── Task 3 → Partition 3

 └── Task 4 → Partition 4

Therefore:

One task generally processes one partition for a stage.

7. Narrow vs. Wide Transformations

This is one of the most important concepts in Spark.

Narrow Transformation

In a Narrow Transformation, each output partition depends on a small number of input partitions, typically without requiring a Shuffle across the cluster.

Examples:

  • map()
  • filter()
  • flatMap()

Example

Worker 1                 Worker 1

Partition 1  ─────────→  Partition 1

Worker 2                 Worker 2

Partition 2  ─────────→  Partition 2

Data can generally remain on the same worker.

Wide Transformation

A Wide Transformation requires data to be redistributed across partitions, generally involving a Shuffle.

Examples:

  • reduceByKey()
  • groupByKey()
  • join()
  • distinct()
  • sortBy()

Example

Worker 1                         Worker 1

Partition 1 ──────┐         ┌──→ Partition 1

                  │         │

                  ├─ SHUFFLE┤

                  │         │

Worker 2 ─────────┘         └──→ Partition 2

Partition 2

Comparison

Feature

Narrow Transformation

Wide Transformation

Shuffle

No

Yes

Network Transfer

Minimal / none

Significant

Performance

Generally faster

Generally more expensive

Stage Boundary

No

Yes

Examples

map(), filter()

reduceByKey(), groupByKey()

Remember: Wide Transformation = Shuffle = Stage Boundary

8. reduceByKey() vs. groupByKey()

Both operations work with key-value data, but they behave very differently.

reduceByKey()

reduceByKey() performs local aggregation before the Shuffle whenever possible.

Example:

Worker 1:

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Local aggregation:

Apple → 3

Only the aggregated result needs to be transferred during Shuffle.

Advantages

  • Reduces network traffic.
  • Uses local aggregation.
  • More efficient for aggregations.
  • Reduces memory pressure compared with sending all raw values.

groupByKey()

groupByKey() transfers all values associated with a key across the network before grouping them.

Example:

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

Apple → 1

All values may be transferred before grouping:

Apple → [1, 1, 1, 1]

This can generate significant network and memory overhead.

Comparison

Feature

reduceByKey()

groupByKey()

Local Aggregation

Yes

No

Shuffle Data

Reduced

Potentially much larger

Network Traffic

Lower

Higher

Memory Pressure

Lower

Higher

Preferred for Aggregation

✅ Yes

❌ Usually avoid when aggregation can be performed directly

Rule of Thumb: When performing an aggregation by key, prefer reduceByKey() over groupByKey() whenever the operation allows it.

9. Advanced RDD Optimization Techniques

Broadcast Join

A standard join between two large RDDs can require significant network Shuffle.

However, if one dataset is very small compared with the other, a Broadcast Join can be much more efficient.

Example

Suppose:

  • orders = 1 GB
  • customers = 1 MB

Instead of shuffling the large orders dataset, Spark can broadcast the small customer dataset to the worker nodes.

Broadcast Join Process

Step 1 — Broadcast Small Dataset

The Driver sends the small dataset to the worker nodes.

Step 2 — Local Lookup

Each worker stores the broadcast dataset and performs local lookups.

Step 3 — Avoid Large Shuffle

The large RDD does not need to be redistributed simply to access the small lookup dataset.

Conceptual Architecture

                 Driver

                    │

                    │ Broadcast

                    ↓

          ┌─────────┼─────────┐

          ↓         ↓         ↓

       Worker 1  Worker 2  Worker 3

          │         │         │

          ↓         ↓         ↓

       Local      Local      Local

       Lookup     Lookup     Lookup

          ↑         ↑         ↑

       Orders     Orders     Orders

Example

# Broadcast Small Dataset

customers_broadcast = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(

    customers_rdd.collectAsMap()

)

# Map-side local join on Large RDD

joined_rdd = orders_rdd.map(

    lambda x: (

        x,

        customers_broadcast.value.get(x.customer_id)

    )

)

Key Idea

Broadcast the small dataset; avoid shuffling the large dataset.

10. Partition Management: repartition() vs. coalesce()

Both functions modify the number of partitions, but their behavior is different.

Property

repartition()

coalesce()

Direction

Increase or decrease partitions

Primarily decreases partitions

Shuffle

Full Shuffle

Avoids full Shuffle when reducing partitions

Distribution

Generally produces more evenly distributed partitions

May result in uneven partition sizes

Best Use Case

Increasing parallelism or redistributing data

Reducing partitions after filtering

Cost

More expensive due to Shuffle

Generally cheaper when reducing partitions

repartition()

Use when you need to:

  • Increase the number of partitions.
  • Decrease partitions while accepting a full Shuffle.
  • Redistribute data more evenly.

Example:

rdd.repartition(10)

coalesce()

Use primarily when reducing the number of partitions.

Example:

rdd.coalesce(5)

A common use case is after a heavy filter() operation has significantly reduced the amount of data.

Quick Rule:
Increase partitions → repartition()
Reduce partitions cheaply → coalesce()

11. In-Memory Management: cache() vs. persist()

Spark transformations are lazy.

If an RDD is used repeatedly across multiple Actions, Spark may recompute its lineage each time unless the RDD is persisted.

Without Caching

RDD

 ↓

Transformation

 ↓

Action 1 → Recompute

 ↓

Action 2 → Recompute

 ↓

Action 3 → Recompute

With Caching

RDD

 ↓

Transformation

 ↓

Cache / Persist

 ↓

Memory

 ↓

Action 1

Action 2

Action 3

cache()

cache() is a convenient shortcut for persisting an RDD using Spark's default storage level.

For RDDs, this is commonly:

MEMORY_ONLY

rdd.cache()

persist()

persist() provides greater control over the storage level.

Common options include:

Storage Level

Meaning

MEMORY_ONLY

Store data in memory

MEMORY_AND_DISK

Store in memory; spill to disk if required

MEMORY_ONLY_SER

Store serialized objects in memory

DISK_ONLY

Store data only on disk

Example:

rdd.persist()

or:

rdd.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)

cache() vs. persist()

cache() = Simple default persistence

persist() = Configurable persistence

Quick Revision

Concept

Remember

Lambda

Anonymous inline function for short logic

Spark map()

Distributed transformation

parallelize()

Creates an RDD from a local collection

Partition

Logical unit of distributed data processing

Narrow Transformation

No Shuffle; dependencies remain local

Wide Transformation

Requires Shuffle across partitions

Job

Triggered by an Action

Stage

Separated by Shuffle boundaries

Task

Processes a partition within a stage

reduceByKey()

Local aggregation + Shuffle; preferred for aggregation

groupByKey()

Shuffles raw values; generally more expensive

Broadcast Join

Sends small dataset to workers to avoid large Shuffle

repartition()

Full Shuffle; can increase or decrease partitions

coalesce()

Primarily reduces partitions without full Shuffle

cache()

persist()

Allows explicit storage-level selection

Important Concepts to Remember

1. Narrow transformations do not require a Shuffle; Wide transformations do.

2. Wide transformations create Shuffle boundaries and therefore separate Spark Stages.

3. A Job is triggered by an Action.

4. A Task generally processes one partition for a particular Stage.

5. reduceByKey() is generally preferred over groupByKey() for aggregation because it performs local aggregation before Shuffle.

6. Broadcast Join is useful when one dataset is small enough to distribute to all worker nodes.

7. repartition() involves a full Shuffle, while coalesce() is primarily used to reduce partitions more efficiently.

8. Cache/persist reused RDDs to avoid repeatedly recomputing their lineage.

9. cache() provides convenient default persistence; persist() gives explicit control over the storage level.

Week 4 Mental Model

PySpark Basics

Python Function → Lambda → Spark Transformation

RDD Processing

RDD → Partition → Transformation → Shuffle (if Wide) → Action

Spark Execution

Action → Job → Stages → Tasks → Partitions

Performance

Narrow → No Shuffle → Faster

Wide → Shuffle → Network I/O → More Expensive

Aggregation

reduceByKey() → Local Aggregation → Less Shuffle

groupByKey() → Shuffle Raw Values → More Expensive

Partition Management

Reduce → coalesce()

Reuse

WEEK 5

Spark APIs — DataFrames & Spark SQL

1. Introduction to Higher-Level APIs

Apache Spark provides multiple APIs for processing distributed data.

At a high level, Spark APIs can be divided into:

  • Low-Level APIs: RDDs
  • Higher-Level APIs: DataFrames and Spark SQL

RDDs contain distributed data without explicit schema information, whereas DataFrames and Spark SQL work with structured data containing columns, data types, and schema metadata.

Low-Level vs. High-Level Spark APIs

RDDs — Low-Level APIs

DataFrames & Spark SQL — High-Level APIs

Raw, unstructured data

Structured data

Data distributed across partitions

Data organized into rows and columns

No explicit schema context

Explicit schema and metadata

More manual optimization

Automatic optimization through Catalyst

More developer control

Easier and more optimized query processing

Key Concept

RDD → Data + Partitions

DataFrame → Data + Partitions + Schema

Spark SQL → DataFrame/Table + SQL Interface + Optimization

Persistent vs. Temporary Data

One important distinction is between Spark SQL tables and DataFrames.

Spark SQL / Spark Tables

Spark SQL tables are persistent.

  • Physical data is stored on persistent storage such as:
  • HDFS
  • Amazon S3
  • Azure ADLS Gen2
  • Table metadata/schema is maintained in a central Metastore.
  • Tables continue to exist after the current Spark session ends.
  • They can be accessed by different Spark applications or sessions.

DataFrames

DataFrames are effectively RDDs enriched with schema.

  • DataFrames are session-scoped.
  • Their temporary metadata is maintained in the Spark session.
  • They disappear when the Spark session terminates unless persisted as a table or written to storage.

Why Are Higher-Level APIs Faster?

DataFrames and Spark SQL provide Spark with structural information about the data.

This allows Spark's Catalyst Optimizer to:

  1. Understand the structure of the data.
  2. Analyze the user's query.
  3. Create an optimized logical execution plan.
  4. Push filters closer to the data source.
  5. Eliminate unnecessary columns.
  6. Optimize the physical execution plan.
  7. Reduce unnecessary resource consumption.

Key Takeaway

RDDs tell Spark HOW to process data.
DataFrames and Spark SQL allow Spark to understand WHAT you want to achieve and optimize the execution.

2. DataFrame Reader Framework

The DataFrame Reader provides a unified way to load external data into a DataFrame.

Standard Syntax

orders_df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .option("header", "true") \

    .option("inferSchema", "false") \

    .load("/public/trendytech/orders_wh/*")

Important Options

Option

Purpose

format()

Specifies the input file format

option("header", "true")

Indicates that the first row contains column names

option("inferSchema", "false")

Prevents Spark from automatically inferring data types

load()

Reads the actual data

inferSchema Performance Warning

Avoid using:

.option("inferSchema", "true")

in production pipelines whenever possible.

Schema inference requires Spark to examine the data to determine appropriate data types. This can result in additional scanning and execution overhead.

Production Recommendation

Define the schema explicitly instead of relying on inference.

3. File Format Reader Shortcuts

Spark provides shortcuts for common file formats.

CSV

df_csv = spark.read.csv(

    "/path/to/data.csv",

    header=True,

    inferSchema=False

)

JSON

df_json = spark.read.json("/path/to/data.json")

Parquet

df_parquet = spark.read.parquet("/path/to/data.parquet")

Parquet is a columnar file format and contains schema information within the file.

ORC

df_orc = spark.read.orc("/path/to/data.orc")

Spark Table

df_table = spark.read.table("database_name.table_name")

4. DataFrames vs. Spark SQL Tables

DataFrames and Spark SQL views can be used together.

The general flow is:

DataFrame → Temporary View → Spark SQL

and the resulting table/view can then be queried back through Spark.

DataFrame → SQL View

orders_df.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")

Query the View

result_df = spark.sql("""

    SELECT *

    FROM orders

""")

5. Temporary Views

Spark provides several methods for creating temporary views.

createTempView()

Creates a session-scoped temporary view.

orders_df.createTempView("orders")

If a view with the same name already exists, Spark throws an error.

createOrReplaceTempView()

Creates a session-scoped temporary view and replaces an existing view with the same name.

orders_df.createOrReplaceTempView("orders")

This is commonly used during development.

createGlobalTempView()

Creates a global temporary view that can be accessed across multiple Spark sessions within the same Spark application.

orders_df.createGlobalTempView("orders")

Global temporary views are accessed through the global_temp database.

spark.sql("""

    SELECT *

    FROM global_temp.orders

""")

createOrReplaceGlobalTempView()

Creates or replaces a global temporary view.

orders_df.createOrReplaceGlobalTempView("orders")

Quick Comparison

Method

Scope

Replaces Existing View?

createTempView()

Current Spark session

No

createOrReplaceTempView()

Current Spark session

Yes

createGlobalTempView()

All sessions in the Spark application

No

createOrReplaceGlobalTempView()

All sessions in the Spark application

Yes

6. Managed vs. External Tables

When creating persistent tables through Spark SQL / Hive Metastore, tables can be broadly classified as:

  1. Managed Tables
  2. External Tables

Managed Table

A managed table is one where Spark manages both:

  • Metadata
  • Physical data

Typical structure:

Managed Table

      |

      +---- Metadata → Hive Metastore

      |

      +---- Data → Spark Warehouse

DROP TABLE Behavior

When a managed table is dropped:

Metadata → Deleted

Physical Data → Deleted

External Table

An external table stores metadata in the Metastore while the actual data remains in an externally specified location.

External Table

      |

      +---- Metadata → Hive Metastore

      |

      +---- Data → External Storage Location

DROP TABLE Behavior

When an external table is dropped:

Metadata → Deleted

Physical Data → Preserved

Managed vs. External Tables

Feature

Managed Table

External Table

Data ownership

Spark manages metadata and data

Spark manages metadata only

Storage location

Default warehouse directory

Explicit LOCATION

Metadata

Hive Metastore

Hive Metastore

DROP TABLE

Deletes metadata + data

Deletes metadata only

Data preserved after DROP?

❌ No

✅ Yes

Typical use

Dedicated pipelines

Shared enterprise data

Example: Managed Table

CREATE TABLE orders (

    order_id BIGINT,

    customer_id BIGINT,

    order_status STRING

);

Example: External Table

CREATE TABLE orders (

    order_id BIGINT,

    customer_id BIGINT,

    order_status STRING

)

LOCATION '/data/orders';

7. DML Operations: Apache Spark vs. Databricks / Delta Lake

Standard file formats such as CSV and Parquet do not natively provide the same transactional capabilities as Delta Lake.

Open-Source Apache Spark

Generally supports:

  • SELECT
  • INSERT INTO

Standard CSV/Parquet tables do not natively support:

  • UPDATE
  • DELETE

Databricks / Delta Lake

Delta Lake provides support for:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE
  • MERGE

This enables ACID-style transactional operations on data.

8. DataFrame API vs. Spark SQL API

The same analytical requirement can generally be implemented using either:

  • DataFrame API
  • Spark SQL

Example 1: Top 15 Customers by Order Count

DataFrame API

result_df = orders_df.groupBy("customer_id") \

                     .count() \

                     .sort("count", ascending=False) \

                     .limit(15)

Spark SQL API

result_sql = spark.sql("""

    SELECT customer_id, COUNT(order_id) AS count

    FROM orders

    GROUP BY customer_id

    ORDER BY count DESC

    LIMIT 15

""")

Example 2: Active Customer Count

DataFrame API

active_customers = orders_df \

    .select("customer_id") \

    .distinct() \

    .count()

Spark SQL API

active_customers_sql = spark.sql("""

    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers

    FROM orders

""")

10. Cluster-Level Resource Optimization

Spark performance depends heavily on appropriate executor configuration.

Example Worker Node

Assume:

  • 10 Worker Nodes
  • 16 CPU Cores per Worker
  • 64 GB RAM per Worker

The goal is to divide each worker's resources into balanced Spark executors.

11. Extreme Executor Strategies

There are two extreme approaches:

Strategy 1: Thin Executors

One executor gets:

  • 1 CPU core
  • 4 GB RAM

Therefore:

16 executors per worker

Problems

  1. Multithreading within each JVM is eliminated.
  2. Broadcast variables may need separate copies in many executors.
  3. Memory can be duplicated unnecessarily.

Strategy 2: Fat Executors

One executor gets:

  • 16 CPU cores
  • 64 GB RAM

Therefore:

1 executor per worker

Problems

  1. HDFS I/O throughput can suffer with too many concurrent threads.
  2. Large JVM memory pools can lead to long Garbage Collection pauses.
  3. A single large executor can become a bottleneck.

12. Balanced Executor Strategy

A balanced approach is preferred.

Worker Node

Worker Node

16 CPU Cores

64 GB RAM

        |

        |-- Reserve 1 Core + 1 GB RAM

        |

        +-- Available to Spark

             15 Cores

             63 GB RAM

Use:

5 CPU cores per executor

Therefore:

15 available cores ÷ 5 cores per executor

= 3 executors per worker

13. Executor Memory Calculation

Step 1: Calculate Available Resources

Total worker resources:

16 CPU cores + 64 GB RAM

Reserve:

1 CPU core + 1 GB RAM

Therefore:

Available CPU = 16 - 1

              = 15 cores

Available RAM = 64 - 1

              = 63 GB

Step 2: Calculate Executors per Worker

Using 5 cores per executor:

Executors per worker

= 15 / 5

= 3 executors

Step 3: Calculate Raw RAM per Executor

Raw RAM per executor

= 63 GB / 3

= 21 GB

Step 4: Calculate Memory Overhead

The notes use:

Overhead = max(384 MB, 7% × Executor Memory)

For a 21 GB executor:

7% × 21 GB

≈ 1.5 GB

Therefore:

Usable Executor RAM

= 21 GB - 1.5 GB

≈ 19 GB

14. Final Cluster Configuration

For 10 worker nodes:

10 Workers

×

3 Executors per Worker

=

30 Executors

One executor is reserved for the YARN ApplicationMaster according to the configuration described in the notes.

Therefore:

30 - 1

=

29 Usable Executors

Final Configuration

Resource

Configuration

Worker Nodes

10

CPU per Worker

16 cores

RAM per Worker

64 GB

Executors per Worker

3

Total Executors

30

ApplicationMaster Allocation

1

Usable Executors

29

CPU per Executor

5 cores

Usable Heap RAM per Executor

~19 GB

16. Key Interview Points

1. Why are DataFrames generally preferred over RDDs?

Because DataFrames provide schema information that allows Spark's Catalyst Optimizer to optimize the execution plan.

2. What happens when a managed table is dropped?

Both metadata and physical data are deleted.

3. What happens when an external table is dropped?

The metadata is deleted, but the underlying physical data remains.

4. What is the danger of collect()?

It brings the complete dataset to the Driver and can cause Out Of Memory (OOM) errors.

5. What is the difference between a temporary and global temporary view?

A normal temporary view is available within the current Spark session, while a global temporary view can be accessed across sessions within the same Spark application.

6. Why avoid inferSchema in production?

It introduces additional data scanning and can increase execution time; explicit schema definition is preferred.

7. What is the purpose of executor sizing?

To balance CPU, memory, I/O throughput, parallelism, and garbage-collection overhead for efficient Spark execution.

Week 6: Spark DataFrame Transformations & Deep Dive

1. Schema Management: Inference vs. Enforcement

Schema inference allows Spark to automatically guess data types by scanning input data. However, it is not recommended for production workloads.

Disadvantages of Schema Inference

  1. Inaccurate Data Types: Dates or timestamps may be incorrectly inferred as strings, or integers as longs.
  2. Performance Overhead: Spark must scan the entire dataset (or a large sample) twice to infer column types, adding significant execution time.

Sampling Ratio Alternative: If inference is mandatory during initial exploratory testing, use .option("samplingRatio", 0.1) to force Spark to scan only a 10% subset of records.

Development Example

df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .option("header", "true") \

    .option("inferSchema", "true") \

    .option("samplingRatio", 0.1) \

    .load("/public/yelp-dataset/yelp_user.csv")

Enforcing Schema — Production Best Practice

Schema enforcement explicitly defines data types upfront, preventing extra data scans and ensuring data consistency.

If a data value fails type casting during read, Spark sets that specific cell value to null without crashing the query.

Schema Enforcement Approaches

Approach

Description

DDL String Schema

Compact SQL-like string defining column names and data types

Programmatic StructType

Programmatic schema definition using StructType and StructField

Approach 1: DDL String Schema

A compact DDL string defines column names and data types.

orders_schema = "order_id long, order_date string, cust_id long, order_status string"

df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .schema(orders_schema) \

    .load("/public/trendytech/datasets/orders_sample1.csv")

Approach 2: Programmatic StructType & StructField

This approach is useful for nested structures and programmatic data pipelines.

from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, LongType, StringType, IntegerType, DateType

orders_schema_struct = StructType([

    StructField("orderid", LongType(), nullable=True),

    StructField("orderdate", DateType(), nullable=True),

    StructField("customerid", IntegerType(), nullable=True),

    StructField("orderstatus", StringType(), nullable=True)

])

df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .schema(orders_schema_struct) \

    .load("/public/trendytech/datasets/orders_sample1.csv")

2. Handling Date & Timestamp Formats

The default date pattern expected by Apache Spark is:

yyyy-MM-dd

If incoming raw date values do not match this pattern, reading directly into DateType can result in null values or parsing errors.

Strategies to Handle Custom Date Patterns

Strategy 1: Explicit Date Format Option

Specify the exact custom pattern during the read operation.

df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .schema(orders_schema) \

    .option("dateFormat", "MM-dd-yyyy") \

    .load("/public/trendytech/datasets/orders_sample1.csv")

Important: Month formatting is case-sensitive.

MM = Month
mm = Minutes

Using lowercase mm when you mean month can result in incorrect date parsing.

Strategy 2: Read as String and Cast

A recommended approach is to load raw date columns as StringType first and then explicitly convert them using to_date().

from pyspark.sql.functions import to_date

# Load raw date as StringType

raw_df = spark.read \

    .schema("order_id long, order_date string, cust_id long, order_status string") \

    .csv("/public/trendytech/datasets/orders_sample1.csv")

# Convert string to DateType

transformed_df = raw_df.withColumn(

    "order_date_parsed",

    to_date("order_date", "MM-dd-yyyy")

)

3. DataFrame Read Modes

When reading structured data, corrupt or malformed records are processed according to the configured Read Mode.

Read Mode

Default

Behaviour on Malformed Records

permissive

Yes

Sets corrupted/mismatched fields to null while preserving valid fields

dropmalformed

No

Drops the entire corrupted row

failfast

No

Immediately throws an exception and stops Spark job execution

Example

df = spark.read \

    .format("csv") \

    .schema(orders_schema) \

    .option("mode", "dropmalformed") \

    .load("/public/trendytech/datasets/orders_sample1.csv")

Quick Memory Trick

PERMISSIVE → Preserve

DROPMALFORMED → Drop

FAILFAST → Fail

4. DataFrame Creation Patterns & RDD Conversion

Methods to Instantiate DataFrames

1. Reading External Files

df1 = spark.read.csv("path/to/file.csv")

2. Querying Spark SQL Tables / Views

df2 = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM default.orders")

df3 = spark.table("default.orders")

3. Generating Numeric Ranges

df_range = spark.range(0, 10, 2)

Produces an id column containing:

0, 2, 4, 6, 8

4. Converting In-Memory Python Lists

orders_list = [

    (1, '2013-07-25 00:00:00.0', 11599, 'CLOSED'),

    (2, '2013-07-25 00:00:00.0', 256, 'PENDING_PAYMENT')

]

Two-Step Name Assignment

df_list = spark.createDataFrame(orders_list) \

    .toDF("order_id", "order_date", "customer_id", "order_status")

One-Step Full Schema Enforcement

schema_str = "order_id long, order_date string, cust_id int, order_status string"

df_list_enforced = spark.createDataFrame(

    orders_list,

    schema=schema_str

)

Converting RDDs to DataFrames

DataFrames are conceptually RDDs bound to an explicit schema.

RDDs can be converted to DataFrames using two approaches:

Approach

Syntax

Approach 1 — SparkSession

spark.createDataFrame(rdd, schema)

Approach 2 — RDD Method

rdd.toDF(schema)

Sample RDD

raw_rdd = spark.sparkContext.parallelize([

    (1, '2013-07-25 00:00:00.0', 11599, 'CLOSED'),

    (2, '2013-07-25 00:00:00.0', 256, 'PENDING_PAYMENT')

])

Approach 1: Using SparkSession

df_from_rdd1 = spark.createDataFrame(

    raw_rdd,

    schema=schema_str

)

Approach 2: Using RDD's toDF() Method

df_from_rdd2 = raw_rdd.toDF([

    "order_id",

    "order_date",

    "customer_id",

    "order_status"

])

5. Working with Complex & Nested Schemas

JSON records and complex data formats often contain nested structures such as structs and maps.

Nested JSON Example

{"customer_id": 1, "fullname": {"firstname": "sumit", "lastname": "mittal"}, "city": "bangalore"}

{"customer_id": 2, "fullname": {"firstname": "ram", "lastname": "kumar"}, "city": "hyderabad"}

Approach 1: Nested DDL String

nested_ddl = "customer_id long, fullname struct<firstname:string, lastname:string>, city string"

df_nested_ddl = spark.read \

    .format("json") \

    .schema(nested_ddl) \

    .load("path/to/nested_customers.json")

Approach 2: Nested Programmatic StructType

nested_struct = StructType([

    StructField("customer_id", LongType()),

    StructField("fullname", StructType([

        StructField("firstname", StringType()),

        StructField("lastname", StringType())

    ])),

    StructField("city", StringType())

])

df_nested_struct = spark.read \

    .format("json") \

    .schema(nested_struct) \

    .load("path/to/nested_customers.json")

6. Key DataFrame Column Transformations

Transformation

Functional Purpose

Syntax Example

withColumn()

Adds a new column or overwrites an existing column

df.withColumn("new_col", expr("subtotal * 0.1"))

withColumnRenamed()

Renames an existing column without changing its data type or value

df.withColumnRenamed("old_name", "new_name")

drop()

Removes one or more columns

df.drop("cust_id", "order_date")

select() vs. selectExpr()

select()

Used for selecting existing column names or column objects.

SQL expressions must be wrapped inside the expr() function.

selectExpr()

Accepts raw SQL expression strings directly.

Example

from pyspark.sql.functions import expr

df_select = df.select(

    "order_item_id",

    expr("CASE WHEN product_name LIKE '%Nike%' THEN product_price * 1.2 ELSE product_price END AS adjusted_price")

)

Using selectExpr():

df_select_expr = df.selectExpr(

    "order_item_id",

    "CASE WHEN product_name LIKE '%Nike%' THEN product_price * 1.2 ELSE product_price END AS adjusted_price"

)

Quick Comparison

Method

SQL Expression Handling

select()

Requires expr()

selectExpr()

Accepts SQL expressions directly

7. Deduplication: distinct() vs. dropDuplicates()

Sample Duplicate Data

data = [

    (1, "Kapil", 34),

    (1, "Kapil", 34),

    (1, "Satish", 26),

    (2, "Satish", 26)

]

df_dup = spark.createDataFrame(

    data,

    ["id", "name", "age"]

)

distinct()

Deduplicates records by evaluating all columns simultaneously.

df_unique_all = df_dup.distinct()

Example

The following two rows are duplicates:

1, Kapil, 34

1, Kapil, 34

distinct() removes one of them.

dropDuplicates()

Deduplicates records based on a specific subset of key columns.

df_unique_subset = df_dup.dropDuplicates(["name", "age"])

Quick Comparison

Method

Deduplication Criteria

distinct()

All columns

dropDuplicates()

Selected columns

8. Deep Dive into SparkSession & Deployment Modes

Role of SparkSession

Prior to Spark 2.0, applications managed separate contexts:

  • SparkContext → RDD APIs
  • SQLContext → DataFrames
  • HiveContext → Hive Metastore access

Modern Spark unifies these under a single entry point:

SparkSession

SparkSession Encapsulation

                        +--------------------+

                         |    SparkSession    |

                         +--------------------+

                           /        |        \

                          v         v         v

                 SparkContext  SQLContext  HiveContext

                  (RDD APIs)  (DataFrames) (Metastore)

Shared Contexts & Multiple Sessions

A single Spark Application can run only one SparkContext.

However, multiple isolated SparkSession objects can be instantiated within the same application using:

spark.newSession()

These sessions:

  • Run independently.
  • Have separate temporary views.
  • Can have separate settings.
  • Share the underlying SparkContext.

Primary SparkSession

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder \

    .appName("Production Pipeline") \

    .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", "/user/itv005857/warehouse") \

    .enableHiveSupport() \

    .master("yarn") \

    .getOrCreate()

Creating an Isolated Secondary Session

isolated_session = spark.newSession()

9. Deployment Modes: Client vs. Cluster

Spark applications can run in two common deployment modes:

  1. Client Mode
  2. Cluster Mode

Client Deployment Mode

Typical Use: Interactive development

Examples:

  • Jupyter Notebooks
  • REPL
  • Interactive development environments

Architecture

            CLIENT / GATEWAY NODE

             +-------------------+

             |                   |

             |  Driver Process   |

             |      (Master)     |

             |                   |

             +-------------------+

                      |

                      v

             YARN CLUSTER

       +----------+ +----------+ +----------+

       | Executor | | Executor | | Executor |

       +----------+ +----------+ +----------+

Characteristics

  • The Driver process runs locally on the client/submission/gateway machine.
  • Executors run on the YARN cluster.
  • Useful for interactive development.

Risk

If the client machine disconnects or shuts down, the driver fails and the cluster job terminates.

Cluster Deployment Mode

Typical Use: Production environments

Architecture

            CLIENT / GATEWAY NODE

             +-------------------+

             | Submit Application|

             +-------------------+

                      |

                      v

             YARN CLUSTER

       +----------+ +----------+ +----------+

       |  Driver  | | Executor | | Executor |

       +----------+ +----------+ +----------+

Characteristics

  • The Driver process runs inside the cluster.
  • The driver runs within an ApplicationMaster container on one of the cluster worker nodes.
  • The client only submits the application.

Benefits

  • Better isolation from the local workstation.
  • The application continues running even if the submitting machine disconnects.
  • Driver–executor communication remains within the cluster.
