WEEK 7: APACHE SPARK CACHING IN-DEPTH

1. Monitoring & Debugging: Spark UI and History Server

Monitoring job execution and resource consumption in Apache Spark relies mainly on two interfaces:

Spark UI vs. Spark History Server

Feature

Spark UI

Spark History Server

Availability

During job execution

After job completion

Purpose

Real-time monitoring

Post-mortem analysis

Data Source

Active SparkContext

Event logs

Main Use

Debug active jobs

Analyze completed jobs

Important Tabs

Jobs, Stages, Storage, Executors, SQL

Same historical execution information

Spark History Server

The Spark History Server reads event logs generated by completed Spark applications.

It is useful for:

  • Analyzing completed jobs
  • Post-mortem debugging
  • Performance auditing
  • Reviewing historical Spark applications

It becomes particularly useful after the application's SparkContext has terminated.

Spark UI

The Spark UI runs while the Spark application is active.

By default, it is commonly available on:

http://<driver-host>:4040

The Spark UI provides real-time information about:

  • Jobs
  • Stages
  • Tasks
  • Executors
  • Storage
  • DAG execution
  • Cached datasets
  • Resource utilization

Key Difference

Spark UI

    ↓

Real-Time Monitoring

    ↓

Application Currently Running

Spark History Server

    ↓

Historical Monitoring

    ↓

Application Already Completed

2. Fundamentals of Caching and Persistence

Spark uses lazy evaluation.

When transformations are applied to an RDD or DataFrame, Spark does not immediately execute them.

Instead, Spark builds a logical execution plan and executes it only when an action is triggered.

Without Caching

Suppose we have:

Source Data

    ↓

Transformation 1

    ↓

Transformation 2

    ↓

Action 1

After Action 1 finishes, Spark does not automatically keep the transformed dataset in memory.

If another action is executed:

Source Data

    ↓

Transformation 1

    ↓

Transformation 2

    ↓

Action 2

Spark may need to recompute the transformations again.

Therefore:

Action 1

    ↓

Full computation

Action 2

    ↓

Full computation AGAIN

With Caching

If the intermediate dataset is cached:

Source Data

    ↓

Transformation 1

    ↓

Transformation 2

    ↓

Cache

    ↓

Action 1

The resulting dataset is stored according to the selected storage level.

A subsequent action can reuse the cached data:

                        ┌──→ Action 1

                         │

Source → Transformations → Cache

                         │

                         └──→ Action 2

This avoids repeating expensive transformations.

When Should You Cache?

Cache when:

  • The dataset is reused multiple times.
  • The transformation logic is expensive.
  • The dataset is reasonably sized.
  • Multiple downstream actions depend on the same dataset.

Avoid caching when:

  • The dataset is used only once.
  • The dataset is extremely large.
  • The dataset cannot fit effectively into available cluster storage.
  • Recomputing the dataset is cheaper than maintaining the cache.

Lazy Evaluation of cache()

Calling:

df.cache()

does not immediately load the DataFrame into memory.

Caching is lazy.

The data is actually materialized when an action is executed.

Example:

df.cache()

df.count()

Here:

df.cache()

    ↓

Marks DataFrame for caching

df.count()

    ↓

Action

    ↓

Data is computed and cached

3. Data Serialization and Storage Formats

Cached data can be represented in two major forms:

  1. Deserialized
  2. Serialized

Deserialized Data

Data is stored as actual Java/Python objects in memory.

Advantages

  • Faster CPU access
  • No deserialization required
  • Convenient for direct processing

Disadvantages

  • Requires more memory
  • Object headers create additional memory overhead

Serialized Data

Data is converted into a compact binary representation.

Advantages

  • Requires less memory
  • More space efficient

Disadvantages

  • Requires CPU time to serialize and deserialize data
  • Slightly slower access compared with directly available objects

Comparison

Property

Deserialized

Serialized

Representation

Java/Python objects

Binary byte stream

Memory usage

Higher

Lower

CPU usage

Lower

Higher

Access speed

Faster

Slower

Space efficiency

Lower

Higher

Simple Rule

Deserialized

    ↓

More Memory

Less CPU

Serialized

    ↓

Less Memory

More CPU

4. cache() vs. persist()

Caching and persistence allow Spark to store intermediate datasets for reuse.

cache()

cache() is a convenient shortcut for using the default storage level.

For an RDD:

rdd.cache()

The default storage level is:

MEMORY_ONLY

For a DataFrame:

df.cache()

The default storage level is:

MEMORY_AND_DISK

RDD Default Caching

rdd.cache()

Equivalent conceptually to:

rdd.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY)

The RDD attempts to remain in memory.

If a partition cannot be retained in memory, Spark can recompute that partition from lineage when required.

DataFrame Default Caching

df.cache()

Uses:

MEMORY_AND_DISK

Data is stored in memory where possible.

If memory is insufficient, partitions can spill to local disk.

persist()

persist() provides more control over the storage level.

Example:

from pyspark.storagelevel import StorageLevel

df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)

Other storage levels include:

StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY

StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK

StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY

StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY_2

Storage Level Concept

A storage level can be represented conceptually as:

StorageLevel(

    useDisk,

    useMemory,

    useOffHeap,

    deserialized,

    replication

)

For example:

df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)

means the cached data is stored only on disk.

Another example:

df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)

allows Spark to use both memory and disk.

Replication

Spark can maintain multiple copies of cached partitions.

For example:

df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY_2)

The _2 indicates a replication factor of 2.

This means cached partitions can have two copies across the cluster.

5. Locality Levels

Spark attempts to execute tasks as close as possible to the data.

This minimizes unnecessary network communication.

Two important locality levels are:

  • PROCESS_LOCAL
  • NODE_LOCAL

PROCESS_LOCAL

The data is already available inside the executor's process/JVM.

For example:

Executor JVM

    ↓

Cached Data in Memory

    ↓

Task

No disk or network transfer is required.

Therefore:

PROCESS_LOCAL

    ↓

Fastest

NODE_LOCAL

The data is located on the same physical worker node but is not already available inside the executor's memory.

For example:

Worker Node

    ↓

Local Disk / HDFS Block

    ↓

Executor

    ↓

Task

The task needs local disk access to retrieve the data.

Comparison

Locality

Data Location

Relative Speed

PROCESS_LOCAL

Executor memory

Fastest

NODE_LOCAL

Same worker node

Slower than process local

General Principle

Closer to Data

      ↓

Less Data Movement

      ↓

Better Performance

6. Spark SQL Caching

Spark SQL provides commands for caching tables and views.

CACHE TABLE

CACHE TABLE caching_demo_db.orders1;

This caches the table.

CACHE LAZY TABLE

CACHE LAZY TABLE caching_demo_db.orders1;

This marks the table for caching but delays materialization until the data is actually accessed.

Removing a Cached Table

UNCACHE TABLE caching_demo_db.orders1;

This removes the specified table from the cache.

Clearing All Cached Tables

CLEAR CACHE;

This clears all cached tables/views in the active session.

Important Difference

CACHE TABLE

    ↓

Eager caching

CACHE LAZY TABLE

    ↓

Lazy caching

7. Cache Invalidation and REFRESH TABLE

Spark interacts with multiple layers of data and metadata.

A simplified architecture is:

1. Backend Storage

   HDFS / S3 / ADLS

          ↓

2. Spark Catalog / Metadata

          ↓

3. Memory Cache

Suppose a new file is manually added to HDFS.

The backend storage changes:

HDFS

 ↓

New File Added

But Spark's existing metadata and cache may not immediately know about the change.

Therefore, Spark may need to refresh the table.

REFRESH TABLE table_name;

This forces Spark to refresh its knowledge of the table's underlying data.

Internal vs. External Data Changes

Changes through Spark

If data is modified through Spark APIs, Spark can manage its metadata and cache state.

Changes outside Spark

If files are manually added, deleted, or modified in HDFS/S3, Spark may need an explicit refresh.

Example:

spark.sql("REFRESH TABLE table_name")

8. When Caching Can Hurt Performance

Caching is not always beneficial.

For example, Parquet files already contain useful metadata and columnar structures.

Parquet can support:

  • Column pruning
  • Predicate filtering
  • Metadata-based optimizations
  • Row-group-level optimizations
  • Dictionary encoding

If such data is cached in a less efficient representation, Spark may consume significantly more memory.

Therefore:

Caching ≠ Always Faster

The correct rule is:

Cache when:

    Expensive computation

        +

    Multiple reuse

        +

    Reasonable dataset size

Otherwise, caching can consume valuable cluster memory without providing meaningful performance benefits.

WEEK 8: APACHE SPARK ARCHITECTURE & ADVANCED AGGREGATIONS

1. Spark on YARN Execution Architecture

Apache Spark can run on top of Hadoop YARN.

The primary YARN components involved are:

  • Resource Manager
  • Node Manager
  • ApplicationMaster
  • Spark Driver
  • Spark Executors

YARN Architecture

                   +----------------------+

                    |   Resource Manager   |

                    |       (Master)       |

                    +----------------------+

                              |

              +---------------+---------------+

              |                               |

              v                               v

     +------------------+            +------------------+

     |   Node Manager   |            |   Node Manager   |

     |    Worker 1      |            |    Worker 2      |

     |                  |            |                  |

     | +--------------+ |            | +--------------+ |

     | | Application  | |            | |   Executor   | |

     | |    Master    | |            | |  Container   | |

     | | Spark Driver | |            | |              | |

     | +--------------+ |            | +--------------+ |

     +------------------+            +------------------+

Execution Flow

Step 1: Application Submission

The client submits a Spark application.

For example:

spark-submit my_application.py

Step 2: Driver Allocation

The YARN Resource Manager coordinates with a Node Manager to launch the ApplicationMaster.

In Spark cluster mode:

ApplicationMaster

        ↓

Spark Driver

Step 3: Resource Negotiation

The ApplicationMaster communicates with the Resource Manager to obtain resources for Spark executors.

Step 4: Executor Launch

Executors are launched inside YARN containers.

The overall flow becomes:

Client

  ↓

Resource Manager

  ↓

ApplicationMaster

  ↓

Spark Driver

  ↓

Executors

  ↓

Tasks

2. Client Mode vs. Cluster Mode

Spark applications can commonly be deployed in:

  1. Client Mode
  2. Cluster Mode

Client Mode

In client mode, the Spark Driver runs on the machine from which the application is submitted.

Client / Gateway Machine

        |

        +-- Spark Driver

        |

        v

YARN Cluster

        |

        +-- Executor 1

        +-- Executor 2

        +-- Executor 3

Advantages

  • Useful for interactive development
  • Convenient for notebooks
  • Useful for REPL/shell-based development

Disadvantage

If the client machine disconnects or shuts down, the Driver may fail and the Spark application can terminate.

Cluster Mode

In cluster mode, the Driver runs inside the cluster.

Client Machine

      |

      | Submit Application

      v

YARN Cluster

      |

      +-- ApplicationMaster / Driver

      |

      +-- Executor 1

      +-- Executor 2

      +-- Executor 3

Advantages

  • Driver is independent of the submitting workstation
  • Suitable for production workloads
  • Better isolation from client-side failures

Comparison

Feature

Client Mode

Cluster Mode

Driver Location

Client/Gateway machine

Inside cluster

Typical Usage

Development / Interactive

Production

Client Disconnect

Can terminate application

Application can continue

Driver Isolation

Lower

Higher

Easy Interview Answer

Client mode is mainly useful for interactive development, while cluster mode is preferred for production because the Driver runs inside the cluster rather than on the submitting machine.

3. Five Ways of Referencing Columns in PySpark

PySpark provides multiple ways to reference DataFrame columns.

1. String Notation

Useful for straightforward column references.

df.select("order_id", "order_status")

2. DataFrame Prefix Notation

Useful when working with multiple DataFrames, especially joins.

df.select(orders_df.order_id, customers_df.cust_id)

This can help resolve ambiguity between columns having the same name.

3. Bracket / Dictionary Notation

df.select(df["order_date"])

4. Column Object Notation

Use col() or column() to work with column objects and their methods.

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, column

df.select(

    col("cust_id"),

    column("order_status")

)

Example:

df.where(

    col("order_status").like("PENDING%")

)

5. Expression Notation

The expr() function allows SQL expressions to be written directly.

from pyspark.sql.functions import expr

df.select(

    expr("cust_id + 1 AS new_cust_id")

)

Quick Reference

Method

Example

Common Use

String

"order_id"

Simple column selection

DataFrame prefix

df.order_id

Joins / ambiguity

Bracket

df["order_id"]

Column reference

col() / column()

col("order_id")

Programmatic operations

expr()

expr("cust_id + 1")

SQL expressions

4. Types of Aggregations

Aggregations can be broadly categorized into:

  1. Simple Aggregations
  2. Grouping Aggregations
  3. Windowing Aggregations

Simple Aggregations

Simple aggregation processes multiple rows and produces a single result.

Examples:

  • count()
  • sum()
  • avg()
  • countDistinct()

Example:

from pyspark.sql.functions import count, countDistinct, sum, avg

df.select(

    count("*").alias("total_records"),

    countDistinct("invoiceno").alias("unique_invoices"),

    sum("quantity").alias("total_qty"),

    avg("unitprice").alias("avg_price")

).show()

Conceptually:

Multiple Rows

      ↓

Aggregation

      ↓

Single Result

5. Grouping Aggregations

Grouping aggregation first divides records into groups and then performs calculations for every group.

Example:

from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, expr

df.groupBy("country", "invoiceno") \

    .agg(

        sum("quantity").alias("total_qty"),

        expr("sum(quantity * unitprice) AS total_invoice_val")

    ) \

    .sort("invoiceno") \

    .show()

Conceptually:

All Rows

    ↓

Group By Key

    ↓

Aggregate Each Group

    ↓

One Result Row Per Group

6. Windowing Aggregations

Window functions perform calculations across related rows without collapsing the rows into one row per group.

This is the major difference between:

GROUP BY

and:

WINDOW FUNCTION

GROUP BY

Multiple rows

     ↓

Aggregation

     ↓

One row per group

Window Function

Multiple rows

     ↓

Calculation across related rows

     ↓

Original rows remain

7. Window Specification

A Window Specification commonly consists of:

1. partitionBy()

Defines the logical groups within which the calculation is performed.

2. orderBy()

Defines the ordering of rows inside each partition.

3. Frame Boundaries

Defines which rows are included in the calculation.

Common functions include:

rowsBetween()

rangeBetween()

Running Total Example

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

from pyspark.sql.functions import sum

running_window = Window \

    .partitionBy("country") \

    .orderBy("weeknum") \

    .rowsBetween(

        Window.unboundedPreceding,

        Window.currentRow

    )

df_with_running = df.withColumn(

    "running_total",

    sum("invoicevalue").over(running_window)

)

Conceptually:

Country

   ↓

Sort by Week

   ↓

Week 1 → Week 1 Total

Week 2 → Week 1 + Week 2

Week 3 → Week 1 + Week 2 + Week 3

...

8. rank() vs. dense_rank() vs. row_number()

These functions are commonly used for ranking records within a window.

Consider:

Student

Marks

Ankur

100

Satish

100

Kapil

100

Kaushik

99

Ram

99

Rohit

98

The ranking results are:

Student

Marks

rank()

dense_rank()

row_number()

Ankur

100

1

1

1

Satish

100

1

1

2

Kapil

100

1

1

3

Kaushik

99

4

2

4

Ram

99

4

2

5

Rohit

98

6

3

6

rank()

Rows with the same value receive the same rank.

However, the next rank skips numbers.

Example:

1, 1, 1, 4

dense_rank()

Rows with the same value receive the same rank, but ranks do not contain gaps.

Example:

1, 1, 1, 2

row_number()

Every row receives a unique sequential number.

Example:

1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

Code Example

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

from pyspark.sql.functions import rank, dense_rank, row_number, desc

rank_window = Window \

    .partitionBy("country") \

    .orderBy(desc("invoicevalue"))

df_ranked = df \

    .withColumn("rank", rank().over(rank_window)) \

    .withColumn("dense_rank", dense_rank().over(rank_window)) \

    .withColumn("row_num", row_number().over(rank_window))

9. lead() and lag()

Window functions can also be used to compare the current row with previous or future rows.

lag()

lag() retrieves a value from a previous row.

lag("invoicevalue", 1)

means:

Current Row

    ↓

Look 1 row backward

lead()

lead() retrieves a value from a subsequent row.

lead("invoicevalue", 1)

means:

Current Row

    ↓

Look 1 row forward

Example

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

from pyspark.sql.functions import lag, lead

window_lead_lag = Window \

    .partitionBy("country") \

    .orderBy("weeknum")

df_comparison = df \

    .withColumn(

        "prev_week_invoice",

        lag("invoicevalue", 1).over(window_lead_lag)

    ) \

    .withColumn(

        "next_week_invoice",

        lead("invoicevalue", 1).over(window_lead_lag)

    )

Conceptually:

Previous Row ← Current Row → Next Row

     lag()          lead()

       ↓               ↓

Previous Value    Next Value

10. Pivoting Log Data

Pivoting converts row-oriented data into a column-oriented summary.

For example, suppose server logs contain:

loglevel    month

INFO        January

ERROR       January

INFO        February

WARN        February

A pivot can transform the data into:

            January    February

INFO            1           1

ERROR           1           0

WARN            0           1

Standard Pivot

pivoted_df = log_df \

    .groupBy("loglevel") \

    .pivot("month") \

    .count()

11. Pivot Performance Optimization

When the pivot column contains unknown values, Spark may need to scan the dataset to discover all distinct pivot values.

For example:

log_df \

    .groupBy("loglevel") \

    .pivot("month") \

    .count()

Spark may first need to discover all unique months.

This introduces an additional scan.

Optimized Pivot

If the possible values are already known, provide them explicitly.

months = [

    "January",

    "February",

    "March",

    "April",

    "May",

    "June",

    "July",

    "August",

    "September",

    "October",

    "November",

    "December"

]

optimized_pivot_df = log_df \

    .groupBy("loglevel") \

    .pivot("month", months) \

    .count()

Why is this better?

Without Explicit Values

Dataset

   ↓

Discover DISTINCT months

   ↓

Perform Pivot

With explicit values:

Known Month List

       ↓

Perform Pivot Directly

Therefore, providing the pivot values can eliminate the extra distinct-value discovery scan.

Week 9: Apache Spark Internals & DataFrame Writer API

1. DataFrame Writer API & Write Modes

The DataFrame Writer API (df.write) is used to write transformed DataFrame results to internal data lakes such as HDFS, ADLS Gen2, and AWS S3, as well as external data targets such as relational databases, NoSQL systems, and data warehouses.

Basic DataFrame Writer Syntax

orders_df.write \

    .format("parquet") \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .option("path", "/user/itv006763/sparkwritedemo") \

    .save()

Supported Write Modes

Mode

Behavior

overwrite

Replaces existing files/directories at the target destination.

append

Adds new output files alongside existing data.

ignore

Silently skips the write if the target already exists.

errorIfExists

Default mode. Throws an AnalysisException if the target already exists.

Key Point

Write Mode = What should Spark do if the target already exists?

  • overwrite → Replace it
  • append → Add to it
  • ignore → Do nothing
  • errorIfExists → Throw an error

2. Storage Techniques: Partitioning vs. Bucketing

Spark provides partitioning and bucketing to organize data physically and reduce unnecessary data scanning during queries.

Partitioning vs. Bucketing

PARTITIONING (partitionBy)              BUCKETING (bucketBy)

• Low-cardinality columns               • High-cardinality columns

  Example: country, status                Example: customer_id, id

• Creates folders                       • Creates bucket files

• Enables partition pruning             • Optimizes joins and scans

2.1 Partitioning — partitionBy()

Partitioning is best suited for low-cardinality columns that are frequently used in filtering conditions.

Examples:

  • order_status
  • country
  • state

How Partitioning Works

Spark creates separate directories for each unique partition value.

For example:

orders/

├── order_status=CLOSED/

├── order_status=COMPLETE/

├── order_status=PENDING/

└── order_status=CANCELLED/

If a query asks for:

WHERE order_status = 'CLOSED'

Spark can scan only the CLOSED directory instead of the entire dataset.

This is called Partition Pruning.

Single-Level Partitioning

orders_df.write \

    .format("parquet") \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .partitionBy("order_status") \

    .save("/path/to/partitioned_orders")

Multi-Level Partitioning

Multiple columns can be used to create hierarchical directories.

customer_df.write \

    .format("parquet") \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .partitionBy("customer_state", "customer_city") \

    .save("/path/to/nested_partitions")

This produces a structure similar to:

customer_state=Karnataka/

    customer_city=Bangalore/

customer_state=Telangana/

    customer_city=Hyderabad/

Best Practice

Use partitioning when the column has low cardinality.

Avoid partitioning on extremely high-cardinality columns such as:

customer_id

order_id

transaction_id

because this can create a very large number of directories and small files.

2.2 Bucketing — bucketBy()

Bucketing is designed for high-cardinality columns.

Examples:

  • customer_id
  • order_id
  • user_id

Instead of creating one folder for every unique value, Spark distributes records across a fixed number of bucket files.

Bucketing Formula

Bucket Number = hash(column) % number_of_buckets

Example

customer_final_df.write \

    .format("parquet") \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .bucketBy(8, "customer_id") \

    .sortBy("customer_id") \

    .saveAsTable("itv006753_bucketing_db.customersnew")

Here:

  • Number of buckets = 8
  • Bucket column = customer_id
  • Data is sorted by customer_id
  • Output is saved as a Spark SQL table

Important

bucketBy() is used with:

.saveAsTable()

rather than a simple file-path .save() workflow.

2.3 Partitioning vs. Bucketing — Comparison

Feature

Partitioning

Bucketing

API

partitionBy()

bucketBy()

Ideal column

Low cardinality

High cardinality

Example

country, status

customer_id, order_id

Physical structure

Folders/directories

Bucket files

Main optimization

Partition pruning

Bucket pruning / SMB joins

Typical write

.save() or table

.saveAsTable()

Number of partitions/buckets

Based on unique values

Fixed number specified by developer

Remember

Low Cardinality → Partitioning

High Cardinality → Bucketing

3. Initial Partition Calculation Mechanics

Initial partitions determine the number of parallel tasks Spark can use when reading files into DataFrames.

The source material gives the following formula:

{Partition Size}

\min
\left(
\text{maxPartitionBytes},
\frac{\text{File Size}}{\text{defaultParallelism}}
\right)

The default value of:

spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes

is 128 MB.

Example 1: 1.1 GB File, 2 Cores

File Size = 1.1 GB

Default Parallelism = 2

Partition Size

= min(128 MB, 1.1 GB / 2)

= 128 MB

Partitions

= 1.1 GB / 128 MB

≈ 9 partitions

Example 2: 1.1 GB File, 16 Cores

File Size = 1.1 GB

Default Parallelism = 16

Partition Size

= min(128 MB, 1.1 GB / 16)

= 75 MB

Partitions

= 1.1 GB / 75 MB

≈ 16 partitions

Key Learning

The number of initial partitions depends on:

  1. File size
  2. spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes
  3. defaultParallelism

4. Splittable vs. Non-Splittable Files

Not every file can be divided into multiple input partitions.

Splittable Formats

Examples given in the source:

  • Uncompressed CSV/Text
  • Parquet
  • ORC
  • Avro

These can generally be split into multiple partitions.

Non-Splittable Formats

Examples given in the source:

  • Gzip-compressed CSV
  • Gzip-compressed JSON
  • Snappy-compressed CSV/JSON

These can result in one partition per file, creating a potential single-threaded bottleneck.

Important Concept

Large Splittable File

        ↓

Multiple Input Partitions

        ↓

Multiple Tasks

        ↓

Parallel Processing

Whereas:

Large Non-Splittable File

        ↓

One Input Partition

        ↓

One Task

        ↓

Potential Bottleneck

5. Submitting Production Jobs Using spark-submit

Interactive notebooks typically use Client Mode, while production applications are commonly submitted using spark-submit in Cluster Mode.

Production Submission Example

spark3-submit \

  --deploy-mode cluster \

  --master yarn \

  --num-executors 4 \

  --executor-cores 5 \

  --executor-memory 19G \

  --driver-cores 2 \

  --driver-memory 4G \

  --conf spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled=false \

  /path/to/production_pipeline.py

Important Parameters

Parameter

Purpose

--deploy-mode cluster

Runs driver inside the cluster

--master yarn

Uses YARN as resource manager

--num-executors 4

Requests 4 executors

--executor-cores 5

Gives each executor 5 cores

--executor-memory 19G

Gives each executor 19 GB memory

--driver-cores 2

Gives driver 2 CPU cores

--driver-memory 4G

Gives driver 4 GB memory

--conf

Sets Spark configuration properties

Configuration Precedence

From highest priority to lowest priority:

1. SparkSession.builder configuration

            ↓

2. spark-submit arguments

            ↓

3. spark-defaults.conf

Therefore:

Application code > spark-submit > spark-defaults.conf

Week 10: Apache Spark Optimizations — Part 1

1. Internal Working of groupBy() & Empty Partition Problem

A groupBy() operation is a wide transformation because data needs to be shuffled across the cluster.

By default, Spark SQL uses:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200

This means Spark initially creates 200 shuffle partitions.

Example

Suppose a dataset contains 9 distinct order statuses.

Raw Dataset

    ↓

Local Partial Aggregation

    ↓

Shuffle

    ↓

200 Shuffle Partitions

Only the partitions corresponding to the actual keys may contain data.

Partitions 1–9

→ Active

Partitions 10–200

→ Empty

Therefore, Spark may end up creating many unnecessary tasks.

Problem

If:

Distinct Keys = 9

Shuffle Partitions = 200

then potentially:

9 active partitions

191 empty partitions

The empty tasks still create:

  • Scheduler overhead
  • Task-launch overhead
  • Unnecessary execution planning

2. Adaptive Query Execution — AQE

Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) dynamically changes Spark's execution plan using runtime statistics.

According to the source:

  • Introduced in Spark 3.0
  • Enabled by default in Spark 3.2+

Enable AQE

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", True)

AQE has three major optimization capabilities:

                   AQE

       ┌───────────────────────────────┐

       │                               │

       ↓                               ↓

Coalesce Shuffle                 Handle Skewed

Partitions                       Partitions

       │                               │

       └──────────────┬────────────────┘

                      ↓

              Switch Join Strategy

2.1 AQE — Coalescing Shuffle Partitions

AQE can combine small or empty shuffle partitions after observing the actual runtime data.

Without AQE

200 shuffle partitions

        ↓

Only 9 contain useful data

        ↓

191 unnecessary tasks

With AQE

200 shuffle partitions

        ↓

Runtime statistics

        ↓

Small/empty partitions combined

        ↓

Fewer useful partitions

        ↓

Less task overhead

Key Benefit

AQE dynamically adjusts partitioning based on actual runtime data rather than relying solely on static configuration.

2.2 AQE — Dynamic Partition Skew Handling

A data skew occurs when one partition contains significantly more data than others.

Example

Suppose:

COMPLETE → 80% of all records

PENDING  → 10%

CANCELLED → 5%

OTHERS   → 5%

The partition containing COMPLETE can become much larger than other partitions.

This creates a straggler task.

AQE can detect the skewed partition and split it into smaller sub-partitions during execution.

Result

Large Skewed Partition

        ↓

AQE detects skew

        ↓

Split into smaller partitions

        ↓

More balanced execution

2.3 AQE — Dynamic Join Strategy Switching

AQE can also change the join strategy at runtime.

For example:

Initial plan:

Sort-Merge Join

        ↓

Runtime filtering reduces dataset size

        ↓

Dataset now fits broadcast threshold

        ↓

AQE switches to:

Broadcast Hash Join

This can significantly improve join performance.

3. Join Types in PySpark

Join Type

PySpark Keyword

Behavior

Inner

"inner"

Keeps only matching records from both DataFrames.

Left Outer

"left" / "left_outer"

Keeps all left records; unmatched right columns become NULL.

Right Outer

"right" / "right_outer"

Keeps all right records; unmatched left columns become NULL.

Full Outer

"full" / "full_outer"

Keeps all records from both DataFrames.

Left Semi

"left_semi"

Returns left records that have a match in the right DataFrame. Right-side columns are not included.

Left Anti

"left_anti"

Returns left records that have no match in the right DataFrame.

4. Spark Join Execution Strategies

Spark can use different physical strategies depending on dataset sizes and execution conditions.

Three Important Strategies

1. Broadcast Hash Join

2. Shuffle Hash Join

3. Sort-Merge Join

4.1 Broadcast Hash Join — BHJ

Broadcast Hash Join is generally used when one DataFrame is sufficiently small.

The source specifies the default broadcast threshold as:

spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = 10 MB

Working

Suppose:

Orders     = 1 GB

Customers  = 5 MB

Spark can:

Small Customers DF

        ↓

Driver

        ↓

Broadcast

        ↓

All Executors

Large Orders DF

        ↓

No large-table shuffle

        ↓

Local Hash Lookup

Advantage

The large DataFrame does not need to be shuffled across the network.

Key Point

Small table + large table → Broadcast Hash Join

4.2 Shuffle Hash Join — SHJ

Shuffle Hash Join is applicable when datasets require shuffling but one side can still be hashed efficiently within each partition.

Working

DataFrame A

     ↓

Shuffle

     ↓

Partition by Join Key

     ↓

Hash

DataFrame B

     ↓

Shuffle

     ↓

Partition by Join Key

     ↓

Hash

        ↓

Join matching partitions

The smaller partition is used to build an in-memory hash table.

4.3 Sort-Merge Join — SMJ

Sort-Merge Join is commonly used when joining two large DataFrames that cannot be broadcast.

It involves three major steps:

1. Shuffle

      ↓

2. Sort

      ↓

3. Merge

Step 1 — Shuffle

Records are distributed according to the join key.

Step 2 — Sort

Each partition sorts records by the join key.

Step 3 — Merge

The sorted datasets are merged to find matching keys.

Key Point

Two large DataFrames → Shuffle + Sort + Merge

5. Sort-Merge-Bucket Join — SMB Join

When two very large tables are joined using a standard Sort-Merge Join, Spark may have to perform:

Shuffle

   ↓

Sort

   ↓

Merge

For very large datasets, the shuffle and sorting operations can be extremely expensive.

Bucketing can eliminate this repeated work.

SMB Join Requirements

For Spark to take advantage of a Sort-Merge-Bucket Join, the tables should be:

  1. Bucketed on the same join key
  2. Using the same number of buckets
  3. Sorted by the join key

Step 1 — Bucket Orders Table

orders_df.write \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .bucketBy(8, "cust_id") \

    .sortBy("cust_id") \

    .saveAsTable("bucketed_db.orders_table")

Step 2 — Bucket Customers Table

customers_df.write \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .bucketBy(8, "customer_id") \

    .sortBy("customer_id") \

    .saveAsTable("bucketed_db.customers_table")

Both tables use:

Number of buckets = 8

Orders join key    = cust_id

Customers join key = customer_id

The columns have different names but represent the corresponding join keys.

Step 3 — Perform the Join

joined_df = spark.sql("""

    SELECT *

    FROM bucketed_db.orders_table o

    JOIN bucketed_db.customers_table c

      ON o.cust_id = c.customer_id

""")

Why SMB Join Is Faster

Without bucketing:

Orders

   ↓

Shuffle

   ↓

Sort

   ↓

        JOIN

   ↑

Sort

   ↑

Shuffle

   ↑

Customers

With compatible bucketing:

Orders Bucket 1 ──────────┐

                          ├── JOIN

Customers Bucket 1 ──────┘

Orders Bucket 2 ──────────┐

                          ├── JOIN

Customers Bucket 2 ──────┘

...

Because the data is already organized into matching buckets and sorted by the join key, Spark can avoid the expensive shuffle and sort phases.

Core Idea

Pre-bucketing prepares the data for future large-scale joins.

Week 10 — Quick Revision

groupBy()

groupBy()

   ↓

Wide Transformation

   ↓

Shuffle

   ↓

Default: 200 shuffle partitions

AQE

AQE

├── Coalesces small/empty shuffle partitions

├── Handles partition skew

└── Can switch join strategies at runtime

Join Strategy Cheat Sheet

Situation

Preferred Strategy

Small + Large DataFrame

Broadcast Hash Join

Large + Medium DataFrame

Shuffle Hash Join

Large + Large DataFrame

Sort-Merge Join

Large pre-bucketed tables

Sort-Merge-Bucket Join

Most Important Optimization Concepts

Partitioning

      ↓

Partition Pruning

Bucketing

      ↓

Large-table Join Optimization

AQE

      ↓

Runtime Optimization

Broadcast Join

      ↓

Avoid Large Table Shuffle

SMB Join

      ↓

Avoid Repeated Shuffle + Sort

⭐ Interview Memory Line

Broadcast when one side is small, AQE when runtime data changes the plan, and bucketing when repeatedly joining very large tables on the same key.

WEEK 11: APACHE SPARK MEMORY MANAGEMENT & FILE FORMATS

1. Executor Memory Architecture

When requesting memory for an executor container, such as --executor-memory 2G, Spark divides the memory into several functional regions.

Executor Memory Breakdown

Container Memory

  • Off-Heap / Memory Overhead
  • Memory overhead
  • Optional PySpark memory
  • Optional off-heap allocations
  • JVM Heap Memory
  • Reserved Memory
  • Unified Memory
  • Storage Memory
  • Execution Memory
  • User Memory

1.1 Reserved Memory

  • Fixed size: 300 MB
  • Used internally by Spark.
  • This memory is reserved for Spark's internal engine and runtime processes.

1.2 User Memory

User Memory is approximately 40% of usable JVM heap memory.

It is used for:

  • User-defined data structures
  • Custom UDF variables
  • Metadata required for raw RDD transformations

Formula:

User Memory = (Java Heap − 300 MB) × (1 − spark.memory.fraction)

1.3 Unified Memory

Unified Memory is approximately 60% of usable JVM heap memory.

It is shared between:

Storage Memory

  • Cached DataFrames
  • Persistent tables
  • Broadcast variables

Execution Memory

  • Shuffles
  • Joins
  • Sorts
  • Aggregations

1.4 Memory Overhead

Memory overhead is outside the JVM heap and helps prevent memory-related failures caused by:

  • OS processes
  • PySpark processes
  • Non-JVM tasks

Formula:

Memory Overhead = max(384 MB, 10% × spark.executor.memory)

2. Dynamic Memory Eviction Rules

Spark allows Storage and Execution Memory to dynamically borrow unused space from one another.

Scenario A: Execution Needs More Memory

Storage → Execution

Execution can evict cached blocks from Storage Memory when additional memory is required for operations such as:

  • Sorts
  • Joins
  • Aggregations

Scenario B: Storage Needs More Memory

Execution → Storage: NOT allowed

Storage cannot evict memory actively being used by execution tasks.

If there is insufficient memory:

  • Cached data may spill to disk.
  • The requested data may fail to cache.

Key Rule to Remember

Execution can evict Storage, but Storage cannot evict active Execution.

3. Aggregation Engines: Hash Aggregate vs. Sort Aggregate

Spark SQL can use different physical operators for grouping aggregations.

3.1 Hash Aggregate

Hash aggregation is generally faster and operates approximately in:

O(N)

Characteristics:

  • Uses hash tables.
  • Updates aggregate values directly.
  • Works efficiently with suitable mutable data types.
  • Generally avoids the additional sorting overhead of SortAggregate.

3.2 Sort Aggregate

Sort aggregation generally has:

O(N log N)

Characteristics:

  • Requires data to be sorted by grouping keys.
  • Introduces additional CPU overhead.
  • Can be used when HashAggregate is not suitable.

Comparison

Feature

Hash Aggregate

Sort Aggregate

Time Complexity

O(N)

O(N log N)

Main Mechanism

Hash table

Sorting

Performance

Generally faster

Generally slower

Memory

Uses hash-based aggregation

Requires sorting

Use

Suitable data types / aggregation plans

Fallback or suitable cases

Key Takeaway

The source material emphasizes that data types can influence the aggregation strategy. A grouping key represented as a String may lead Spark toward SortAggregate, while suitable numeric or timestamp types may allow HashAggregate.

4. Spark Optimizer Architecture: Catalyst

The Catalyst Optimizer transforms high-level DataFrame or SQL operations into optimized execution plans.

Catalyst Optimization Pipeline

DataFrame / SQL Query

↓

1. Unresolved Logical Plan

↓

2. Analyzed Logical Plan

↓

3. Optimized Logical Plan

↓

4. Physical Plan

↓

5. Code Generation

4.1 Unresolved Logical Plan

At this stage, Spark checks the query structure and syntax.

It has not yet fully resolved:

  • Tables
  • Columns
  • Data types

4.2 Analyzed Logical Plan

Spark uses the Catalog to resolve:

  • Table names
  • Column names
  • Data types
  • Functions

The result is a fully resolved logical plan.

4.3 Optimized Logical Plan

Spark applies logical optimization rules such as:

  • Predicate Pushdown — filters data as early as possible.
  • Projection / Column Pruning — reads only required columns.

4.4 Physical Plan

Spark selects actual execution strategies.

Examples:

  • Broadcast Hash Join
  • Sort-Merge Join
  • Hash Aggregate
  • Sort Aggregate

4.5 Code Generation

Spark can generate optimized Java bytecode through Whole-Stage Code Generation for efficient execution.

5. File Formats: Row-Based vs. Column-Based

File format selection has a direct impact on:

  • Storage requirements
  • Network bandwidth
  • Query performance
  • Compression
  • Read/write performance

5.1 Row-Based Formats

Examples:

  • CSV
  • Avro

Data is stored row by row.

Advantages

  • Efficient for writing complete records.
  • Useful for ingestion and landing-zone workloads.

Disadvantages

  • Less efficient when queries require only a subset of columns.
  • Can result in higher I/O during analytical queries.

5.2 Column-Based Formats

Examples:

  • Parquet
  • ORC

Data is stored column by column.

Advantages

  • Efficient analytical reads.
  • Better compression.
  • Supports column pruning.
  • Supports predicate pushdown.

6. Text-Based File Formats

Common examples:

  • CSV
  • JSON
  • XML

Main Drawbacks

Values are generally represented as text, meaning Spark may need to parse strings into appropriate data types.

This can introduce:

  • Additional CPU overhead
  • Larger storage requirements
  • Higher I/O

JSON and XML can also be bulky compared with specialized Big Data file formats.

7. Avro vs. Parquet vs. ORC

Feature

Apache Avro

Apache Parquet

Apache ORC

Layout

Row-based

Columnar

Columnar

Primary Use Case

Data ingestion / landing zones

Analytical querying with Spark

Analytical querying with Hive

Write Performance

Fast

Slower

Slower

Read Performance

Slower

Fast

Fast

Compression

Moderate

High

Very High

Schema Evolution

Supported

Supported

Supported

Simple Rule

Avro → Good for ingestion

Parquet → Excellent for Spark analytics

ORC → Commonly associated with Hive analytics

8. Parquet Internal Architecture

A Parquet file is organized into:

  1. Row Groups
  2. Column Chunks
  3. Pages

Conceptually:

Parquet File

→ Row Group 1

→ Column Chunk 1

→ Page 1, Page 2, Page 3

→ Column Chunk 2

→ Page 1, Page 2, Page 3

→ Row Group 2

→ ...

The file also contains metadata describing the structure and statistics.

8.1 Row Groups

A Row Group contains a collection of rows.

Each Row Group contains separate Column Chunks for each column.

Example:

Row Group 1

  • Column Chunk: order_id
  • Column Chunk: order_date
  • Column Chunk: customer_id

8.2 Column Chunks

A Column Chunk contains the data for one column within a Row Group.

This column-oriented organization enables Spark to avoid reading columns that are not required.

8.3 Pages

Column Chunks are further divided into Pages.

Pages can contain statistics that help Spark determine whether particular data needs to be read.

9. Parquet Query Optimizations

9.1 Column Pruning

Suppose a table contains:

  • order_id
  • order_date
  • customer_id
  • order_amount
  • order_status

If the query only requires:

order_id

order_amount

Spark can avoid reading the other columns.

This reduces:

  • Disk I/O
  • Network I/O
  • Memory consumption

9.2 Predicate Pushdown

Parquet stores statistics such as:

  • Minimum value
  • Maximum value

for relevant data regions.

Suppose a Row Group contains:

order_id:

min = 1

max = 20,000

and the query asks for:

order_id = 50,000

Spark can determine that this Row Group cannot contain the requested value and skip reading it.

Key Idea

Column Pruning → Skip unnecessary columns

Predicate Pushdown → Skip unnecessary data

10. Parquet Encoding Techniques

Parquet uses lightweight encoding techniques before applying general-purpose compression.

10.1 Dictionary Encoding

Repeated values are stored using dictionary IDs instead of repeating the full value.

Example:

Bangalore

Bangalore

Bangalore

Hyderabad

Hyderabad

can be represented conceptually using:

1

1

1

2

2

with a dictionary:

1 → Bangalore

2 → Hyderabad

10.2 Bit Packing

Bit packing reduces the number of bits required to store integer values.

Instead of allocating unnecessary bits for every value, only the required number of bits is used.

10.3 Delta Encoding

Instead of storing every value independently, Parquet can store the difference between consecutive values.

Example:

100

105

110

115

can conceptually become:

100

+5

+5

+5

10.4 Run-Length Encoding (RLE)

Repeated consecutive values can be represented using a value and its count.

Example:

A A A A A B B B

can conceptually become:

A × 5

B × 3

11. Compression Codecs

Compression codecs are used with container formats such as Parquet and ORC.

Codec

Compression Speed

Compression Ratio

Splittable

Typical Use

Snappy

Moderate

No by itself; works efficiently within Parquet/ORC

Default-style choice for Parquet/ORC

LZO

Moderate

Yes, with indexing

High-speed processing

Gzip

High

Bzip2

Very High

Yes

General Trade-Off

Faster compression → Usually lower compression ratio

Higher compression ratio → Usually higher CPU cost

12. Schema Evolution in Parquet

Parquet supports schema evolution.

When reading Parquet datasets with compatible schema changes, Spark can merge schemas using:

df = spark.read \

    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \

    .parquet("/public/trendytech/datasets/parquet-schema-evol-demo1")

The important option is:

mergeSchema = true

This allows Spark to combine compatible schemas across Parquet files.

End-to-End Enterprise Big Data & PySpark Project

1. Project Lifecycles & Agile Project Delivery

Building an enterprise-grade Big Data pipeline requires balancing technical design with business domain context.

Projects are delivered iteratively using Agile Methodology and Scrum Frameworks.

Agile Iterative Sprint Lifecycle

                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐

                     └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘

                                            │

                                            ▼

                     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐

                     │               SPRINT BACKLOG                │

                     │                                             │

Agile vs. Waterfall Model

Waterfall Model

  • Linear and sequential.
  • Requirements are frozen upfront.
  • Late architectural modifications can be costly.

Agile Framework (Scrum)

  • Iterative and adaptive.
  • Work is broken down into 1–2 week Sprints.
  • Produces incremental and testable pipeline features.

2. Enterprise Problem Statement: Credit Risk Analysis

To demonstrate a production architecture, consider a FinTech Lending Institution Case Study.

Business Goal

The business goal is to analyze historical borrower data to compute an automated Credit Risk Score that determines:

  • Loan approvals
  • Interest rates

3. Data Ingestion & Hash Surrogate Keys

The raw dataset consists of a 1.7 GB monolithic CSV file containing:

  • 118 attributes
  • 2.2+ million records

The ingestion pipeline splits this raw data into distinct functional domain datasets:

1. customers_data

Contains borrower profiles.

2. loans_data

Contains:

  • Applied loan amounts
  • Loan terms
  • Interest rates

3. loan_repayments

Contains:

  • Historical principal
  • Interest
  • Payment dates

4. loan_defaulters

Contains:

  • Historical delinquencies
  • Public records
  • Bankruptcies

Generating Deterministic Hash Keys (emp_id)

Because raw borrower records lack a unique primary key (member_id contains nulls), a surrogate key called emp_id is generated.

A SHA-256 algorithm is applied across 9 composite key attributes.

from pyspark.sql.functions import sha2, concat_ws

# Generating a deterministic composite primary key

composite_cols = [

    'emp_title',

    'emp_length',

    'home_ownership',

    'annual_inc',

    'zip_code',

    'addr_state',

    'grade',

    'sub_grade',

    'verification_status'

]

# SHA-256 produces a 256-bit (64 hex character) unique hash code

customers_raw_df = raw_df.withColumn(

    "emp_id",

    sha2(concat_ws("||", *composite_cols), 256)

)

4. Multi-Stage Data Cleaning & Standardization

Data Cleaning Pipeline

Raw Ingestion Data

        │

        ▼

Schema Enforcement & Renaming

        │

        ▼

Regex Text Parsing

        │

        ▼

Outlier & Null Imputation

        │

        ▼

Cleaned Output Storage

Stage 1: Cleaning customers_data

1. Explicit Schema Assignment

Loads raw data using explicit:

  • Float
  • Integer
  • String

data types.

2. Column Renaming

Standardizes ambiguous attribute names.

Examples:

annual_inc  →  annual_income

addr_state  →  address_state

3. Audit Columns

Appends ingestion timestamps using:

withColumn("ingest_date", current_timestamp())

4. Regex Cleaning (emp_length)

Strips non-digit characters using regex \D.

Example:

"10+ years" → 10

from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_replace, col

# Replace all non-digits (\D) with empty strings and cast to Integer

cleaned_emp_df = df.withColumn(

    "emp_length",

    regexp_replace(col("emp_length"), r"(\D)", "").cast("int")

)

5. Imputing Nulls

Fills missing emp_length values with the column average:

.na.fill(

    avg_emp_duration,

    subset=["emp_length"]

)

6. State Code Normalization

Enforces 2-character state codes and replaces invalid text with:

"NA"

Stage 2: Cleaning loans_data

1. Term Conversion

Converts raw string terms such as:

" 36 months"

into numeric years.

(

    (

        regexp_replace(

            "loan_term_months",

            " months",

            ""

        ).cast("float") / 12

    ).cast("int")

)

2. Categorical Lookup Mapping

Maps low-frequency loan purposes into an "other" category.

when(

    col("loan_purpose").isin(lookup_list),

    col("loan_purpose")

).otherwise("other")

Stage 3: Cleaning loan_repayments & loan_defaulters

1. Total Payment Correction

Reconstructs zero total payments when principal was received.

from pyspark.sql.functions import when, col

# Rebuilding total payment if total_payment_received is incorrectly 0.0

repayments_df = df.withColumn(

    "total_payment_received",

    when(

        (col("total_payment_received") == 0.0) &

        (col("total_principal_received") != 0.0),

        col("total_principal_received") +

        col("total_interest_received") +

        col("total_late_fee_received")

    ).otherwise(col("total_payment_received"))

)

2. Null Replacement

Replaces 0.0 sentinel values in date fields with None / null.

3. Defaulter Categorization

Splits defaulter data into two separate Parquet storage targets:

Delinquencies

delinq_2yrs > 0

Public Records / Inquiries

pub_rec > 0

OR

inq_last_6mths > 0

Downstream teams such as BI Analysts and ML Engineers require different access patterns to cleaned datasets.

Serving Layer Access Architecture

CONSOLIDATED REAL-TIME VIEW              PRE-CALCULATED MATERIALIZED TABLE

 ┌─────────────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────────────────┐

 │ CREATE VIEW                 │          │ CREATE TABLE                    │

 │                             │          │                                 │

 │ • Executes 5-table JOIN     │          │ • Populated by weekly batch job │

 │   dynamically               │          │ • Fast, zero-join read speeds  │

 │ • Always up-to-date         │          │ • Data up to 7 days old        │

 └─────────────────────────────┘          └─────────────────────────────────┘

External Tables for Multi-Team Access

For shared access across teams, datasets are exposed through External Tables registered in the Hive Metastore.

External tables preserve the physical Parquet data on disk even if the table metadata is dropped.

-- Creating an External Table on Top of Cleaned Parquet Data

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE lending_club.customers (

    member_id STRING,

    emp_title STRING,

    emp_length INT,

    home_ownership STRING,

    annual_income FLOAT,

    address_state STRING,

    total_high_credit_limit FLOAT,

    ingest_date TIMESTAMP

)

STORED AS PARQUET

LOCATION '/public/trendytech/lendingclubproject/cleaned/customers_parquet';

6. Business Logic: Credit Risk Scoring Engine

The automated Credit Risk Score evaluates three weighted financial pillars.

Formula

Credit Risk Score

= (0.20 × Payment History Points)

  • (0.45 × Defaulters History Points)
  • (0.35 × Financial Health Points)

Credit Risk Score Weighting Distribution

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ PAYMENT HISTORY — 20%                                        │

│                                                              │

│ • Last Payment vs. Monthly Installment Ratio                 │

│ • Total Payment Received vs. Principal Funded Ratio           │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ DEFAULTERS HISTORY — 45%                                     │

│                                                              │

│ • Delinquency Count (2 Years)                                │

│ • Public Records & Bankruptcies                              │

│ • Credit Inquiries (Last 6 Months)                           │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ FINANCIAL HEALTH — 35%                                       │

│                                                              │

│ • Loan Status (Fully Paid, Current, Grace Period, Charged Off)│

│ • Home Ownership (Own, Rent, Mortgage)                       │

│ • Credit Limit Utilization & Grade Points                    │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Dynamic Point Parameterization

Hardcoding point boundaries directly into queries is discouraged in production.

Dynamic limits are passed through configuration parameters.

# Registering dynamic score thresholds in SparkConf

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.unacceptable_rated_pts", 0)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.very_bad_rated_pts", 100)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.bad_rated_pts", 250)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.good_rated_pts", 500)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.very_good_rated_pts", 650)

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.excellent_rated_pts", 800)

Assigned Final Loan Grade

Risk Status

500 – 650

9. Unit Testing Framework with pytest

Testing pipeline functions requires isolated test execution using pytest.

tests/conftest.py

Centralized fixture file:

import pytest

from lib.Utils import get_spark_session

@pytest.fixture

def spark():

    """Sets up a local SparkSession for testing and tears it down after tests run."""

    spark_session = get_spark_session("LOCAL")

    yield spark_session

    spark_session.stop()

tests/test_retail.py

import pytest

from lib.DataReader import read_customers, read_orders

from lib.DataManipulation import filter_closed_orders

def test_customer_count(spark):

    """Verifies customer DataFrame read row count."""

    customer_df = read_customers(spark, "LOCAL")

    assert customer_df.count() == 12435

@pytest.mark.transformation

def test_filter_closed_orders(spark):

    """Verifies status filtering transformation logic."""

    orders_df = read_orders(spark, "LOCAL")

    closed_orders_count = filter_closed_orders(orders_df).count()

    assert closed_orders_count == 7556

Executing Pytest Suites

Run All Tests

python -m pytest

Discovers and executes all test functions beginning with test_.

Run Tests in Verbose Mode

python -m pytest -v

Run Only Transformation Tests

python -m pytest -m transformation

Runs test functions tagged with:

@pytest.mark.transformation

10. Production Logging via Log4j

Using plain print() statements in production code:

  • Slows down execution.
  • Cannot write to centralized log files.
  • Lacks configurable severity levels.

Spark includes Log4j to support structured, performance-friendly logging.

Log4j Priority Hierarchy

DEBUG  <  INFO  <  WARN  <  ERROR  <  FATAL

Lowest Severity                       Highest Severity

Log4j Wrapper Class

# lib/logger.py

class Log4j:

    def __init__(self, spark):

        # Obtain the JVM LogManager instance from the active SparkContext

        log4j = spark._jvm.org.apache.log4j

        self.logger = log4j.LogManager.getLogger(

            "com.trendytech.retail.application"

        )

    def info(self, message):

        self.logger.info(message)

    def warn(self, message):

        self.logger.warn(message)

    def error(self, message):

        self.logger.error(message)

Configuring Custom Log4j Properties

To instruct Spark to use custom Log4j parameters, add the Log4j configuration file option during SparkSession creation.

SparkSession.builder \

    .config(

        "spark.driver.extraJavaOptions",

        "-Dlog4j.configuration=file:log4j.properties"

    ) \

    .getOrCreate()

WEEK 14: VERSION CONTROL (GIT/GITHUB) & CI/CD PIPELINES WITH JENKINS

1. Code Versioning & Collaboration: Git vs. GitHub

Modern data engineering teams use version control systems to:

  • Collaborate on application code
  • Track code changes
  • Maintain commit history
  • Manage branches
  • Review changes through Pull Requests
  • Maintain clean release cycles
  • Automate CI/CD workflows

Git vs. GitHub

Git — Local Version Control Engine

Git runs on the developer's local machine and is responsible for:

  • Tracking changes
  • Managing local branches
  • Creating commits
  • Maintaining local commit history
  • Managing the local .git repository

GitHub — Remote Repository Host

GitHub hosts repositories remotely and enables:

  • Team collaboration
  • Remote repository management
  • Pull Requests (PRs)
  • Code reviews
  • Branch management
  • CI/CD integration

Local vs. Remote Repository Architecture

LOCAL WORKSTATION (Git)                         REMOTE CENTRAL HOST (GitHub)

+----------------------------------+            +----------------------------------+

|  Working Directory (Unstaged)    |            |  GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket     |

|             |                    |            |                                  |

|          git add .               |            |  Main Branch (Production)        |

|             ↓                    |            |  Dev Branch                      |

|  Staging Area (Index)            |            |  Feature Branches                |

|             |                    |            |                                  |

|       git commit                 |            |                                  |

|             ↓                    |   git push |                                  |

|  Local Repository (.git)         | ---------->|                                  |

+----------------------------------+            +----------------------------------+

Key Difference

Git manages version control locally, while GitHub provides a remote platform for collaboration, code review, and CI/CD integration.

2. Core Git Workflow & Essential Commands

2.1 Three-State Git Architecture

Git manages code through three primary states.

1. Working Directory — Unstaged

Contains:

  • Modified files
  • Newly created files
  • Untracked files

These changes have not yet been selected for the next commit.

2. Staging Area — Index

Files are moved into the staging area using:

git add .

The staging area defines which changes will be included in the next commit.

3. Local Repository — Committed

The staged changes are permanently recorded in the local Git history using:

git commit -m "commit message"

Three-State Code Lifecycle

Working Directory

        |

     git add

        ↓

Staging Area

        |

    git commit

        ↓

Local Repository

Easy Way to Remember

Working Directory → Staging Area → Repository

git add → git commit

3. Essential Git Commands

3.1 Initialization & Synchronization

git init

Initializes a brand-new Git repository in the current directory.

git init

git clone

Downloads an existing remote repository to the local machine.

git clone <repo-url>

git remote add origin

Connects a local repository to a remote GitHub repository.

git remote add origin <repo-url>

git pull

Fetches and merges the latest commits from a remote branch.

git pull origin <branch>

git push

Uploads local committed changes to the remote repository.

git push origin <branch>

3.2 Staging & Committing

git status

Displays:

  • Modified files
  • Untracked files
  • Staged files
  • Current repository status

git status

git add .

Stages all modified and newly created files.

git add .

git commit

Creates a commit containing the staged changes.

git commit -m "commit message"

3.3 Branch Management

Display local branches

git branch

Rename current branch to main

git branch -M main

Create and switch to a new branch

git checkout -b <new-branch>

Delete a local branch

git branch -d <branch-name>

4. Advanced Git Operations

Advanced Git workflows include:

  • Undoing changes
  • Forking repositories
  • Stashing uncommitted work
  • Managing upstream repositories

4.1 Undoing Changes

Different Git commands are used depending on the state of the change.

State of Changes

Recovery Command

Unstaged modifications

git restore <file>

Staged changes

git restore --staged <file>

Committed changes — keep code

git reset HEAD~1

Committed changes — wipe code

git reset --hard <commit-hash>

Unstaged Modifications

Discard local modifications:

git restore <file-name>

Staged Changes

Move a staged file back to the unstaged state:

git restore --staged <file-name>

Soft Reset / Commit Reset

Undo the most recent commit while retaining the changes in the working directory:

git reset HEAD~1

Hard Reset

Move the repository back to a particular commit and discard subsequent changes:

git reset --hard <commit-hash>

Important: git reset --hard can permanently remove local changes.

5. Forking & Open-Source / Organizational Contributions

A Fork creates a copy of an upstream repository under your own GitHub account.

Typical Fork Workflow

Original Repository

        |

      Fork

        ↓

Personal GitHub Repository

        |

      Clone

        ↓

Local Repository

        |

 Feature Branch

        |

     Commit

        |

      Push

        ↓

Pull Request

        |

        ↓

Original Repository

Steps

1. Fork

Create a copy of the upstream repository in your personal GitHub account.

2. Clone & Branch

Clone the fork locally and create a feature branch.

3. Push & Pull Request

Commit the changes, push them to your fork, and open a Pull Request against the original repository.

4. Sync with Upstream

Add the original repository as an upstream remote:

git remote add upstream <original-repo-url>

Pull the latest changes:

git pull upstream main

6. Git Stashing

Git Stash temporarily stores uncommitted changes so that you can switch tasks without creating a commit.

git stash

Stores current modifications.

git stash

git stash -u

Stores modifications along with untracked files.

git stash -u

git stash list

Displays all available stash entries.

git stash list

git stash pop

Restores the most recent stash and removes it from the stash stack.

git stash pop

git stash clear

Removes all stash entries.

git stash clear

7. Enterprise Branching & Deployment Strategy

Enterprise projects commonly isolate development, testing, and production environments using dedicated branches.

Enterprise Branching Flow

Feature Branch

      ↓

    DEV

      ↓

    TEST

      ↓

    UAT

      ↓

   MAIN / PROD

7.1 Feature Branch

Example:

feature-RA-XXXX

Used for:

  • Individual developer work
  • JIRA-ticket-specific changes
  • Isolated development

Feature branches are generally deleted after merging.

7.2 DEV Branch

Used to:

  • Integrate changes from multiple developers
  • Perform initial functional checks

7.3 TEST Branch

Used for:

  • Automated integration testing
  • Quality Assurance (QA)
  • Controlled test execution

7.4 UAT Branch

UAT = User Acceptance Testing

Business stakeholders validate whether the application meets the required business expectations.

7.5 MAIN / PROD

Contains production-ready code.

Production deployments are performed from the stable production branch.

8. CI/CD Pipelines & Jenkins

8.1 Continuous Integration

Continuous Integration (CI) automatically builds and tests code when changes are pushed to the repository.

Typical CI activities include:

  • Installing dependencies
  • Building the application
  • Running unit tests
  • Running lint checks
  • Validating the code

8.2 Continuous Deployment

Continuous Deployment (CD) automates the packaging and deployment of application artifacts to target environments.

CI/CD Pipeline

+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+

|    BUILD    | --> |    TEST     | --> |   PACKAGE   | --> |   DEPLOY    |

|             |     |             |     |             |     |             |

| VirtualEnv  |     | Pytest Runs |     | Create Zip /|     | SCP / SSH   |

| Dependencies|     | Lint Checks |     | Jar Artifact|     | to Cluster  |

+-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+     +-------------+

Pipeline Stages

1. Build

  • Create environment
  • Install dependencies

2. Test

  • Execute Pytest
  • Run lint checks

3. Package

  • Create ZIP/JAR/application artifact

4. Deploy

  • Transfer the artifact
  • Deploy to the target cluster/environment

9. Jenkinsfile

Jenkins pipelines can be defined as code using a root-level Jenkinsfile.

pipeline {

    agent any

    environment {

        LABS = credentials('labcreds')

    }

    stages {

        stage('Build') {

            steps {

                echo "Building environment and installing dependencies..."

                sh 'pip3 install --user pipenv'

                sh '~/.local/bin/pipenv --rm || exit 0'

                sh '~/.local/bin/pipenv install'

            }

        }

        stage('Test') {

            steps {

                echo "Executing automated unit testing suite..."

                sh '~/.local/bin/pipenv run pytest -v'

            }

        }

        stage('Package') {

            steps {

                echo "Packaging PySpark application artifacts..."

                sh 'zip -r retailproject.zip .'

            }

        }

        stage('Deploy') {

            steps {

                echo "Deploying artifact to gateway edge node..."

                sh '''

                    sshpass -p $LABS_PSW scp -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -r . \

                    $LABS_USR@g02.itversity.com:/home/itv005857/retailproject

                '''

            }

        }

    }

}

Important Jenkins Concepts

Concept

Meaning

pipeline

Defines the Jenkins pipeline

agent any

Allows execution on any available Jenkins agent

environment

Defines environment variables

credentials()

Retrieves credentials stored securely in Jenkins

stages

Groups the pipeline's major phases

stage()

Defines an individual pipeline phase

steps

Contains commands executed within a stage

sh

Executes shell commands

WEEK 15: APACHE HIVE & METASTORE INTEGRATION

1. OLTP vs. OLAP

OLTP — Online Transaction Processing

OLTP systems support day-to-day operational workloads.

Typical characteristics:

  • Inserts
  • Updates
  • Deletes
  • Individual record reads
  • Low latency
  • High concurrency
  • Relational databases
  • Schema-on-write

Examples include:

  • MySQL
  • Oracle
  • Other relational databases

OLAP — Online Analytical Processing

OLAP systems support large-scale analytical workloads.

Typical characteristics:

  • Historical analysis
  • Large scans
  • Aggregations
  • High throughput
  • Distributed processing
  • Schema-on-read

Apache Hive is commonly used as a SQL abstraction layer over distributed storage.

OLTP vs. OLAP Comparison

Dimension

OLTP

OLAP / Hive

Primary Workload

High-concurrency operations

Large-scale historical analysis

Operations

Inserts, Updates, Deletes, Single Reads

Large reads, scans and aggregations

Underlying Systems

MySQL, Oracle, RDBMS

Hive / Distributed Warehouses

Schema

Schema-on-Write

Schema-on-Read

Latency

Low

Higher

Throughput

Lower

Extremely High

Data Scale

Relatively smaller operational datasets

Massive analytical datasets

Key Difference

OLTP is optimized for operational transactions, while OLAP is optimized for large-scale analytical processing.

2. Apache Hive Architecture

Apache Hive provides an SQL-like abstraction layer called HQL (Hive Query Language) over distributed storage such as:

  • HDFS
  • Amazon S3
  • ADLS

Hive can work with distributed compute engines such as:

  • MapReduce
  • Tez
  • Spark

Hive Architecture

                        +-------------------+

                         |  Beeline Client   |

                         |  JDBC Interface   |

                         +---------+---------+

                                   |

                                   ↓

                         +-------------------+

                         |    HiveServer2    |

                         | Query Execution   |

                         +---------+---------+

                                   |

                    +--------------+--------------+

                    |                             |

                    ↓                             ↓

          +-------------------+         +---------------------------+

          | Hive Metastore    |         | Distributed Storage       |

          |       (HMS)       |         | & Compute                 |

          |                   |         |                           |

          | Schemas           |         | Storage: HDFS/S3/ADLS     |

          | Column Types      |         | Compute: MR/Tez/Spark     |

          | File Locations    |         |                           |

          +-------------------+         +---------------------------+

2.1 Hive Metastore (HMS)

The Hive Metastore stores metadata about tables, including:

  • Table schemas
  • Column names
  • Column data types
  • File locations

The metadata itself is stored in a relational database such as MySQL.

Why use an RDBMS for the Metastore?

A relational database provides efficient and low-latency metadata management and schema updates.

2.2 HiveServer2

HiveServer2:

  • Receives client queries
  • Accepts JDBC/ODBC requests
  • Processes HQL
  • Compiles queries into distributed jobs
  • Returns query results

2.3 Beeline

Beeline is a JDBC-based command-line client used to connect to HiveServer2.

Example:

beeline -u "jdbc:hive2://m02.itversity.com:10000/;auth=noSasl"

Architecture Flow

Beeline

   ↓

HiveServer2

   ↓

Hive Metastore + Compute Engine

   ↓

HDFS / S3 / ADLS

3. Hive Table Types

Hive primarily supports two important table types:

  1. Managed Tables
  2. External Tables

3.1 Managed Table

A Managed Table is controlled by Hive.

Hive manages:

  • Table metadata
  • Physical data

The default warehouse location is controlled by:

hive.metastore.warehouse.dir

DROP Behavior

When a managed table is dropped:

DROP TABLE table_name;

Both:

  • Metadata
  • Physical data

are deleted.

3.2 External Table

An External Table is useful when the underlying data is shared with other systems or teams.

Hive manages:

  • Table metadata

The actual data remains in the custom storage location.

DROP Behavior

When an external table is dropped:

  • Metastore metadata is removed
  • Physical files remain intact

Managed vs. External Tables

Property

Managed Table

External Table

Hive owns metadata

Yes

Yes

Hive owns data

Yes

No

Storage location

Default warehouse

Custom LOCATION

DROP TABLE

Deletes metadata + data

Deletes metadata only

Best Use Case

Hive-managed lifecycle

Shared datasets / external systems

3.3 Creating an External Hive Table

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders_external (

    order_id INT,

    order_date STRING,

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING

)

ROW FORMAT DELIMITED

FIELDS TERMINATED BY ','

STORED AS TEXTFILE

LOCATION '/user/itv005857/hive_datasets/orders';

Key Point

External tables are useful when Hive should manage the metadata without owning or deleting the underlying data files.

4. Hive Performance Optimizations

Two major storage optimization techniques are:

  • Partitioning
  • Bucketing

4.1 Partitioning

Partitioning divides data into directories/folders based on a column.

Example:

/warehouse/orders/

│

├── order_status=CLOSED/

│   └── part-0000

│

└── order_status=COMPLETE/

    └── part-0000

Best Use Case

Partitioning works well with low-cardinality columns, such as:

  • order_status
  • country

Main Benefit

Partition Pruning

If a query filters on a partition column, Hive can skip directories that do not match the filter.

5. Bucketing

Bucketing divides data into a fixed number of files/buckets based on a hash function.

Example:

/warehouse/orders/

├── 000000_0    → Bucket 1

├── 000001_0    → Bucket 2

├── 000002_0    → Bucket 3

└── 000003_0    → Bucket 4

Best Use Case

Bucketing is useful for high-cardinality columns, such as:

  • order_id
  • Customer identifiers

Example:

CLUSTERED BY (order_id) INTO 4 BUCKETS

Main Benefits

  • Optimizes joins
  • Helps point lookups
  • Supports bucket-based join strategies

6. Partitioning vs. Bucketing

Feature

Partitioning

Bucketing

Physical Structure

Folders / directories

Files

Best Column Type

Low cardinality

High cardinality

Example

country, order_status

order_id, customer_id

Main Optimization

Partition Pruning

Bucket-based joins / lookups

Number of Values

Relatively few

Potentially many

Primary Benefit

Avoids scanning unnecessary directories

Organizes records into fixed bucket files

Easy Way to Remember

Partitioning → Folders

Bucketing → Files

7. Hive Join Optimization Strategies

Hive supports multiple join optimization techniques.

7.1 Map-Side Join / Broadcast Join

Trigger

Used when one table is small enough to fit into memory.

The source material specifies a default threshold of approximately:

25 MB

Mechanism

  1. Small table is loaded into memory.
  2. An in-memory Hash Table is created.
  3. The small table is distributed to nodes.
  4. The Reduce phase is bypassed.

Benefit

Avoids the expensive Reduce phase and improves join performance.

8. Bucket Map Join

Bucket Map Join is useful when the datasets are too large to broadcast completely.

Requirements

Both tables must:

  • Be bucketed on the join key
  • Have compatible bucket counts

The number of buckets in one table should be an integer multiple of the other.

Example:

Table A → 4 buckets

Table B → 8 buckets

8 is an integer multiple of 4.

Mechanism

Instead of loading an entire table into memory, Hive processes matching buckets individually.

9. Sort-Merge-Bucket (SMB) Join

SMB Join is optimized for large datasets where both tables are already bucketed and sorted.

Requirements

Both tables must:

  1. Be bucketed on the join key
  2. Have the same number of buckets
  3. Be sorted by the join key

Example:

Table A → 8 buckets

Table B → 8 buckets

Join Key → customer_id

Sorted By → customer_id

Mechanism

Hive sequentially merges corresponding bucket files.

This avoids:

  • Network shuffling
  • In-memory sorting

Key Difference

Bucket Map Join

→ Bucket counts can be integer multiples

SMB Join

→ Exact same number of buckets

→ Same join key

→ Pre-sorted on join key

10. Hive SMB Join Configuration

The following settings are used to enable/optimize SMB joins:

SET hive.input.format=org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.BucketizedHiveInputFormat;

SET hive.auto.convert.sortmerge.join=true;

SET hive.optimize.bucketmapjoin=true;

SET hive.optimize.bucketmapjoin.sortedmerge=true;

SET hive.enforce.bucketing=true;

SET hive.enforce.sorting=true;

11. Transactional ACID Tables in Hive

Hive supports ACID transactions for workloads that require operations such as:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE

ACID stands for:

A — Atomicity

C — Consistency

I — Isolation

D — Durability

These capabilities can be useful for workloads such as Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) and streaming updates.

11.1 Hive ACID Storage Structure

Hive stores transactional changes using base and delta files.

HDFS Directory/

├── base_0000001/

│   └── Initial snapshot

│

├── delta_0000002_0000002/

│   └── New inserts / updates

│

├── delta_0000003_0000003/

│   └── New inserts / updates

│

└── delete_delta_0000004_0000004/

    └── Recorded deletions

Read-Time Processing

At read time, Hive combines:

Base

 +

Delta

 +

Delete Delta

 ↓

Final Logical Dataset

12. Requirements for Full ACID Tables

According to the provided course material, full Hive ACID tables must:

  1. Be Managed Tables
  2. Use the ORC file format
  3. Be Bucketed
  4. Have:

TBLPROPERTIES ('transactional'='true')

12.1 Enabling Hive ACID Support

SET hive.support.concurrency=true;

SET hive.txn.manager=org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.lockmgr.DbTxnManager;

12.2 Creating a Full ACID Table

CREATE TABLE orders_trx (

    order_id INT,

    order_date STRING,

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING

)

CLUSTERED BY (order_id) INTO 4 BUCKETS

STORED AS ORC

TBLPROPERTIES ('transactional'='true');

Remember

Full ACID Hive Table

Managed

   +

ORC

   +

Bucketed

   +

transactional=true

13. Insert-Only Transactional Tables

Hive also supports insert-only transactional tables.

These tables are useful when the workload only requires:

INSERT

and does not require:

UPDATE

DELETE

Key Difference

According to the provided material:

Insert-only transactional tables support all file formats, including CSV/Text.

They are created using:

TBLPROPERTIES (

    'transactional'='true',

    'transactional_properties'='insert_only'

)

14. MSCK REPAIR TABLE

The Problem

Hive's Metastore maintains information about table partitions.

Suppose a partition directory is manually added to HDFS:

hadoop fs -cp ...

Hive may not automatically know that the new partition exists.

Example

Hive Metastore

      |

      | Does not know

      ↓

HDFS

├── order_status=CLOSED

├── order_status=COMPLETE

└── order_status=PENDING  ← Manually added

The Metastore needs to be synchronized with the actual partition directories.

MSCK REPAIR TABLE

Use:

MSCK REPAIR TABLE database_name.table_name;

This scans the relevant HDFS directory structure and updates the Hive Metastore with partitions that were added outside Hive/Spark.

Key Takeaway

MSCK REPAIR TABLE synchronizes partition metadata in the Hive Metastore with partition directories physically present in storage.
