Week 16: Resource Estimation, Production Debugging & Interview Preparation

1. Resource Estimation Framework for PySpark Jobs

Accurately sizing cluster resources for production PySpark jobs requires balancing data volume, hardware configuration, and SLA requirements. Simply allocating more resources does not always make a job faster.

Core Estimation Factors

1. Data Volume & Memory Expansion

Data stored on disk is usually compressed and serialized. Once loaded into memory, its representation can expand significantly.

A practical estimation rule is:

[
\text{Memory Requirement} \approx \text{Disk Data Size} \times 4\text{–}6
]

For example:

  • 100 GB of input data
  • Approximate in-memory requirement = 400–600 GB

This expansion factor is particularly important when estimating executor memory for operations such as:

  • Aggregations
  • Joins
  • Sorting
  • Shuffles
  • Caching

2. SLA Requirements

Resource allocation should also depend on how quickly the job needs to finish.

For example:

  • If a 100 GB job can run for 2 hours → fewer resources may be acceptable.
  • If the same job must complete in 15 minutes → significantly more parallelism may be required.

Therefore:

Resource estimation is not only about data size; it is also about the required completion time.

3. Hardware Baseline

A commonly used baseline in the course is:

  • 5 CPU cores per executor
  • Approximately 1 GB execution memory per CPU core

Using 5 cores per executor helps balance:

  • Parallelism
  • HDFS/network I/O
  • Garbage Collection
  • Executor overhead

2. Example: 100-Node Cluster

Assume:

100 Nodes

Each Node:

16 CPU Cores

64 GB RAM

Reserve resources for the operating system:

OS Reservation:

1 CPU Core

1 GB RAM

Therefore:

Available per Node:

15 CPU Cores

63 GB RAM

With 5 cores per executor:

Executors per Node = 15 / 5

                   = 3 Executors

Each executor gets approximately:

5 CPU Cores

19 GB RAM

Therefore, the entire cluster can support approximately:

100 Nodes × 3 Executors

= 300 Executors

300 Executors × 5 Cores

= 1,500 CPU Cores

Cluster Summary

Resource

Value

Nodes

100

Cores per Node

16

RAM per Node

64 GB

Usable Cores per Node

15

Usable RAM per Node

63 GB

Executors per Node

3

Cores per Executor

5

RAM per Executor

~19 GB

Total Executors

300

Total Available Cores

1,500

3. Scenario A — 100 GB Aggregation Job

Suppose we have:

Input Data = 100 GB

Partition Size = 128 MB

Approximate number of input partitions:

[
100GB / 128MB \approx 800
]

So we have approximately:

800 input partitions

Stage 1 — Reading Input

If we want to process all 800 partitions simultaneously:

Required CPU Cores = 800

With 5 cores per executor:

[
800 / 5 = 160
]

Therefore:

160 executors

are required.

Stage 1

800 Input Partitions

        ↓

800 CPU Cores

        ↓

160 Executors

        ↓

5 Cores / Executor

Stage 2 — Shuffle

The default value of:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200

would produce approximately:

[
100GB / 200 = 500MB
]

per shuffle partition.

That is considerably larger than the 128 MB input-partition target.

Considering memory expansion, a 500 MB partition could require:

[
500MB \times 4 = 2GB
]

or even more depending on the workload.

This can cause:

  • Memory pressure
  • Disk spilling
  • Garbage Collection
  • Executor OOM

Solution

Increase:

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 800)

Now:

[
100GB / 800 = 125MB
]

per shuffle partition, which is close to the 128 MB baseline.

Key Idea

Shuffle partition sizing is important because the default 200 partitions may be too few for large datasets.

Option 1 — Maximum Parallelism

Executors = 160

Cores = 800

Stage 1:

800 partitions → 1 wave

Stage 2:

800 shuffle partitions → 1 wave

This gives maximum parallelism but uses more resources.

Option 2 — Moderate Resource Footprint

Suppose we use:

80 Executors

5 cores each

= 400 cores

Then:

Stage 1:

800 partitions / 400 cores

= 2 waves

For Stage 2, using 400 shuffle partitions:

[
100GB / 400 = 250MB
]

per shuffle partition.

So:

Executors = 80

CPU Cores = 400

Stage 1 → 2 waves

Stage 2 → 400 shuffle partitions

Important Trade-off

Strategy

Resources

Parallelism

Cost

Maximum

160 executors

Very High

Higher

Moderate

80 executors

Medium

Lower

The goal is not always maximum parallelism.

The goal is an appropriate balance between execution time and resource consumption.

4. Scenario B — Large-Scale Join

Consider:

Orders = 100 GB

Customers = 50 GB

Total:

[
100GB + 50GB = 150GB
]

With 128 MB partitions:

[
150GB / 128MB \approx 1,200
]

So we have approximately:

1,200 input partitions

Maximum Parallelism

To process all 1,200 partitions simultaneously:

Required Cores = 1,200

With 5 cores per executor:

[
1200 / 5 = 240
]

Therefore:

240 executors

would be required.

Shuffle partitions can similarly be set around:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 1200

Optimized Resource Allocation

Instead of 240 executors, suppose we use:

120 Executors

× 5 Cores

= 600 Cores

Stage 1

1,200 partitions

600 available cores

Therefore:

1,200 / 600

= 2 waves

Stage 2

Set:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 600

Then:

[
150GB / 600 = 250MB
]

per shuffle partition.

So the job uses:

120 Executors

600 Cores

Stage 1 → 2 waves

Stage 2 → 600 shuffle partitions

5. Dynamic Resource Allocation

Static resource allocation can result in idle executors.

For example:

Stage 1 → Heavy workload

Stage 2 → Medium workload

Stage 3 → Small workload

If the cluster always maintains the same number of executors, resources can remain unused during lighter stages.

Dynamic Resource Allocation allows Spark to:

  • Add executors when there is a backlog of tasks
  • Remove idle executors
  • Adapt resource consumption to workload requirements

Configuration

spark.conf.set("spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled", True)

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors",

    10

)

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors",

    200

)

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.dynamicAllocation.initialExecutors",

    20

)

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.dynamicAllocation.schedulerBacklogTimeout",

    "1s"

)

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout",

    "60s"

)

Important Parameters

Parameter

Meaning

enabled

Turns Dynamic Allocation on/off

minExecutors

Minimum number of executors

initialExecutors

Starting number

maxExecutors

Maximum allowed

schedulerBacklogTimeout

Time before Spark requests additional executors

executorIdleTimeout

Time after which idle executors can be removed

6. Practical PySpark Coding Problems

Problem 1 — Remove Duplicate Records from Parquet

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder \

    .appName("Deduplication") \

    .getOrCreate()

source_path = "path/to/input/data.parquet"

target_path = "path/to/output/results"

df = spark.read.parquet(source_path)

df_clean = df.dropDuplicates()

df_clean.write \

    .mode("overwrite") \

    .parquet(target_path)

Key Concept

dropDuplicates()

removes duplicate rows across all columns.

7. Problem 2 — collect_list

Suppose the input is:

("a", "aa", 1)

("a", "aa", 2)

("b", "bb", 5)

("b", "bb", 3)

("b", "bb", 4)

Create:

from pyspark.sql.functions import collect_list

data = [

    ("a", "aa", 1),

    ("a", "aa", 2),

    ("b", "bb", 5),

    ("b", "bb", 3),

    ("b", "bb", 4)

]

df = spark.createDataFrame(

    data,

    ["col1", "col2", "col3"]

)

result_df = df.groupBy(

    "col1",

    "col2"

).agg(

    collect_list("col3").alias("col3")

)

result_df.show()

The same can be done using Spark SQL:

df.createOrReplaceTempView("my_table")

result_sql = spark.sql("""

    SELECT

        col1,

        col2,

        collect_list(col3) AS col3

    FROM my_table

    GROUP BY col1, col2

""")

Key Concept

collect_list() converts multiple values belonging to a group into an array.

8. Problem 3 — Exploding Nested Arrays

Suppose a JSON record contains:

{

  "dept_id": 101,

  "e_id": [10101, 10102, 10103]

}

Read it:

json_df = spark.read.json(

    "path/to/nested_file.json"

)

Use explode():

from pyspark.sql.functions import explode

exploded_df = json_df.select(

    "dept_id",

    explode("e_id").alias("e_id")

)

exploded_df.show()

Conceptually:

Before:

dept_id     e_id

101         [10101, 10102, 10103]

After:

dept_id     e_id

101         10101

101         10102

101         10103

Key Concept

explode() converts an array element into separate rows.

9. Problem 4 — Handling Multi-Character Delimiters

Standard CSV readers may not directly handle unusual delimiters such as:

~|

Example:

Name~/Age

Brayan, Gomez~|25

John, Cleark~|30

Read as raw text:

input_df = spark.read.text(

    "/path/to/messedupfile.txt"

)

Extract the header:

header_row = input_df.first()[0]

schema_cols = header_row.split("~/")

Remove the header:

data_df = input_df.filter(

    input_df.value != header_row

)

Parse using an RDD:

parsed_df = data_df.rdd \

    .map(lambda row: row[0].split("~|")) \

    .toDF(schema_cols)

parsed_df.show()

Key Concept

When a standard reader cannot handle the file structure, one approach is:

Text File

   ↓

DataFrame

   ↓

RDD

   ↓

Custom Parsing

   ↓

DataFrame

10. Problem 5 — Calculate Team Size

Given:

data = [

    (1, 8),

    (2, 8),

    (3, 8),

    (4, 7),

    (5, 9),

    (6, 9)

]

employee_df = spark.createDataFrame(

    data,

    ["employee_id", "team_id"]

)

First group employees:

from pyspark.sql.functions import (

    collect_list,

    size,

    explode

)

result_df = employee_df \

    .groupBy("team_id") \

    .agg(

        collect_list("employee_id")

        .alias("employee_list")

    ) \

    .withColumn(

        "team_size",

        size("employee_list")

    ) \

    .selectExpr(

        "explode(employee_list) as employee_id",

        "team_size"

    )

result_df.show()

Processing Flow

Employee Records

       ↓

groupBy(team_id)

       ↓

collect_list(employee_id)

       ↓

size(employee_list)

       ↓

explode(employee_list)

       ↓

Employee + Team Size

This combines three important Spark functions:

collect_list()

size()

explode()

11. Production Debugging & Root Cause Analysis

A production Spark job can fail because of:

  • Driver memory issues
  • Executor memory issues
  • Data skew
  • Excessive shuffling
  • Insufficient partitions
  • Excessive caching
  • Disk spilling
  • Inefficient file formats
  • Poor aggregation strategies

A useful first distinction is:

               Spark Application

                       |

             +---------+---------+

             |                   |

        Driver OOM           Executor OOM

             |                   |

       Driver process       Worker process

12. Driver OOM

A common cause is:

df.collect()

If the DataFrame is very large, collect() attempts to bring the entire dataset into the driver's memory.

Common Causes

  • Calling .collect() on large DataFrames
  • Broadcasting excessively large tables
  • Excessive driver-side logs/buffers

Example

Avoid:

data = df.collect()

for large datasets.

Instead, keep processing distributed whenever possible.

13. Executor OOM

Executor OOM happens when an individual executor cannot handle its workload.

Common Causes

  • Too few shuffle partitions
  • Data skew
  • Excessive caching
  • Large partitions
  • Insufficient executor memory

Possible Solutions

Increase:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions

Filter data earlier:

df = df.filter(...)

or increase executor memory when appropriate:

--executor-memory

14. Diagnosing Data Skew Using Spark UI

A classic skew pattern is:

Task 1    → 10 seconds

Task 2    → 11 seconds

Task 3    → 9 seconds

...

Task 199  → 10 seconds

Task 200  → 2 hours

This indicates that one partition contains substantially more data than others.

Why?

Suppose:

Customer A → 10 records

Customer B → 15 records

Customer C → 20 records

BIG_CUSTOMER → 50 million records

When grouped or joined by customer ID, the BIG_CUSTOMER records can end up concentrated in a single partition.

This is data skew.

15. Fixing Data Skew

Two approaches highlighted in the material are:

1. AQE Skew Join

Enable:

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled",

    True

)

Spark's Adaptive Query Execution can detect and mitigate skewed partitions during execution.

2. Salting

For heavily skewed keys, manually modify the join key by adding a salt value.

Conceptually:

Original Key:

customer_123

Salted:

customer_123_1

customer_123_2

customer_123_3

...

This distributes a heavily concentrated key across multiple partitions.

16. Disk Spill

When Spark does not have enough execution memory, it can spill intermediate data to disk.

Spark UI may show:

Spill (Memory)

Spill (Disk)

Large spill values can indicate memory pressure.

Potential Solutions

  • Increase the number of shuffle partitions
  • Reduce partition size
  • Filter data earlier
  • Review memory allocation
  • Consider off-heap memory where appropriate

The course material also highlights:

spark.memory.fraction

spark.memory.offHeap.size

as memory-related configuration areas.

17. Optimizing Aggregations

From Week 11, remember the distinction:

HashAggregate

       ↓

Fast

       ↓

Works efficiently with suitable primitive/mutable types

SortAggregate

       ↓

Sorting overhead

       ↓

Can be slower

When appropriate, using primitive types such as:

Integer

Long

Timestamp

can allow Spark to use more efficient aggregation strategies.

18. Optimizing Storage Reads

Use columnar formats such as:

Parquet

ORC

and compression such as:

Snappy

Advantages include:

  • Reduced storage footprint
  • Reduced I/O
  • Column pruning
  • Predicate pushdown
  • Better query performance

Partitioning is useful when queries frequently filter on low-cardinality columns.

For recurring large-table joins, pre-bucketing may also be considered.

19. Production Debugging Decision Tree

A useful way to approach a failing Spark job:

                Spark Job Slow / Failed

                         |

                         v

                   Check Spark UI

                         |

          +--------------+--------------+

          |                             |

     One task slow                 All tasks slow

          |                             |

     Data Skew?                   Resource issue?

          |                             |

      Yes → AQE /                    Check:

       Salting                   partitions

                                    memory

                                    cores

                                    I/O

          |

          v

    Check OOM / Spill

          |

    +-----+------+

    |            |

 Driver OOM   Executor OOM

    |            |

 collect()    skew / partitions

 broadcast    cache / memory

20. Interview Preparation — High-Value Questions

Resource Estimation

Q1. Why can't we simply allocate maximum resources to every Spark job?

Because more resources do not automatically produce proportional performance improvements. Excessive resources can increase cost while resources remain underutilized.

Q2. Why is data size multiplied by 4–6 during memory estimation?

Disk data is typically compressed/serialized, while in-memory representations can be significantly larger. The course uses 4×–6× as a practical estimation factor.

Q3. Why are 5 cores per executor commonly used in the baseline?

The course uses 5 cores as a balanced baseline to maintain parallelism while avoiding excessive GC and I/O pressure.

Shuffle

Q4. What happens if spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is too low?

Each shuffle partition becomes larger, increasing memory pressure and potentially causing:

  • Spill
  • Slow tasks
  • Executor OOM

Q5. How do you choose the number of shuffle partitions?

Consider:

Total shuffle data

        ↓

Desired partition size

        ↓

Number of shuffle partitions

        ↓

Available CPU parallelism

Dynamic Allocation

Q6. What is Dynamic Resource Allocation?

It allows Spark to dynamically add and remove executors based on workload demand.

Debugging

Q7. How can you identify data skew from Spark UI?

Look for a stage where most tasks finish quickly but one or a few tasks take significantly longer.

Q8. How can you fix data skew?

Common approaches from the course:

  • AQE skew join
  • Salting
  • Better partitioning strategies

Driver vs Executor

Q9. What is a common cause of Driver OOM?

Calling:

df.collect()

on a large dataset.

Q10. What causes Executor OOM?

Potential causes include:

  • Large partitions
  • Too few shuffle partitions
  • Data skew
  • Excessive caching
  • Insufficient executor memory

The 10 things I'd memorize from Week 16

  1. Disk data can expand 4–6× in memory.
  2. 5 cores/executor is the baseline used in the course.
  3. More resources ≠ automatically faster jobs.
  4. Too few shuffle partitions → large partitions → OOM/spill.
  5. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions controls shuffle parallelism.
  6. Dynamic Allocation adds/removes executors based on demand.
  7. .collect() on huge data can cause Driver OOM.

  9. Fix skew using AQE skew join or salting.
  10. Use Parquet/ORC + compression + partitioning for efficient data access.

WEEK 17

Cloud Computing Foundations & Azure Global Infrastructure

1. Cloud Computing Foundations & Economic Models

Cloud computing provides on-demand availability of computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, and networking over the internet.

Cloud services generally follow a pay-as-you-go delivery model, allowing organizations to consume resources based on their requirements rather than purchasing and maintaining physical infrastructure.

On-Premise vs. Cloud

                   ON-PREMISE vs. CLOUD

      ON-PREMISE (CapEx Dominant)              CLOUD COMPUTING (OpEx Dominant)

   ┌───────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────────────┐

   │ • Significant upfront costs  │         │ • Zero upfront investment      │

   │ • Dedicated IT infrastructure│         │ • Pay based on usage            │

   │ • Capacity waste possible    │         │ • On-demand dynamic scaling     │

   │ • Hardware procurement slow   │         │ • High agility & instant deploys│

   └───────────────────────────────┘         └────────────────────────────────┘

Capital Expenditure (CapEx)

CapEx refers to the large upfront investment required to purchase physical infrastructure.

Examples include:

  • Physical servers
  • Networking hardware
  • Cooling systems
  • Data-center infrastructure
  • Real estate

The purchased equipment depreciates over time. Scaling generally requires purchasing additional hardware.

Operational Expenditure (OpEx)

OpEx refers to variable operational costs where organizations pay for resources according to their consumption.

Cloud environments allow organizations to:

  • Pay based on usage
  • Scale resources up or down
  • Deploy infrastructure quickly
  • Avoid large upfront hardware investments

CapEx vs. OpEx

Feature

On-Premise — CapEx

Cloud — OpEx

Upfront Cost

Significant initial investment

No upfront capital investment

Ongoing Costs

Relatively static maintenance costs

Dynamic, usage-based

Maintenance

Managed by in-house teams

Primarily handled by cloud provider

Scaling

Slow and limited by physical capacity

Fast and elastic

Deployment

Requires hardware procurement

Resources can be provisioned quickly

2. Core Cloud Characteristics

Cloud computing provides several important characteristics that distinguish it from traditional infrastructure.

2.1 Agility

Agility is the ability to provision and deploy IT infrastructure rapidly.

Traditional infrastructure may require months for procurement and installation, whereas cloud infrastructure can often be provisioned within minutes.

2.2 Scalability

Scalability is the ability to increase or decrease resources according to workload requirements.

There are two primary types.

Vertical Scaling — Scale Up / Scale Down

Increasing or decreasing the CPU and RAM of an existing machine.

Before:

VM → 4 CPU + 16 GB RAM

Scale Up:

VM → 8 CPU + 32 GB RAM

Horizontal Scaling — Scale Out / Scale In

Adding or removing multiple compute nodes.

Before:

[ VM 1 ]

Scale Out:

[ VM 1 ] [ VM 2 ] [ VM 3 ] [ VM 4 ]

Scale In:

[ VM 1 ] [ VM 2 ]

2.3 Elasticity

Elasticity is the ability of a cloud environment to dynamically and automatically adjust resources based on real-time demand.

Example:

Low Traffic

     ↓

2 VMs

Traffic Increases

     ↓

5 VMs

Traffic Decreases

     ↓

2 VMs

Scalability vs. Elasticity

  • Scalability: Ability to increase or decrease capacity.
  • Elasticity: Ability to dynamically and automatically adjust capacity according to demand.

2.4 Fault Tolerance

Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to remain operational even when individual components fail.

It is achieved using redundancy and failure-isolation mechanisms.

2.5 Disaster Recovery (DR)

Disaster Recovery refers to architectural strategies that allow systems to recover from major outages or disasters.

A common approach is maintaining failover infrastructure in another region.

Primary Region

      │

      │ Failure

      ↓

Secondary Region

      │

      ↓

Service Recovery

2.6 High Availability (HA)

High Availability focuses on keeping systems operational with minimal unexpected downtime.

The availability formula is:

[
Availability =
\frac{Total\ Uptime}
{Total\ Uptime + Downtime}
]

Higher availability means less downtime.

3. Cloud Service Models & Deployment Strategies

Cloud services are commonly divided into three major service models:

                    CLOUD SERVICE MODELS

        IaaS                  PaaS                  SaaS

     Azure VM             Azure SQL DB          Microsoft 365

        │                     │                     │

        ▼                     ▼                     ▼

   More control          Less infrastructure     Fully managed

   More management       management              application

3.1 Infrastructure as a Service — IaaS

IaaS provides fundamental infrastructure such as:

  • Virtual machines
  • Compute
  • Networking
  • Storage

Example:

Azure Virtual Machines

The customer manages the operating system, runtime, applications, and data.

The cloud provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

3.2 Platform as a Service — PaaS

PaaS provides a managed platform where users can focus primarily on their application and data.

Examples:

  • Azure SQL Database
  • Databricks

The cloud provider manages infrastructure and much of the underlying platform.

3.3 Software as a Service — SaaS

SaaS provides complete applications that users access directly.

Examples:

  • Microsoft 365
  • Google Drive

The vendor manages the underlying infrastructure, platform, and application.

IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS

Layer

IaaS

PaaS

SaaS

Customer

Vendor-managed

Memory Trick

IaaS → Infrastructure

PaaS → Platform

SaaS → Software

The further you move from IaaS toward SaaS, the more infrastructure management is handled by the provider.

4. Cloud Deployment Models

4.1 Public Cloud

Infrastructure is provided by a cloud provider and made available to customers over the internet.

Examples:

  • Microsoft Azure
  • Amazon Web Services
  • Google Cloud Platform

Advantages:

  • High elasticity
  • Low initial investment
  • Rapid provisioning

4.2 Private Cloud

Infrastructure is dedicated exclusively to one organization.

Advantages:

  • Greater control
  • Strong security and compliance capabilities

Disadvantage:

  • Higher infrastructure and operational requirements

4.3 Hybrid Cloud

A hybrid cloud combines public and private cloud infrastructure.

For example:

            HYBRID CLOUD

       Private Cloud              Public Cloud

      ┌──────────────┐           ┌──────────────┐

      │ Sensitive    │           │ Scalable     │

      │ workloads    │◄─────────►│ workloads    │

      └──────────────┘           └──────────────┘

Sensitive workloads can remain in private infrastructure while scalable workloads can use public-cloud resources.

5. Azure Resource Management & Account Hierarchy

Azure organizes resources using a hierarchical structure:

                MANAGEMENT GROUPS

                       │

                       ▼

                  SUBSCRIPTION

                       │

                       ▼

                 RESOURCE GROUP

                       │

                       ▼

                    RESOURCE

5.1 Management Groups

Management Groups are containers used to manage:

  • Access
  • Policies
  • Governance

across multiple Azure subscriptions.

5.2 Subscription

A Subscription is an important boundary for:

  • Billing
  • Access control
  • Resource management

Examples may include different billing or organizational subscriptions.

5.3 Resource Group

A Resource Group (RG) is a logical container for resources that share a common lifecycle.

Examples of resources inside a Resource Group:

Resource Group

├── Virtual Machine

├── Storage Account

├── Database

└── Networking Resources

Important Resource Group Rules

  1. Every resource must belong to exactly one Resource Group.
  2. Resource Groups cannot be nested.
  3. Resources can be moved between Resource Groups.
  4. Resources in the same Resource Group can exist in different physical regions.
  5. The Resource Group itself stores metadata in its assigned region.

5.4 Resources

Resources are individual Azure services.

Examples:

  • Virtual Machines
  • Storage Accounts
  • Databases
  • Networking components

5.5 Azure Resource Manager — ARM

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the management layer through which Azure resources are controlled.

Requests can originate from:

  • Azure Portal
  • Azure CLI
  • PowerShell
  • SDKs
  • REST APIs

Azure Portal

Azure CLI

PowerShell

SDK

REST API

      │

      ▼

 Azure Resource Manager

      │

      ▼

 Azure Resources

6. Azure Global Infrastructure

Azure infrastructure can be understood using the following hierarchy:

                AZURE GLOBAL INFRASTRUCTURE

                      GEOGRAPHY

                         │

                         ▼

                    REGION PAIR

                     /        \

                    /          \

               REGION A      REGION B

                  │              │

                  ▼              ▼

             Availability    Availability

                Zones            Zones

                  │

                  ▼

             Data Centers

7. Data Centers

A Data Center is a physical facility containing interconnected servers and infrastructure.

It contains:

  • Servers
  • Networking
  • Power systems
  • Cooling systems
  • Physical infrastructure

A data center represents the physical foundation of cloud infrastructure.

8. Azure Regions

An Azure Region is a geographical area containing one or more data centers connected through a low-latency network.

Region selection can depend on:

  • Proximity to users
  • Service availability
  • Pricing
  • Availability Zone support
  • Regulatory requirements

Example from the course material:

India Geography

       │

       ├── Central India — Pune

       │

       └── South India — Chennai

9. Availability Zones

An Availability Zone is a physically separate data-center location within an Azure region.

Availability Zones have independent:

  • Power
  • Cooling
  • Networking

They protect workloads from failures affecting an individual data-center location.

Zone-Enabled Region

A region is considered Zone Enabled when it contains three or more independent Availability Zones, according to the course material.

Zonal vs. Zone-Redundant Services

Zonal Service

A resource is pinned to a specific Availability Zone.

Examples:

  • Azure Virtual Machines
  • Managed Disks

Zone-Redundant Service

Azure automatically replicates the service across multiple Availability Zones.

Examples:

  • Azure SQL
  • Storage Accounts

10. Azure Region Pairs

Azure regions are paired with another region within the same geography.

The purpose is to provide resilience against region-wide disasters.

            GEOGRAPHY

                 │

          ┌──────┴──────┐

          ▼             ▼

       REGION A  ◄──► REGION B

       Primary       Paired

Examples from the course material:

  • Central India ↔ South India
  • East US ↔ West US

Region pairs help organizations design disaster recovery strategies.

11. Azure Geographies

A Geography represents a broad geographical boundary containing one or more Azure regions.

Examples:

  • India
  • United States
  • Europe

Geographies are important for:

  • Data residency
  • Regulatory compliance
  • Data sovereignty

12. Azure Compute — Virtual Machines

An Azure Virtual Machine (VM) is an IaaS compute service.

A VM provides:

  • CPU
  • Memory
  • Storage
  • Guest operating system
  • Network connectivity

Multiple VMs can run on a physical host through a Hypervisor.

             PHYSICAL SERVER

                    │

                Hypervisor

          ┌─────────┼─────────┐

          ▼         ▼         ▼

         VM 1      VM 2      VM 3

        Linux     Linux     Windows

The hypervisor provides isolation between virtual machines while allowing hardware resources to be shared efficiently.

13. Virtual Machine Scale Sets — VMSS

Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) allow Azure to automatically deploy and manage groups of identical VMs.

VMSS can:

  • Deploy identical VM instances
  • Scale out during increased demand
  • Scale in during reduced demand
  • Balance workloads across instances

            VM SCALE SET

              Load

               │

      ┌────────┼────────┐

      ▼        ▼        ▼

    VM 1      VM 2      VM 3

Traffic increases

        │

        ▼

      VM 4

      VM 5

14. Fault Domains & Update Domains

Azure provides two important concepts for availability sets.

14.1 Fault Domain — FD

A Fault Domain represents a physical grouping of hardware that shares common infrastructure such as:

  • Power source
  • Network switch
  • Physical rack

Fault Domains protect against localized physical hardware failures.

Fault Domain 0             Fault Domain 1

┌───────────────┐          ┌───────────────┐

│ Rack 1        │          │ Rack 2        │

│ VM 1          │          │ VM 2          │

│ Power Supply  │          │ Power Supply  │

└───────────────┘          └───────────────┘

14.2 Update Domain — UD

An Update Domain is a logical grouping of infrastructure that undergoes maintenance or software patching together.

The objective is to ensure that not all VMs are unavailable at the same time.

Update Domain 0 → Maintenance

Update Domain 1 → Running

Update Domain 2 → Running

             ↓

Update Domain 0 → Running

Update Domain 1 → Maintenance

Update Domain 2 → Running

15. Availability Sets

An Availability Set groups VMs across multiple Fault Domains and Update Domains within a single data center.

It protects against:

  • Rack failures
  • Hardware failures
  • Planned maintenance events

               AVAILABILITY SET

                       │

          ┌────────────┴────────────┐

          ▼                         ▼

     Fault Domain 0           Fault Domain 1

          │                         │

        VM 1                      VM 2

The key limitation is that Availability Sets do not protect against a complete data-center outage.

16. Availability Zones vs. Availability Sets

Feature

Availability Set

Availability Zone

Scope

Within one data center

Across separate data centers

Protection

Rack/hardware failures

Data-center failures

Fault Domain

Yes

Physical separation

Update Domain

Yes

Not the primary concept

Resilience Level

Lower

Higher

Typical Use

Intra-datacenter availability

Datacenter-level resilience

Easy Way to Remember

Availability Set → Separate VMs inside a data center

Availability Zone → Separate VMs across data centers

17. Azure Availability SLA Comparison

The course material presents the following availability targets:

Configuration

Failure Scenario

Azure Guaranteed SLA

Approx. Annual Maximum Downtime

Single VM

Basic instance failure

99.9%

~8 hours 45 minutes

Availability Set — ≥2 VMs

Intra-datacenter rack failure

99.95%

~4 hours 22 minutes

Availability Zones — ≥2 zones

Data-center-level outage

99.99%

~52 minutes

Availability Calculation

[
Availability =
\frac{Uptime}{Uptime + Downtime}
]

As the number of 9s increases, the permitted downtime decreases.

99.9%    → ~8h 45m downtime/year

99.95%   → ~4h 22m downtime/year

99.99%   → ~52m downtime/year

Final Mental Model

Cloud gives you elastic infrastructure. Azure organizes that infrastructure through subscriptions and resource groups, physically distributes it across regions and availability zones, and provides compute services such as VMs and VM Scale Sets with multiple mechanisms for high availability and fault tolerance.

Week 18: Azure Storage Services & Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2)

1. Azure Storage Account

An Azure Storage Account is a foundational cloud storage service designed to provide highly durable, scalable, and secure storage.

It supports multiple storage services:

                [ Azure Storage Account ]

  +------------------+------------------+-------------------+------------------+

  | Blob / Containers|  Table Storage   |    File Share     |  Queue Storage   |

  +------------------+------------------+-------------------+------------------+

  | Unstructured     | Semi-structured  | SMB / Network     | Asynchronous     |

  | object storage   | NoSQL tables     | file mounts for   | message queuing  |

  | for raw files    |                  | legacy workloads  | across apps      |

  +------------------+------------------+-------------------+------------------+

Core Storage Services

Service

Purpose

Blob Storage

Stores unstructured objects such as files, images, CSV, JSON, Parquet, etc.

Table Storage

NoSQL key-value storage for semi-structured data

File Storage

Managed file shares accessible using SMB

Queue Storage

Asynchronous message queuing between applications

2. Azure Storage Access Tiers

Azure Blob Storage provides different access tiers based on how frequently data is accessed.

Hot Tier

  • Designed for frequently accessed data
  • Higher storage cost
  • Lower access/retrieval cost
  • Suitable for active datasets

Cool Tier

  • Designed for infrequently accessed data
  • Lower storage cost than Hot
  • Higher retrieval cost
  • Intended for data stored for at least 30 days

Archive Tier

  • Designed for rarely accessed historical data
  • Lowest storage cost
  • Highest retrieval cost
  • Intended for data stored for at least 180 days

Rehydration

Data stored in Archive cannot be accessed immediately like Hot or Cool data.

It must first undergo rehydration, which moves it back into an online access tier.

This process can take several hours.

Early Deletion

Deleting or moving data before the minimum retention period can result in early deletion charges:

  • Cool → minimum 30 days
  • Archive → minimum 180 days

3. Azure Storage Redundancy

Azure provides multiple replication strategies to protect against hardware, data-center, and regional failures.

Redundancy

Replication

Protection

LRS

3 copies within one data center

Server, disk, or rack failure

ZRS

3 synchronous copies across Availability Zones

Data-center failure

GRS

LRS in primary + LRS in secondary region

Regional disaster

RA-GRS

GRS + read access to secondary

Regional outage with read availability

GZRS

ZRS in primary + LRS in secondary

Zone + regional failures

LRS — Locally Redundant Storage

Primary Data Center

       |

   +---+---+

   |   |   |

 Copy Copy Copy

Three copies are maintained within the same physical data center.

Protects primarily against localized hardware failures.

ZRS — Zone-Redundant Storage

            Azure Region

          /       |       \

       Zone 1   Zone 2   Zone 3

         |        |        |

       Copy     Copy     Copy

Data is synchronously replicated across Availability Zones.

Protects against an entire data center becoming unavailable.

GRS — Geo-Redundant Storage

Primary Region                 Secondary Region

     |                               |

    LRS                             LRS

  3 copies                        3 copies

        Total = 6 copies

Three copies exist in the primary region and three in the paired secondary region.

RA-GRS

Provides the same geo-redundancy as GRS while also allowing read access to the secondary region.

GZRS — Geo-Zone-Redundant Storage

Combines zone-level redundancy in the primary region with geo-redundancy to a secondary region.

Primary Region

  Zone 1

  Zone 2       --> ZRS

  Zone 3

       |

       | Geo Replication

       v

Secondary Region

      LRS

4. Standard Blob Storage vs. ADLS Gen2

Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2) is built on Azure Blob Storage and optimized for large-scale analytics workloads.

The major distinction is the Hierarchical Namespace (HNS).

       Standard Blob Storage          ADLS Gen2

        HNS Disabled                  HNS Enabled

             |                             |

       Flat namespace              Hierarchical namespace

             |                             |

        Blob objects                Directories + files

             |                             |

       Limited ACL model             POSIX-style ACLs

Standard Blob Storage

  • Flat namespace
  • Objects are stored within containers
  • No true directory hierarchy
  • Directory operations can require object-level operations

ADLS Gen2

  • Hierarchical Namespace enabled
  • Supports directories and nested folders
  • Supports granular file and directory permissions
  • Optimized for Big Data analytics

5. Hierarchical Namespace (HNS)

HNS transforms the flat Blob namespace into a hierarchical directory structure.

For example:

/raw

   /sales

      /2026

         /01

            orders.parquet

         /02

            orders.parquet

/processed

   /sales

      orders.parquet

One important benefit is that directory operations such as rename or move can be handled as metadata operations rather than requiring every underlying file to be copied and deleted individually.

6. POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs)

ADLS Gen2 supports granular permissions at directory and file levels.

Example:

Storage Account

      |

      +-- raw/

      |     |

      |     +-- sales/

      |     +-- finance/

      |

      +-- processed/

Different users or applications can be granted different permissions for different paths.

This makes ADLS Gen2 particularly suitable for enterprise data lakes where multiple teams require controlled access to shared data.

7. Key Takeaways — Week 18

Remember these concepts for interviews:

  1. Azure Storage Account is the foundation for Azure storage services.
  2. Hot, Cool, Archive tiers optimize storage cost according to access frequency.
  3. LRS protects against localized hardware failures.
  4. ZRS protects against Availability Zone failures.
  5. GRS protects against regional disasters.
  6. RA-GRS provides read access to the secondary region.
  7. GZRS combines zone and geographic redundancy.
  8. ADLS Gen2 = Blob Storage + Hierarchical Namespace + Data Lake capabilities.
  9. HNS enables hierarchical directories and efficient directory operations.
  10. ACLs provide granular file- and directory-level access control.

Week 19: Azure Databricks Architecture & Delta Lake Deep Dive

1. Azure Databricks

Azure Databricks is an Apache Spark-based analytics platform optimized for Azure.

It simplifies Spark-based data engineering by providing managed infrastructure, notebooks, cluster management, security integrations, and collaborative development capabilities.

Instead of manually configuring Spark infrastructure, users can provision and manage Spark environments through Databricks.

2. Azure Databricks Architecture

Azure Databricks follows a Control Plane / Data Plane architecture.

             Azure Databricks Architecture

   CONTROL PLANE                         DATA PLANE

   Databricks Managed                   Customer Azure Subscription

+--------------------------+       +------------------------------+

| Web UI                   |       | Compute Clusters              |

| Notebooks                |       | Driver + Worker Nodes         |

| Cluster Manager          | <---->| Virtual Network               |

| Job Scheduler            |       | Subnets                       |

| Workspace Configuration  |       | Azure Storage / Data Lake     |

| Control Metadata         |       | DBFS Root                     |

+--------------------------+       +------------------------------+

Control Plane

Managed by Databricks.

Includes:

  • Web application
  • Notebook interface
  • Cluster management
  • Job scheduling
  • Workspace configuration
  • Control metadata

Data Plane

Contains the actual compute and data resources.

Includes:

  • Driver nodes
  • Worker nodes
  • Virtual networks
  • Subnets
  • Azure Storage
  • Data Lake resources

3. Databricks Pricing Model

Azure Databricks involves two primary cost components:

1. Azure Infrastructure Cost

Includes infrastructure such as:

  • Virtual machines
  • Disks
  • Networking

2. Databricks Software Cost

Databricks charges based on DBUs — Databricks Units.

Therefore:

Total Databricks Cost

        =

Azure Infrastructure Cost

        +

Databricks DBU Cost

4. Databricks Cluster Types

All-Purpose Cluster

Used mainly for interactive development.

Characteristics:

  • Manually started
  • Used for notebooks and development
  • Can remain active until manually terminated
  • Higher cost if left running unnecessarily

Job Cluster

Designed for automated production workloads.

Characteristics:

  • Created when a job starts
  • Runs the workload
  • Automatically terminates after completion
  • Better suited for production pipelines

All-Purpose Cluster

Developer

   |

   v

Notebook

   |

   v

Persistent Cluster

Job Cluster

Workflow

   |

   v

Create Cluster

   |

   v

Execute Job

   |

   v

Terminate Cluster

5. Cluster Modes

Single Node Cluster

One VM acts as both:

  • Driver
  • Worker

Suitable for small workloads and single-user processing.

Standard Cluster

Contains:

             Driver

                |

       +--------+--------+

       |        |        |

    Worker   Worker   Worker

Suitable for distributed Spark processing.

High Concurrency Cluster

Designed for multiple users sharing compute resources.

Provides workload isolation and resource sharing.

6. Databricks Magic Commands

Databricks notebooks support multiple programming languages.

%python

Runs Python code.

%python

df = spark.read.parquet("/data/orders")

%sql

Runs SQL.

%sql

SELECT * FROM orders;

%scala

Runs Scala.

%r

Runs R.

%md

Creates Markdown documentation.

%fs

Provides a shortcut for file-system operations.

7. Databricks Utilities — dbutils

dbutils provides utility functions for common Databricks operations.

File System Utilities

List Files

dbutils.fs.ls("dbfs:/FileStore")

Read File Header

dbutils.fs.head("path", 65536)

Create Directory

dbutils.fs.mkdirs("path")

Move Files

dbutils.fs.mv("src", "dest", recurse=True)

Delete Files

dbutils.fs.rm("path", recurse=True)

8. Notebook Orchestration

Databricks notebooks can invoke other notebooks.

Run Another Notebook

dbutils.notebook.run(

    "path/to/notebook",

    timeout_seconds,

    arguments

)

This is useful for creating modular workflows.

Return a Value

dbutils.notebook.exit("SUCCESS")

The parent notebook can receive the returned value.

9. Databricks Widgets

Widgets allow users to provide parameters dynamically.

Examples include:

  • Dropdown
  • Combobox
  • Multiselect
  • Text input

dbutils.widgets.text(

    "environment",

    "dev",

    "Environment"

)

Retrieve the selected value:

environment = dbutils.widgets.get("environment")

This allows the same notebook to operate against different environments or datasets.

10. Azure Storage Authentication

Databricks can access Azure Storage using different authentication mechanisms.

The three approaches covered are:

Account Access Key

        |

        v

SAS Token

        |

        v

Service Principal / OAuth

11. Account Access Key

An account access key provides broad access to the storage account.

Example:

dbutils.fs.mount(

    source="wasbs://retaildb@storageaccount.blob.core.windows.net",

    mount_point="/mnt/retaildb",

    extra_configs={

        "fs.azure.account.key.storageaccount.blob.core.windows.net":

        "ACCESS_KEY"

    }

)

Limitation

Access keys can provide very broad permissions and therefore have weaker granularity from a security perspective.

12. SAS Token

A Shared Access Signature (SAS) provides more restricted access.

It can be scoped by:

  • Resource
  • Permissions
  • Validity period

Example:

spark.conf.set(

    "fs.azure.account.auth.type.storage.dfs.core.windows.net",

    "SAS"

)

SAS is more granular than an account key because access can be restricted and time-bound.

13. Service Principal / OAuth

A Service Principal represents an application identity in Azure.

It can be used with OAuth authentication and Azure RBAC/ACLs.

Typical credentials include:

Tenant ID

Client ID

Client Secret

Conceptually:

Databricks

    |

    | OAuth

    v

Azure AD / Entra ID

    |

    v

Service Principal

    |

    v

ADLS Gen2

This approach is suitable for enterprise workloads requiring fine-grained identity-based access.

14. Databricks Secret Scopes

Never hardcode sensitive credentials directly inside notebooks.

Instead of:

client_secret = "actual-secret-value"

use a secret scope:

client_secret = dbutils.secrets.get(

    "my_scope",

    "client_secret"

)

The notebook references the secret without exposing the raw credential.

15. Secret Scope Types

Azure Key Vault-Backed Secret Scope

Secrets are maintained in Azure Key Vault.

Advantages:

  • Centralized secret management
  • Can be shared with other Azure applications
  • Enterprise-oriented secret management

Databricks-Backed Secret Scope

Secrets are stored in Databricks' internal encrypted storage.

Example:

databricks secrets create-scope \

--scope demoscopedatabricksbacked

Store a secret:

databricks secrets put \

--scope demoscopedatabricksbacked \

--key storageKey

Retrieve it:

secret_key = dbutils.secrets.get(

    "demoscopedatabricksbacked",

    "storageKey"

)

16. Traditional Data Lake vs. Delta Lake

Traditional data lakes store files such as:

CSV

JSON

Parquet

However, simply storing files does not provide full database-like transaction capabilities.

Common challenges include:

  • Failed writes leaving inconsistent state
  • Concurrent reads and writes
  • Lack of schema enforcement
  • Limited UPDATE/DELETE functionality
  • No native table version history

Delta Lake addresses these limitations.

17. Delta Lake Architecture

The most important concept:

            Delta Table

                  |

        +---------+---------+

        |                   |

   Parquet Files       _delta_log

                            |

                       Transaction

                           Logs

In simplified form:

$$
\boxed{\text{Delta Table} = \text{Parquet Data Files} + \text{Transaction Log}}
$$

The transaction log is stored inside:

_delta_log/

Example:

orders/

│

├── _delta_log/

│   ├── 00000000000000000000.json

│   ├── 00000000000000000001.json

│   └── 00000000000000000002.checkpoint.parquet

│

├── part-00000.parquet

├── part-00001.parquet

└── part-00002.parquet

18. Delta Lake Transaction Log

The transaction log records changes made to the table.

It can contain operations such as:

ADD file

REMOVE file

UPDATE metadata

CHANGE schema

The transaction log allows Spark to determine which Parquet files currently belong to the table.

19. Delta Write Protocol

A simplified Delta write works like this:

1. Write new Parquet files

          |

          v

2. Verify successful write

          |

          v

3. Commit transaction log

          |

          v

4. New table version becomes visible

If the job fails before the transaction is committed, the incomplete files are not considered part of the valid table state.

This is a key mechanism behind Delta Lake's transactional guarantees.

20. Delta Read Protocol

When Spark reads a Delta table:

Delta Table

     |

     v

_delta_log

     |

     v

Determine valid files

     |

     v

Read relevant Parquet files

     |

     v

Return current table state

The transaction log tells the reader which files are active.

21. How UPDATE Works in Delta Lake

Delta Lake does not directly modify a row inside an existing Parquet file.

Suppose:

part-001.parquet

contains a row that needs modification.

Conceptually:

Existing file

part-001.parquet

       |

       | Read + modify

       v

New file

part-005.parquet

The transaction log then records:

REMOVE part-001.parquet

ADD    part-005.parquet

The old file is no longer part of the current table snapshot.

22. How DELETE Works

Similarly, a delete can involve rewriting the relevant data into a new file.

part-001.parquet

       |

       v

Remove deleted rows

       |

       v

part-006.parquet

Transaction log:

REMOVE part-001.parquet

ADD    part-006.parquet

23. COPY INTO

COPY INTO provides an idempotent mechanism for loading external files into Delta tables.

Example:

COPY INTO retaildb.ordersdelta

FROM '/mnt/retaildb/raw_incoming/'

FILEFORMAT = CSV

FORMAT_OPTIONS (

    'header' = 'true',

    'inferSchema' = 'true'

);

It is useful when files arrive incrementally in an external location.

24. Schema Enforcement

Schema enforcement prevents incompatible data from being written into a Delta table.

For example, if the table expects:

customer_id : INT

order_status : STRING

and incoming data has incompatible structure, the write can be rejected.

This helps prevent accidental schema corruption.

25. Schema Evolution

Schema evolution allows the target schema to expand when new columns appear.

Example:

df_new_cols.write \

    .mode("append") \

    .format("delta") \

    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \

    .save("/mnt/retaildb/delta/orders.delta")

Difference

Schema Enforcement

        ↓

Reject incompatible schema

Schema Evolution

        ↓

Allow compatible schema changes

26. Delta Table Constraints

Delta tables can enforce data quality rules.

NOT NULL

ALTER TABLE retaildb.ordersdelta

ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET NOT NULL;

CHECK Constraint

ALTER TABLE retaildb.ordersdelta

ADD CONSTRAINT status_ck

CHECK (

    order_status IN

    ('CLOSED',

     'COMPLETE',

     'PROCESSING',

     'PENDING',

     'ON_HOLD',

     'CANCELED')

);

27. Delta Lake Time Travel

Delta Lake maintains table history through transaction versions.

View History

DESCRIBE HISTORY retaildb.ordersdelta;

Query an Older Version

SELECT *

FROM retaildb.ordersdelta

VERSION AS OF 2;

Query by Timestamp

SELECT *

FROM retaildb.ordersdelta

TIMESTAMP AS OF '2023-09-23T14:01:01.000+0000';

This makes historical analysis and auditing possible.

28. Restore a Delta Table

If an accidental modification occurs, a previous version can be restored.

RESTORE TABLE retaildb.ordersdelta

TO VERSION AS OF 0;

Conceptually:

Version 0

   |

Version 1

   |

Version 2

   |

Version 3  ← Current

   |

   | Restore

   v

Version 0 ← Current state

Week 20: Databricks Lakehouse Architecture, Delta Engine & Medallion Architecture

1. Databricks Lakehouse Architecture Overview

The Lakehouse Architecture combines the scalability and cost efficiency of Data Lakes with the reliability, ACID transactions, and performance features traditionally associated with Data Warehouses.

Traditional 2-Tier Architecture

                    [ Modern 2-Tier Architecture Limitations ]

   Data Sources ---> Data Lake (100 TB Raw/Parquet) ---> Data Warehouse (20 TB Relational)

                    (Data Science & ML Workloads)        (BI & Reporting Workloads)

                                        \                       /

                                         +-- ETL Duplication --+

                                         +-- Increased Costs  --+

                                         +-- Data Staleness   --+

The traditional architecture often requires maintaining both a Data Lake and a Data Warehouse, resulting in:

  • Duplicate data storage
  • Additional ETL pipelines
  • Increased infrastructure and operational costs
  • Data synchronization challenges
  • Potential data staleness

Unified Lakehouse Architecture

                       [ Unified Lakehouse Architecture ]

                             +---------------------------------+

                             |     Databricks Lakehouse        |

                             |   (Single Source of Truth)      |

                             +---------------------------------+

                             | Photon Engine & Delta Engine    |

                             |        Query Acceleration       |

                             +---------------------------------+

                             | Delta Lake (ACID & Trans Logs)  |

                             |        Reliability Layer        |

                             +---------------------------------+

                             | Data Lake (S3, ADLS Gen2, GCS)  |

                             |        Cheap Open Storage       |

                             +---------------------------------+

                                     /             \

                                    v               v

                         Data Science / ML       BI & Reporting

The Lakehouse combines:

  1. Data Lake Storage — S3, ADLS Gen2, or GCS for scalable and inexpensive storage.
  2. Delta Lake — Provides ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and transaction history.
  3. Delta/Photon Engine — Provides optimized query execution and performance improvements.
  4. Unified Access — Supports Data Science, Machine Learning, Streaming, BI, and reporting workloads.

Key Architectural Advantages

1. Eliminates Data Duplication

A Lakehouse reduces the need to maintain separate storage and reporting copies of the same data.

2. Unified Workloads

The same data platform can support:

  • Machine Learning
  • Data Science
  • Streaming
  • Business Intelligence
  • Reporting
  • Analytical workloads

3. Open Data Formats

Lakehouse storage continues to use open formats such as Parquet, while Delta Lake adds transaction-management capabilities through the _delta_log.

Key Concept

Data Lake

   +

Delta Lake

   +

Query Optimization

   =

Lakehouse

2. Delta Engine Performance & Optimization Techniques

The Delta Engine is a high-performance execution layer designed to improve the performance of reads, writes, joins, and aggregations over Delta Lake data.

Major optimization techniques include:

  1. Data Skipping
  2. File Compaction
  3. Z-Ordering
  4. Delta Cache
  5. Auto-Optimization
  6. Photon Execution Engine

                      [ Delta Engine Optimization Pillars ]

  1. Data Skipping          2. Compaction           3. Multi-Dim Clustering

       (Stats)                (OPTIMIZE)                 (Z-Order)

 +--------------------+   +--------------------+   +-------------------------+

 | Uses min/max       |   | Merges small files |   | Co-locates related data |

 | metadata to bypass |   | into larger files  |   | into the same files for |

 | irrelevant files.  |   | for better reads.  |   | better data skipping.   |

 +--------------------+   +--------------------+   +-------------------------+

2.1 Data Skipping via Statistics

Delta Lake maintains file-level statistics such as:

  • Minimum values
  • Maximum values
  • Other file-level metadata

These statistics are recorded in the Delta transaction log.

Example

Suppose a query executes:

SELECT *

FROM orders

WHERE total_amt = 234;

Delta can inspect the file statistics before reading the actual Parquet files.

If a file contains:

File A → min = 1, max = 100

File B → min = 101, max = 200

File C → min = 201, max = 300

Then the query can skip Files A and B because 234 cannot exist in those files.

Query: total_amt = 234

File A: 1 ───────── 100       SKIP

File B: 101 ─────── 200       SKIP

File C: 201 ─────── 300       READ

Benefit

Data skipping reduces unnecessary physical file scans and improves query performance.

Delta vs. Standard Parquet

The source material highlights that Delta maintains centralized transaction-log metadata, allowing the query engine to use statistics for file skipping before reading the underlying data files.

2.2 Delta Cache vs. Spark Cache

Delta Cache and Spark Cache operate at different levels.

Delta Cache

Delta Cache stores remote Data Lake files on the local SSD storage of worker nodes in an optimized intermediate format.

Characteristics:

  • Works with Parquet/Delta formats.
  • Uses local SSD storage.
  • Reduces repeated remote storage reads.
  • Automatically handles stale cached blocks when source files change or clusters restart.

Example configuration:

spark.conf.set(

    "spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled",

    "true"

)

Spark Cache

Spark .cache() stores DataFrame/RDD representations in memory, using JVM heap or off-heap memory depending on the configuration.

Comparison

Feature

Delta Cache

Spark Cache

Storage

Local SSD

Memory / JVM heap / off-heap

Primary Purpose

Cache remote data files

Cache processed DataFrame/RDD data

Format

Parquet / Delta

DataFrame / RDD representation

Managed By

Databricks I/O caching

Spark caching mechanism

Main Benefit

Reduces remote storage reads

Avoids repeated computation

2.3 File Compaction — Bin Packing & OPTIMIZE

Continuous operations such as:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE
  • Streaming writes

can generate many small files.

A large number of small files causes:

  • More file-open operations
  • Increased metadata overhead
  • More task scheduling overhead
  • Slower query execution

Solution: Bin Packing

The OPTIMIZE command combines smaller files into larger, query-friendly files.

OPTIMIZE taxidb.trips_delta;

Conceptually:

Before OPTIMIZE

File 1 → 10 MB

File 2 → 15 MB

File 3 → 20 MB

File 4 → 12 MB

File 5 → 18 MB

          ↓

       OPTIMIZE

          ↓

File A → Large consolidated file

File B → Large consolidated file

The source material describes optimized physical file blocks as being up to approximately 1 GB.

Important

OPTIMIZE performs file compaction, but by itself it does not provide multidimensional clustering.

For multidimensional data organization, use Z-Ordering.

2.4 Z-Ordering — Multidimensional Clustering

Z-Ordering is a data co-location technique that organizes related rows into the same physical file groups.

It is particularly useful for columns frequently used in:

  • WHERE filters
  • Joins
  • GROUP BY operations

Example

Suppose a table contains employee IDs.

Without Z-Ordering:

File 1 → emp_id: 1, 5, 8

File 2 → emp_id: 2, 4, 9

File 3 → emp_id: 3, 6, 10

Query:

WHERE emp_id = 4

Potentially all three files need to be examined.

With Z-Ordering:

File 1 → emp_id: 1, 2, 3

File 2 → emp_id: 4, 5, 6

File 3 → emp_id: 8, 9, 10

The query can narrow the search to File 2.

Z-Order Example

OPTIMIZE taxidb.trips_delta_new

ZORDER BY (passenger_count);

Key Difference

OPTIMIZE

   ↓

Compacts small files

ZORDER

   ↓

Improves data co-location and data skipping

Z-Ordering is therefore typically used together with OPTIMIZE.

2.5 Vacuuming Old Files — VACUUM

Delta Lake maintains historical table versions to support:

  • Time Travel
  • Snapshot isolation
  • Historical queries

As a result, old Parquet files may remain on storage even after they are no longer part of the current active table state.

VACUUM

The VACUUM command permanently removes physical data files that:

  1. Are no longer referenced by the active Delta transaction log.
  2. Are older than the configured retention period.

The source material specifies the default retention period as 7 days.

Current Delta Table

        |

        +---- Active files → KEEP

        |

        +---- Old unreferenced files → VACUUM

Important Impact

Once historical files are permanently removed using VACUUM, Time Travel may no longer be able to access table versions that depend on those files.

Dry Run

VACUUM taxidb.trips_delta

RETAIN 1 HOURS

DRY RUN;

Permanent Deletion

VACUUM taxidb.trips_delta

RETAIN 1 HOURS;

Retention Safety Check

For retention below 7 days:

SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false;

Important Warning

Reducing retention can remove files required for historical reads. Therefore, short retention periods should be used carefully.

2.6 Auto-Optimization Features

Delta Lake can automatically optimize file sizes during and after writes.

There are two major capabilities:

1. Optimized Writes

Optimized Writes coalesce smaller partitions before writing data to storage.

The goal is to create larger and more efficient data files.

2. Auto Compaction

Auto Compaction performs lightweight file consolidation after writes when a partition accumulates a significant number of small files.

Enabling Auto-Optimization

ALTER TABLE taxidb.trips_delta

SET TBLPROPERTIES (

    'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true',

    'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true'

);

Conceptual Flow

Small Input Partitions

        |

        v

Optimized Writes

        |

        v

Better-Sized Files

        |

        v

Auto Compaction

        |

        v

Reduced Small-File Problem

2.7 Photon Execution Engine

Photon is a native vectorized execution engine implemented in C++ and designed to accelerate Spark SQL and DataFrame workloads in Databricks.

It is particularly useful for:

  • Large joins
  • Complex aggregations
  • Compute-intensive SQL
  • Large-scale analytical workloads

Compatibility

Photon works with:

  • Parquet
  • Delta Lake

Key Concept

Spark SQL / DataFrame Workload

             |

             v

       Photon Engine

             |

             v

Vectorized Native Execution

             |

             v

Improved Query Performance

Photon can be enabled through the Use Photon Acceleration option when configuring appropriate Databricks compute.

3. Delta Architecture — Medallion Design Pattern

The Medallion Architecture organizes Lakehouse data into progressively refined layers.

The three primary layers are:

BRONZE → SILVER → GOLD

Each layer improves data quality and usability.

                    [ Medallion Architecture Workflow ]

  Raw Sources       BRONZE             SILVER              GOLD

 +-----------+    +-------------+    +-------------+    +---------------+

 | Streaming |    | Raw         |    | Cleaned &    |    | Aggregated    |

 | Batch CSV |--->| Ingestion   |--->| Validated    |--->| Business      |

 | RDBMS DBs |    | Append-Only |    | Delta Tables |    | Data / BI     |

 +-----------+    +-------------+    +-------------+    +---------------+

3.1 Bronze Layer

The Bronze layer contains raw ingested data.

Characteristics:

  • Raw data
  • Minimal transformation
  • Often append-only
  • Preserves source information
  • Can contain ingestion metadata

Examples of metadata:

filename

createdon

ingestion timestamp

Purpose

The Bronze layer acts as a raw audit archive and provides a source-of-truth representation of ingested data.

3.2 Silver Layer

The Silver layer contains cleaned and structured data.

Typical operations include:

  • Data validation
  • Filtering invalid records
  • Deduplication
  • Type conversion
  • Data cleansing
  • Schema standardization
  • Business-rule application

Purpose

Silver data is suitable for:

  • Machine Learning
  • Data Science
  • Operational analytics
  • Further business transformations

3.3 Gold Layer

The Gold layer contains business-ready data.

Typical operations include:

  • Aggregations
  • Business calculations
  • Domain-specific transformations
  • Reporting-oriented structures

Purpose

Gold data is primarily used for:

  • BI dashboards
  • Executive reporting
  • Business analytics
  • Analytical applications

Medallion Layer Comparison

Layer

Data State

Main Purpose

Typical Consumers

Bronze

Raw / minimally processed

Source archive & audit

Engineering

Silver

Cleaned / validated / structured

Analytics & ML preparation

Data Scientists / Engineers

Gold

Aggregated / business-ready

Reporting & BI

Business Users / Analysts

Easy Way to Remember

BRONZE = Raw

SILVER = Refined

GOLD   = Business Ready

4. Change Data Feed (CDF) Mechanics

Change Data Feed (CDF) tracks row-level changes occurring between versions of a Delta table.

It can capture:

  • INSERT
  • UPDATE
  • DELETE

CDF provides metadata describing the type and version of each change.

                     [ Change Data Feed Metadata ]

+------------+---------------------+-------------------+----------------------+

| Operation  | _change_type        | _commit_version   | _commit_timestamp    |

+------------+---------------------+-------------------+----------------------+

| INSERT     | insert              | 1                 | 2026-07-25...        |

| UPDATE     | update_preimage     | 2                 | 2026-07-25...        |

| UPDATE     | update_postimage    | 2                 | 2026-07-25...        |

| DELETE     | delete              | 3                 | 2026-07-25...        |

+------------+---------------------+-------------------+----------------------+

CDF Change Types

Change

_change_type

Insert

insert

Update — old value

update_preimage

Update — new value

update_postimage

Delete

delete

4.1 Enabling CDF During Table Creation

CREATE TABLE retaildb.orders (

    order_id INT,

    order_date STRING,

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING

)

USING DELTA

TBLPROPERTIES (

    delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true

);

4.2 Enabling CDF on an Existing Table

ALTER TABLE retaildb.orders

SET TBLPROPERTIES (

    delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true

);

4.3 Enabling CDF as a Session Default

SET spark.databricks.delta.properties.defaults.enableChangeDataFeed = true;

5. Querying Change Data Feed

The table_changes() function can retrieve changes beginning from a specified Delta table version.

From a Specific Version

SELECT *

FROM table_changes('retaildb.orders', 1);

This reads changes beginning from version 1 through the latest available version.

Between Two Versions

SELECT *

FROM table_changes('retaildb.orders', 1, 3);

This retrieves changes across the specified inclusive version range.

CDF Storage

The source material specifies that non-insert DML operations such as:

  • UPDATE
  • DELETE
  • MERGE

can record change events in the _change_data directory within the Delta table path.

6. End-to-End Medallion Pipeline Implementation

The following example demonstrates an enterprise-style Medallion pipeline using:

  • COPY INTO
  • Change Data Feed
  • table_changes()
  • MERGE INTO
  • Delta tables
  • Generated columns
  • Aggregations

Step 1: Create Database

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS retaildb;

Step 2: Create Bronze Layer

The Bronze layer stores raw order data along with ingestion metadata.

CREATE TABLE retaildb.orders_bronze (

    order_id INT,

    order_date STRING,

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING,

    filename STRING,

    createdon TIMESTAMP

)

USING DELTA

LOCATION "dbfs:/FileStore/data/orders_bronze.delta"

PARTITIONED BY (order_status)

TBLPROPERTIES (

    delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true

);

Step 3: Ingest Data Using COPY INTO

COPY INTO is used for idempotent ingestion of new external files.

COPY INTO retaildb.orders_bronze

FROM (

    SELECT

        order_id::INT,

        order_date::STRING,

        customer_id::INT,

        order_status::STRING,

        INPUT_FILE_NAME() AS filename,

        CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() AS createdon

    FROM 'dbfs:/FileStore/raw'

)

FILEFORMAT = CSV

FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true');

Step 4: Create Silver Layer

The Silver table contains cleaned and structured data.

CREATE TABLE retaildb.orders_silver (

    order_id INT,

    order_date DATE,

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING,

    order_year INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (YEAR(order_date)),

    order_month INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (MONTH(order_date)),

    createdon TIMESTAMP,

    modifiedon TIMESTAMP

)

USING DELTA

LOCATION "dbfs:/FileStore/data/orders_silver.delta"

PARTITIONED BY (order_status)

TBLPROPERTIES (

    delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true

);

Step 5: Read Bronze Changes and Merge into Silver

Create a temporary view over the Bronze Change Data Feed:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW orders_bronze_changes AS

SELECT *

FROM table_changes('retaildb.orders_bronze', 1)

WHERE order_id > 0

  AND customer_id > 0

  AND order_status IN (

      'PAYMENT_REVIEW',

      'PROCESSING',

      'CLOSED',

      'SUSPECTED_FRAUD',

      'COMPLETE',

      'PENDING',

      'CANCELLED',

      'PENDING_PAYMENT'

  );

Then merge the changes into Silver:

MERGE INTO retaildb.orders_silver tgt

USING orders_bronze_changes src

   ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN

  UPDATE SET

    tgt.order_status = src.order_status,

    tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id,

    tgt.modifiedon = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN

  INSERT (

      order_id,

      order_date,

      customer_id,

      order_status,

      createdon,

      modifiedon

  )

  VALUES (

      src.order_id,

      TO_DATE(src.order_date),

      src.customer_id,

      src.order_status,

      CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(),

      CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()

  );

Logical Flow

Bronze CDF

    |

    v

Filter Valid Records

    |

    v

table_changes()

    |

    v

MERGE INTO

    |

    +------ MATCHED ------> UPDATE Silver

    |

    +--- NOT MATCHED -----> INSERT Silver

7. Create the Gold Layer

The Gold layer contains aggregated business-level information.

CREATE TABLE retaildb.orders_gold (

    customer_id INT,

    order_status STRING,

    order_year INT,

    num_orders INT

)

USING DELTA

LOCATION "dbfs:/FileStore/data/orders_gold.delta"

TBLPROPERTIES (

    delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true

);

Step 8: Populate Gold Layer

The Silver layer is aggregated to create the business-ready Gold dataset.

INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE retaildb.orders_gold

SELECT

    customer_id,

    order_status,

    order_year,

    COUNT(order_id) AS num_orders

FROM retaildb.orders_silver

GROUP BY

    customer_id,

    order_status,

    order_year;

9. Week 20 — Interview Revision Points

Lakehouse

Q: What is a Lakehouse?

A Lakehouse combines the scalability and low-cost storage of a Data Lake with the reliability and analytical capabilities traditionally associated with Data Warehouses.

Delta Lake

Q: Why is Delta Lake important?

Delta Lake adds ACID transactions, schema management, DML capabilities, transaction history, and Time Travel to Data Lake storage.

Data Skipping

Q: What is Data Skipping?

Data Skipping uses file-level statistics such as minimum and maximum values to avoid scanning files that cannot satisfy a query predicate.

OPTIMIZE

Q: Why do we use OPTIMIZE?

OPTIMIZE compacts small files into larger files, reducing file-management and query overhead.

Z-Ordering

Q: What is Z-Ordering?

Z-Ordering co-locates related data based on selected columns to improve data skipping for frequently filtered or queried columns.

VACUUM

Q: Why is VACUUM used?

VACUUM permanently removes old, unreferenced physical files that are beyond the configured retention period.

Photon

Q: What is Photon?

Photon is a native vectorized execution engine designed to accelerate Spark SQL and DataFrame workloads.

Medallion Architecture

Q: Explain Bronze, Silver, and Gold.

BRONZE → Raw ingestion

SILVER → Cleaned and validated data

GOLD   → Business-ready aggregated data

Change Data Feed

Q: What does CDF provide?

CDF provides row-level change information for operations such as:

INSERT

UPDATE

DELETE

It can be queried using:

table_changes()

Week 20 Key Takeaways

  1. Lakehouse unifies Data Lake and Data Warehouse capabilities.
  2. Delta Lake provides reliability and transactional capabilities on Data Lake storage.
  3. Data Skipping avoids unnecessary file scans using file-level statistics.
  4. OPTIMIZE addresses small-file problems through compaction.
  5. Z-Ordering improves data locality and data skipping.
  6. VACUUM removes old unreferenced physical files.
  7. Delta Cache caches remote data on local SSD storage.
  8. Photon accelerates compute-intensive SQL and DataFrame workloads.
  9. Bronze stores raw data.
  10. Silver stores cleaned and validated data.
  11. Gold stores business-ready aggregated data.
  12. CDF tracks row-level changes between Delta table versions.
  13. COPY INTO supports incremental/idempotent file ingestion.
  14. MERGE INTO is used to synchronize changes between datasets.
  15. A common enterprise pattern is:

Bronze

CDF

Aggregation

Week 21: Databricks Unity Catalog & Enterprise Data Governance

1. Introduction to Unity Catalog

Unity Catalog is a unified, fine-grained data governance solution for data assets such as tables, views, volumes, and files within the Databricks Lakehouse Platform.

Workspace-Level Governance vs. Unity Catalog

             WORKSPACE-LEVEL GOVERNANCE

                         vs.

              CENTRALIZED UNITY CATALOG

 Legacy Workspace Model                 Unity Catalog Model

 Workspace 1        Workspace 2         Workspace 1      Workspace 2

     │                  │                     \              /

 Local Metastore    Local Metastore           \            /

     │                  │                      \          /

 Isolated schemas   Isolated schemas       Centralized Unity

 and permissions    and permissions           Catalog Metastore

Limitations of Workspace-Level Governance

Without Unity Catalog:

  • Metastores are isolated within individual Databricks workspaces.
  • Access control policies are workspace-specific.
  • User directories are siloed.
  • Tables and views registered in one workspace may not be directly available in another.
  • Organizations may need duplicate data registration and fragmented security policies.

Key Pillars of Unity Catalog

  1. Centralized Metadata Management
    A single metastore can be associated with multiple Databricks workspaces.
  2. Standard ANSI SQL Security Model
    Access to database objects can be controlled using SQL commands such as:

GRANT SELECT ON TABLE ...

  1. Fine-Grained Auditing
    User-level query activity, table access, and administrative actions can be audited.
  2. Data Lineage
    Tracks table- and column-level relationships to understand how data moves through pipelines.
  3. Data Discovery
    Users can search for datasets and other data assets using workspace discovery tools.
  4. Delta Sharing
    Provides a mechanism for securely sharing datasets with external parties without copying the underlying data.

2. Setting Up and Configuring a Unity Catalog Metastore

Unity Catalog on Azure requires integration between Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, an Azure Databricks Access Connector, and the Unity Catalog metastore.

             Azure ADLS Gen2 Storage Account

                       │

                       │ Storage Blob Data

                       │ Contributor

                       ▼

        Azure Databricks Access Connector

              System-Assigned Identity

                       │

                       │ Access

                       ▼

              Unity Catalog Metastore

                       │

                       ▼

              Databricks Workspaces

Step 1: Create ADLS Gen2 Storage

Create an Azure Storage Account with:

  • Hierarchical Namespace enabled
  • A container for Unity Catalog storage

Example:

Storage Account:

ttunitycatalogsa

Container:

unityroot

Step 2: Create an Access Connector

Create an Access Connector for Azure Databricks in Azure.

The Access Connector uses a system-assigned managed identity, eliminating the need to manually manage storage access keys or Key Vault secrets for this connection.

Step 3: Assign IAM Permissions

On the ADLS Gen2 storage account:

Access Control (IAM) → Add Role Assignment

Assign:

Storage Blob Data Contributor

to the managed identity of the Access Connector.

Step 4: Create the Unity Catalog Metastore

From the Databricks Account Console, an Account Admin can create the metastore.

Configure:

  • Metastore name
  • Region
  • ADLS Gen2 root storage path
  • Azure Databricks Access Connector resource

Example storage path:

abfss://unityroot@ttunitycatalogsa.dfs.core.windows.net/

Step 5: Attach the Metastore

Finally, attach the newly created Unity Catalog metastore to the required Databricks workspaces.

3. Unity Catalog Three-Level Namespace

Unity Catalog uses a three-level namespace:

catalog.schema.table

The same structure applies to views and other supported objects.

Hierarchy

                             │

              │                             │

        │           │                 │           │

   SCHEMA:       SCHEMA:          SCHEMA:      SCHEMA:

   retaildb        hrdb            retaildb      hrdb

        │                             │

 TABLE     VIEW                 TABLE     TABLE

 sales    v_sales               sales     orders

Namespace Components

1. Catalog

The top-level logical grouping.

Catalogs can be organized according to:

  • Environment
  • dev
  • stage
  • prod
  • Business domain
  • finance
  • marketing
  • retail

2. Schema

The second level, traditionally equivalent to a database.

Schemas contain:

  • Tables
  • Views
  • Volumes

3. Tables / Views / Volumes

The lowest level contains the actual data assets or logical abstractions over data.

4. Managed Tables vs. External Tables

Feature

Managed Tables

External Tables

Data Location

Unity Catalog-managed storage location

Custom external cloud location

Typical Format

Delta

Delta, Parquet, CSV, ORC

Data Ownership

Managed by Unity Catalog

Data remains in external storage

DROP TABLE

Removes metadata and managed data according to Unity Catalog lifecycle behavior

Removes metadata; underlying files remain

Use Case

Databricks-managed data

Data shared with external systems

Example external location:

abfss://data@storageaccount.dfs.core.windows.net/

When to Use Managed Tables

Useful when:

  • Databricks manages the complete data lifecycle.
  • Data is primarily consumed through Databricks.
  • Centralized governance is desired.

When to Use External Tables

Useful when:

  • Data already exists in cloud storage.
  • Multiple systems need to access the same files.
  • External applications or engines also consume the data.

5. Unity Catalog Table Access Permissions

To access:

prod.retaildb.sales

the user needs permissions at each level of the hierarchy.

Catalog

   ▼

USAGE on Catalog

GRANT USAGE ON CATALOG prod

TO `developer-grp`;
