Weeks 28 & 29: Spark Structured Streaming — Micro-Batch Engine, Triggers, Watermarking & Stateful Processing

1. Batch vs. Stream Processing Paradigms

Data processing engines handle data using two fundamental paradigms depending on volume, arrival frequency, and latency requirements.

Processing Paradigm Trade-Offs

Batch Processing

Stream Processing

Processing on bounded, historical datasets at rest

Continuous processing on unbounded streams in motion

Latency: Minutes, Hours, Days

Latency: Seconds, Sub-seconds

High throughput, bulk groups

Immediate insights, incremental processing

Ideal for BI and standard ETL

Ideal for fraud detection and monitoring

Comparative Analysis

Feature

Batch Processing

Stream / Real-Time Processing

Data Scope

Bounded historical files collected over a specific time window

Unbounded continuous data streams arriving dynamically

Data Latency

High tolerance for delays — minutes to days

Strict low-latency demands — seconds to sub-seconds

Computation Model

Scheduled jobs process entire datasets at rest as a single block

Continuous processing on incremental micro-batches or individual events

Primary Use Cases

Financial reporting, end-of-day reconciliation, historical ML training

Real-time credit card fraud detection, website log monitoring, IoT sensor alerts

Hadoop MapReduce vs. Apache Spark

  • Hadoop MapReduce: Exclusively designed for disk-bound batch processing; cannot handle real-time streaming data natively.
  • Apache Spark: A unified general-purpose engine supporting both batch workflows and real-time streaming through its Structured Streaming framework.

2. Spark Structured Streaming Fundamentals & Architecture

Spark Structured Streaming is a scalable, fault-tolerant stream processing engine built on top of the Spark SQL Catalyst engine.

It processes continuous streams as an unbounded table that continuously appends new incoming records.

Unbounded Table Conceptual Model

Stream Input

     |

     v

[ Record 1 | Record 2 | Record 3 | Record N... ]

     |              (Appended continuously)

     v

[ Continuous Execution Engine ]

     |

     v

[ Result Table (Incremental) ]

     |

     v

Append Mode / Update Mode / Complete Mode

     |

     v

Target Sink

Architectural APIs: Legacy DStreams vs. Structured Streaming

1. DStreams API — Spark Streaming

  • Low-level RDD-based streaming abstraction.
  • Does not provide Catalyst SQL optimizations.
  • Does not provide the typed DataFrame-based programming model available in Structured Streaming.

2. Structured Streaming API

  • High-level DataFrame/SQL API.
  • Provides a unified programming model.
  • Batch and streaming applications can share the same transformation logic.

Key Engineering Challenges in Streaming

When operating micro-batch processing over small intervals, standard frameworks encounter four core obstacles:

  1. Backpressure: System performance degrades if incoming batch frequencies outpace the job's processing throughput.
  2. Late-Arriving Records: Network delays can cause events generated at 10:08 AM to physically arrive at 10:20 AM.
  3. State Management: Running aggregations, such as historical user totals, must be tracked across continuous micro-batches.
  4. Fault Tolerance: Intermediate state must be recovered without losing data or creating duplicates after application crashes.

Spark Structured Streaming automates state persistence, micro-batch looping, and checkpoint recovery so developers can focus primarily on business logic.

3. Streaming Data Pipeline Lifecycle: Read, Process, Write

A Spark Structured Streaming application follows a three-stage pipeline:

DataStreamReader (.readStream)

            |

            v

DataFrame Transformations

            |

            v

DataStreamWriter (.writeStream)

Complete Example

# 1. READ: DataStreamReader

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, split, col

spark = SparkSession.builder \

    .appName("StreamingWordCount") \

    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 3) \

    .getOrCreate()

lines = spark.readStream \

    .format("socket") \

    .option("host", "localhost") \

    .option("port", 9999) \

    .load()

# 2. PROCESS: Standard DataFrame Transformations

words = lines.select(explode(split(col("value"), " ")).alias("word"))

word_counts = words.groupBy("word").count()

# 3. WRITE: DataStreamWriter with Checkpointing

query = word_counts.writeStream \

    .outputMode("complete") \

    .format("console") \

    .option("checkpointLocation", "/path/to/checkpoint/dir") \

    .start()

query.awaitTermination()

Streaming Input Sources

File Source

Reads new files landing in a target directory as a continuous stream.

Supported formats include:

  • CSV
  • JSON
  • ORC
  • Parquet
  • Text

Files are processed according to modification time, or in reverse order when latestFirst=true.

Kafka Source

Reads continuous streaming records directly from Apache Kafka topics.

Socket Source

Reads UTF-8 text lines from a network socket using host:port.

Primarily designed for testing and prototyping because it lacks end-to-end replayability.

4. Output Modes

Spark Structured Streaming provides three output modes controlling how result data is written to external sinks.

Output Mode

Behavior

Aggregation Constraint

Append Mode

Only new rows from the latest micro-batch are written to the sink

Does not support streaming aggregations unless a Watermark is defined

Update Mode

Only rows modified or newly inserted in the latest micro-batch are output

Supported with or without aggregations

Complete Mode

Entire updated result table is rewritten on every micro-batch

Requires streaming aggregations such as groupBy or window

1. Append Mode

Only new rows added since the previous batch are written.

APPEND MODE

+-----------------------+

| Only NEW rows added   |

| since last batch are  |

| written.              |

+-----------------------+

2. Update Mode

Only newly inserted or updated rows are written.

This is useful for upsert-style processing.

UPDATE MODE

+-----------------------+

| Only UPDATED / NEW    |

| rows are written.     |

+-----------------------+

3. Complete Mode

The entire updated result table is written on every micro-batch.

COMPLETE MODE

+-----------------------+

| ENTIRE updated result |

| table is rewritten.   |

+-----------------------+

5. Trigger Strategies & Micro-Batch Execution Models

Triggers determine the timing and execution frequency of streaming micro-batches.

Trigger Strategy Types

Trigger

Behavior

Unspecified / Default

Executes the next batch immediately after the current batch completes if new data exists

Fixed Interval

Executes micro-batches at defined time intervals

Available Now

Processes all available data across sequential micro-batches and then terminates

5.1 Unspecified / Default Trigger

With the default trigger, execution continues in a continuous back-to-back fashion.

As soon as one micro-batch finishes, the next batch evaluates immediately if new data is available.

# Default trigger

query = df.writeStream \

    .outputMode("append") \

    .format("parquet") \

    .start()

5.2 Fixed Interval Trigger

A fixed processing interval defines how frequently Spark attempts to execute micro-batches.

# Fixed interval trigger — every 10 seconds

query = df.writeStream \

    .trigger(processingTime="10 seconds") \

    .outputMode("append") \

    .start()

Execution Behavior

Scenario A:

If a batch is configured for a 5-minute interval but completes in 2 minutes, the engine waits for the remaining 3 minutes before starting the next micro-batch.

Scenario B:

If a batch takes 8 minutes and exceeds the configured 5-minute interval, the next batch begins immediately after the previous batch completes.

5.3 Available Now Trigger

availableNow=True processes all currently available incoming data through sequential micro-batches and then automatically terminates the streaming query.

query = df.writeStream \

    .trigger(availableNow=True) \

    .outputMode("append") \

    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/telemetry/checkpoints") \

    .start()

Key Advantage

Available Now combines:

  • Incremental state tracking
  • Streaming checkpointing
  • On-demand batch-style execution
  • Automatic cluster/resource release after processing

This makes it useful when continuous streaming is unnecessary but incremental processing is still desired.

6. Fault Tolerance & Exactly-Once Processing Semantics

To maintain fault tolerance during infrastructure failures or cluster restarts, streaming applications need to support Exactly-Once Semantics.

The objective is to ensure that input records are neither skipped nor duplicated in the final output.

Exactly-Once Execution Architecture

CHECKPOINT LOCATION

        |

        | Tracks offsets and state

        v

REPLAYABLE SOURCE

        |

        | Re-read data after failure

        v

IDEMPOTENT SINK

        |

        v

Final Consistent Output

Four Requirements for Exactly-Once Processing

1. Checkpointing & Write-Ahead Logs (WAL)

The streaming engine stores:

  • Read offsets
  • Metadata
  • State updates

inside a persistent checkpointLocation.

After failure, the application uses the checkpoint to resume execution from the last committed offset.

2. Replayable Source

The source must support re-reading historical uncommitted data from explicit offsets.

Examples:

  • Kafka
  • ADLS / Data Lake files

A socket source is non-replayable.

3. Deterministic Computation

Processing the same input repeatedly should generate the same output.

Example:

sqrt(4) → 2

is deterministic.

Dynamic timestamps and currency conversions may be non-deterministic.

4. Idempotent Sink

The sink must handle re-executed micro-batches safely.

Common approaches include:

  • Overwriting previous records
  • Upserting using MERGE
  • Delta Lake MERGE INTO
  • foreachBatch

7. Stateful Processing & State Store Management

Streaming operations can be classified as Stateless or Stateful.

Stateless Transformations

Stateful Transformations

select

groupBy

filter

Streaming joins

map

Windowing

explode

Stateful aggregations

Each record can be evaluated independently

Requires historical information across micro-batches

State Store

A State Store maintains intermediate values across micro-batches for stateful operations.

The study material describes the State Store as an in-memory key-value store on worker nodes backed by technologies such as RocksDB or HDFS.

Memory Management Risk

Consider an unbounded aggregation:

groupBy(customer_id)

If the stream contains hundreds of millions of active customer IDs without time limits, state can continuously grow and eventually result in executor or driver Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures.

Mitigation

Use:

  • Time-bounded windows
  • Watermarking
  • State eviction

These allow Spark to remove old state from the State Store.

8. Windowing Aggregations & Late-Data Handling

Windowed aggregations calculate metrics over time-bound buckets based on Event Time rather than Processing/Trigger Time.

Event Time vs. Processing Time

Event Time:
The timestamp representing when the event actually occurred.

Processing Time:
The timestamp representing when Spark receives/processes the event.

This distinction is critical because events can arrive late.

8.1 Tumbling Window

A tumbling window consists of fixed-size, contiguous, non-overlapping intervals.

Example:

10:00 ─────── 10:15

10:15 ─────── 10:30

10:30 ─────── 10:45

A 15-minute tumbling window creates independent 15-minute buckets.

8.2 Sliding Window

A sliding window consists of overlapping intervals.

Example:

Window Duration = 15 minutes

Slide Duration  = 5 minutes

10:00 ─────── 10:15

       10:05 ─────── 10:20

              10:10 ─────── 10:25

Comparison

Window

Description

Tumbling

Fixed-size, contiguous, non-overlapping intervals

Sliding

Overlapping intervals defined using window duration and slide duration

9. Watermarking

A Watermark defines an allowed arrival-delay threshold relative to the maximum event time observed by Spark.

Formula

Watermark Boundary

    =

Maximum Event Time Observed

    -

Allowed Late Threshold

Example

Suppose:

Maximum Event Time Observed = 11:45 AM

Allowed Late Threshold      = 30 minutes

Then:

Watermark Boundary = 11:15 AM

Therefore:

Event Time 11:20 AM → ACCEPTED

Event Time 11:05 AM → DROPPED

Why Watermarking Is Important

Watermarking allows Spark to:

  1. Handle late-arriving records within an acceptable threshold.
  2. Drop records that arrive later than the defined boundary.
  3. Evict expired aggregation state.
  4. Prevent indefinite growth of the State Store.
  5. Reduce the risk of OOM failures.

Watermarked Tumbling Window Aggregation

from pyspark.sql.functions import window, col, sum

orders_stream = spark.readStream \

    .format("json") \

    .schema("order_id LONG, order_date TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE") \

    .load("data/inputdir")

windowed_sales = orders_stream \

    .withWatermark("order_date", "30 minutes") \

    .groupBy(

        window(col("order_date"), "15 minutes")

    ) \

    .agg(

        sum("amount").alias("total_sales")

    )

query = windowed_sales.writeStream \

    .outputMode("update") \

    .format("console") \

    .start()

Sliding Window Aggregation

A sliding window can be defined using both duration and slide interval.

Example:

  • Window duration = 15 minutes
  • Slide = 5 minutes

sliding_sales = orders_stream \

    .withWatermark("order_date", "30 minutes") \

    .groupBy(

        window(

            col("order_date"),

            "15 minutes",

            "5 minutes"

        )

    ) \

    .agg(

        sum("amount").alias("total_sales")

    )

10. Streaming Joins

Spark Structured Streaming supports joining:

  1. A streaming DataFrame with a static DataFrame.
  2. Two streaming DataFrames.

10.1 Stream-to-Static Join

A Stream-to-Static Join enriches live streaming events using a static reference dataset.

Example

Streaming Data

(Live ATM Swipes)

        |

        | card_id

        v

Static Customer Table

(Customer Database)

        |

        v

Enriched Streaming Data

Example:

Streaming Transaction

---------------------

transaction_id: TX-991

card_id: 557242753831

amount: $200.00

Static Customer Table

---------------------

card_id: 557242753831

member_id: M-88120

country: United States

The resulting stream contains both transaction and customer information.

Stream-to-Static Left Outer Join

streaming_transactions = spark.readStream \

    .format("kafka") \

    .load()

static_customers = spark.read.table(

    "prod.retail.customers"

)

enriched_stream = streaming_transactions.join(

    static_customers,

    streaming_transactions.card_id == static_customers.card_id,

    "left_outer"

)

Outer Join Restrictions

According to the study material:

  • Left Outer Join: The left side must be Streaming and the right side Static.
  • Right Outer Join: The right side must be Streaming and the left side Static.

Reversing these directional relationships can result in an AnalysisException.

10.2 Stream-to-Stream Join

A Stream-to-Stream Join joins two continuous streaming datasets.

Because Spark must maintain state for both streams, the query requires:

  • Watermarks on both streams.
  • A time-range constraint to limit how long state must be retained.

Example

impressions = spark.readStream \

    .format("kafka") \

    .load() \

    .withWatermark("impression_time", "2 hours")

clicks = spark.readStream \

    .format("kafka") \

    .load() \

    .withWatermark("click_time", "3 hours")

matched_ad_conversions = impressions.join(

    clicks,

    expr("""

        click_ad_id = impression_ad_id AND

        click_time >= impression_time AND

        click_time <= impression_time + interval 1 hour

    """),

    "inner"

)

Key Interview Point

A Stream-to-Stream Join requires bounded state.

Therefore:

Watermark + Time Range Constraint

                ↓

Bounded State

                ↓

Controlled Memory Consumption

11. Upserts in Streaming: Delta Lake + foreachBatch

When streaming data needs to perform micro-batch upserts using Delta Lake, foreachBatch can be used to execute a MERGE INTO operation for every micro-batch.

Custom Micro-Batch Function

def merge_micro_batch(micro_batch_df, batch_id):

    """Executes atomic Delta MERGE INTO for each micro-batch."""

   

    micro_batch_df.createOrReplaceTempView("updates")

    merge_sql = """

        MERGE INTO orders_final_result t

        USING updates s

        ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id

        WHEN MATCHED THEN

          UPDATE SET

            t.products_purchased = s.products_purchased,

            t.orders_placed = s.orders_placed,

            t.amount_spent = s.amount_spent

        WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN

          INSERT (

              customer_id,

              orders_placed,

              products_purchased,

              amount_spent

          )

          VALUES (

              s.customer_id,

              s.orders_placed,

              s.products_purchased,

              s.amount_spent

          )

    """

    micro_batch_df._jdf.sparkSession().sql(merge_sql)

Writing the Streaming Query

query = aggregated_orders.writeStream \

    .format("delta") \

    .outputMode("update") \

    .option(

        "checkpointLocation",

        "/mnt/delta/checkpoints/orders_merge"

    ) \

    .foreachBatch(merge_micro_batch) \

    .start()

Week 30: Apache Kafka Architecture, PySpark Structured Streaming Integration & Production Messaging

1. Apache Kafka Architectural Overview & Distributed Ecosystem

Apache Kafka is an open-source, distributed event-streaming platform designed for high-throughput, scalable, fault-tolerant, real-time messaging and event processing.

Kafka follows a decoupled publish-subscribe architecture:

                        DECOUPLED PUB-SUB ARCHITECTURE

   PRODUCERS                       KAFKA CLUSTER                    CONSUMERS

 ┌─────────────┐              ┌─────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────┐

 │ Applications│              │ Broker 1            │           │ Spark        │

 │ IoT Systems │ ── Publish ─>│ Broker 2            │ ── Pull ─>│ Streaming    │

 │ Web Logs    │              │ Broker 3            │           │ Applications │

 │ Services    │              │ Broker 4            │           │ Other Apps   │

 └─────────────┘              └─────────────────────┘           └──────────────┘

Why Kafka Instead of Network Sockets?

Simple network sockets such as nc -lk can demonstrate streaming concepts, but they are unsuitable for production-grade messaging.

Capability

Network Socket

Apache Kafka

Data persistence

No

Yes

Replayability

No

Yes

Buffering

Limited

Built-in

Multiple consumers

Difficult

Native

Fault tolerance

Very limited

High

Scalability

Limited

High

Consumer offset tracking

No

Yes

Production suitability

Low

High

Kafka's Key Advantages

1. Replayability

Kafka persists messages on disk, allowing consumers to re-read historical messages.

2. Buffering

Kafka decouples producers and consumers. If producers temporarily generate data faster than consumers can process it, Kafka retains the messages until consumers catch up.

3. Multiple Independent Consumers

Different applications can consume the same topic independently through separate consumer groups.

4. Horizontal Scalability

Topics can be divided into multiple partitions and distributed across brokers.

5. Fault Tolerance

Partitions can be replicated across brokers so that data remains available if a broker fails.

2. Kafka Namespace Hierarchy

Kafka's logical organization can be visualized as:

Environment

    │

    └── Kafka Cluster

            │

            ├── Broker 1

            ├── Broker 2

            ├── Broker 3

            └── Broker 4

                    │

                    └── Topics

                          │

                          └── Partitions

                                │

                                └── Offsets

Core Kafka Components

1. Producer

A producer is an application that publishes messages/events to Kafka topics.

Examples:

  • Web applications
  • IoT devices
  • Microservices
  • Application logs
  • Transaction systems

2. Consumer

A consumer is an application that reads messages from Kafka.

Examples:

  • Spark Structured Streaming
  • Databricks
  • Flink
  • Custom Python applications
  • Monitoring systems

3. Broker

A broker is an individual Kafka server responsible for storing and serving partitions.

A Kafka cluster can contain multiple brokers.

4. Topic

A topic is a logical stream of events.

For example:

retail-orders

customer-events

payment-transactions

website-logs

A topic is conceptually similar to a table in a database, but it represents a continuously growing event stream rather than a static dataset.

5. Partition

A topic is divided into partitions for scalability and parallel processing.

Example:

Topic: retail-orders

Partition 0 → [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...]

Partition 1 → [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...]

Partition 2 → [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...]

Partition 3 → [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...]

Each partition is an ordered, append-only log.

6. Offset

An offset is the sequential identifier assigned to a record within a partition.

For example:

Partition 0

Offset 0 → Event A

Offset 1 → Event B

Offset 2 → Event C

Offset 3 → Event D

Offsets are unique within a partition, not across the entire Kafka topic.

Locating a Kafka Record

A specific record can be identified using:

(Topic Name, Partition ID, Partition Offset)

For example:

("retail-orders", 2, 1456)

means:

Record at offset 1456 in partition 2 of the retail-orders topic.

3. Kafka Partitioning & Consumer Groups

Partitioning is one of Kafka's most important mechanisms for achieving parallelism and scalability.

Suppose a topic contains four partitions:

                   TOPIC: retail-orders

        ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐

        │ Partition 0                         │ ──> Consumer 1

        │ Partition 1                         │ ──> Consumer 2

        │ Partition 2                         │ ──> Consumer 3

        │ Partition 3                         │ ──> Consumer 4

        └─────────────────────────────────────┘

With four consumers in the same consumer group, each consumer can process one partition.

Consumer Group

A consumer group is a logical collection of consumers working together to consume a Kafka topic.

The key rule is:

Within a consumer group, a partition can be assigned to only one consumer at a time.

Consumer Group Scaling Rules

Rule 1 — One Partition → One Consumer

A single partition cannot simultaneously be assigned to two consumers within the same consumer group.

This preserves ordering.

Rule 2 — One Consumer Can Read Multiple Partitions

If there are fewer consumers than partitions:

4 Partitions

2 Consumers

Consumer 1 → Partition 0 + Partition 1

Consumer 2 → Partition 2 + Partition 3

Rule 3 — Consumers Cannot Exceed Active Partitions

If there are:

4 partitions

6 consumers

then:

Consumer 1 → Partition 0

Consumer 2 → Partition 1

Consumer 3 → Partition 2

Consumer 4 → Partition 3

Consumer 5 → IDLE

Consumer 6 → IDLE

Therefore:

Maximum active consumers in a group

≈ Number of partitions

4. Kafka Message Keys & Partition Routing

Kafka records can contain:

(Key, Value)

For example:

Key   = customer_id = 256

Value = {

    "order_id": 1001,

    "customer_id": 256,

    "amount": 499.99

}

When a key is supplied, Kafka's partitioning strategy generally uses the key to consistently route records to the same partition.

Why Is This Important?

Suppose:

customer_id = 256

has three orders:

Order 1 → customer 256

Order 2 → customer 256

Order 3 → customer 256

Using customer_id as the Kafka key helps ensure that these records are routed to the same partition.

This is useful when downstream processing requires ordering by customer.

Interview Insight

A good Kafka key should generally:

  • Distribute records reasonably evenly.
  • Preserve ordering where required.
  • Avoid creating a hot partition.

For example:

customer_id

may be a good key for customer-centric event processing.

5. Python Kafka Producer Using Confluent-Kafka

The confluent-kafka Python library provides a high-performance Kafka client.

from confluent_kafka import Producer

import json

conf = {

    "bootstrap.servers": "your-kafka-bootstrap-server:9092",

    "security.protocol": "SASL_SSL",

    "sasl.mechanism": "PLAIN",

    "sasl.username": "YOUR_API_KEY",

    "sasl.password": "YOUR_API_SECRET",

    "client.id": "python-producer-app"

}

producer = Producer(conf)

Sample Payload

customer_id = "256"

payload = {

    "order_id": 2,

    "customer_id": 256,

    "customer_fname": "David",

    "customer_lname": "Rodriguez",

    "city": "Chicago",

    "state": "IL",

    "pincode": 60625,

    "line_items": [

        {

            "order_item_id": 2,

            "order_item_product_id": 1073,

            "order_item_quantity": 1,

            "order_item_product_price": 199.99,

            "order_item_subtotal": 199.99

        }

    ]

}

Delivery Callback

def acked(err, msg):

    if err is not None:

        print(f"Failed to deliver message: {err}")

    else:

        print(

            f"Message produced to Topic: {msg.topic()} "

            f"| Partition: {msg.partition()}"

        )

Producing a Message

producer.produce(

    topic="retail-orders",

    key=customer_id,

    value=json.dumps(payload),

    callback=acked

)

poll() vs flush()

This distinction is frequently asked in interviews.

poll(0)

producer.poll(0)

Processes delivery callbacks and other producer events.

flush()

producer.flush()

Waits for outstanding messages to be delivered before the application exits.

Interview Question

Why does produce() not immediately guarantee that the message has reached Kafka?

Because produce() is asynchronous. The record is initially placed into the producer's local buffer.

The producer then communicates with Kafka brokers in the background.

produce()

   ↓

Local Producer Buffer

   ↓

Kafka Broker

   ↓

Acknowledgement

   ↓

Delivery Callback

6. PySpark Structured Streaming + Kafka

PySpark provides native Kafka integration through:

.format("kafka")

The major distinction is:

spark.read

versus:

spark.readStream

6.1 Batch Reading from Kafka

Batch mode reads a finite snapshot of Kafka records and then terminates.

bootstrap_servers = "your-kafka-bootstrap-server:9092"

topic_name = "retail-orders"

kafka_batch_df = spark.read \

    .format("kafka") \

    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", bootstrap_servers) \

    .option("subscribe", topic_name) \

    .load()

Kafka's key and value columns are binary.

Therefore, they are commonly converted into strings:

formatted_batch_df = kafka_batch_df.selectExpr(

    "CAST(key AS STRING) AS key",

    "CAST(value AS STRING) AS value",

    "topic",

    "partition",

    "offset",

    "timestamp"

)

Important Kafka Metadata

Spark's Kafka DataFrame includes useful metadata:

key

value

topic

partition

offset

timestamp

timestampType

7. Streaming Kafka → PySpark → Delta Lake

For continuous processing:

spark.readStream

is used.

The architecture becomes:

Kafka Topic

     │

     ▼

readStream

     │

     ▼

JSON Parsing

     │

     ▼

DataFrame Transformations

     │

     ▼

Flatten Nested Structures

     │

     ▼

Delta Lake

Reading Kafka as a Stream

kafka_stream_df = spark.readStream \

    .format("kafka") \

    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", bootstrap_servers) \

    .option("subscribe", topic_name) \

    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest") \

    .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 50) \

    .load()

Important Options

startingOffsets

Controls where the streaming query starts reading.

Examples:

earliest

latest

earliest is useful when initially processing historical Kafka data.

maxOffsetsPerTrigger

Controls the maximum number of Kafka records processed in each micro-batch.

Example:

.option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 50)

This can help control workload and prevent large Kafka backlogs from overwhelming the Spark cluster.

8. Parsing JSON from Kafka

Kafka generally provides the message value as binary data.

The first step is converting it to a string:

kafka_stream_df = kafka_stream_df.selectExpr(

    "CAST(value AS STRING) AS raw_json"

)

Then parse JSON using from_json().

from pyspark.sql.functions import from_json, col

orders_schema = """

    order_id LONG,

    customer_id LONG,

    customer_fname STRING,

    customer_lname STRING,

    city STRING,

    state STRING,

    pincode LONG

"""

parsed_stream_df = kafka_stream_df \

    .withColumn(

        "data",

        from_json(col("raw_json"), orders_schema)

    ) \

    .select("data.*")

This converts:

Raw JSON string

       ↓

Structured Spark columns

9. Flattening Nested Arrays Using explode()

Real-world Kafka messages often contain nested arrays.

Example:

{

  "order_id": 1001,

  "customer_id": 256,

  "line_items": [

    {

      "product_id": 101,

      "quantity": 2

    },

    {

      "product_id": 202,

      "quantity": 1

    }

  ]

}

Spark represents line_items as:

ARRAY<STRUCT<...>>

Use:

from pyspark.sql.functions import explode

flattened_df = parsed_stream_df \

    .select(

        "order_id",

        "customer_id",

        explode("line_items").alias("item")

    )

Then extract individual fields:

flattened_df = flattened_df.select(

    "order_id",

    "customer_id",

    col("item.product_id").alias("product_id"),

    col("item.quantity").alias("quantity")

)

The result becomes:

order_id | customer_id | product_id | quantity

------------------------------------------------

1001     | 256         | 101        | 2

1001     | 256         | 202        | 1

Interview Question

What does explode() do?

It converts each element of an array or map into a separate row.

10. Writing Kafka Streams to Delta Lake

After transformation, the stream can be persisted into Delta Lake.

query = flattened_df.writeStream \

    .queryName("KafkaToDeltaIngestion") \

    .format("delta") \

    .outputMode("append") \

    .option(

        "checkpointLocation",

        "/mnt/delta/checkpoints/kafka_orders"

    ) \

    .toTable("retail_db.orders_flattened_bronze")

Architecture

                 KAFKA → SPARK → DELTA

Kafka Topic

    │

    │ JSON Events

    ▼

Spark Structured Streaming

    │

    ├── Parse JSON

    ├── Validate Schema

    ├── Flatten Arrays

    └── Transform

    │

    ▼

Delta Bronze Table

This is a common Bronze-layer ingestion pattern in a Lakehouse architecture.

11. Kafka → PySpark → Kafka Streaming Pipeline

Kafka can also act as both the source and sink.

      SOURCE KAFKA

     retail-orders

           │

           ▼

   Spark Structured

       Streaming

           │

      Filter / Transform

           │

           ▼

       TARGET KAFKA

    chicago-orders

Example:

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, struct, to_json

chicago_orders_df = parsed_stream_df \

    .filter(col("city") == "Chicago") \

    .selectExpr(

        "CAST(customer_id AS STRING) AS key",

        """

        to_json(

            struct(

                order_id,

                customer_id,

                customer_fname,

                customer_lname,

                city,

                state,

                pincode

            )

        ) AS value

        """

    )

Then write to Kafka:

sink_query = chicago_orders_df.writeStream \

    .format("kafka") \

    .outputMode("append") \

    .option(

        "kafka.bootstrap.servers",

        bootstrap_servers

    ) \

    .option(

        "topic",

        "chicago-orders-sink"

    ) \

    .option(

        "checkpointLocation",

        "/mnt/delta/checkpoints/chicago_orders"

    ) \

    .start()

A typical enterprise architecture may look like:

                   ENTERPRISE EVENT STREAMING

 ┌───────────────┐

 │ Applications  │

 │ IoT / APIs    │

 │ Transactions  │

 └───────┬───────┘

         │

 ┌─────────────────────┐

 │    Kafka Cluster    │

 │                     │

 │ Broker 1            │

 │ Broker 2            │

 │ Broker 3            │

 └──────────┬──────────┘

            │

       ┌────┴─────────┐

       │              │

       ▼              ▼

 Consumer Group A   Consumer Group B

       │              │

       ▼              ▼

    Databricks      Analytics App

       │

       ▼

 Structured Streaming

       │

 ┌─────┴───────────┐

 ▼                 ▼

Delta Lake       Kafka Sink

The key architectural benefit is decoupling.

Producers do not need to know:

  • Who consumes their data.
  • How many consumers exist.
  • How quickly consumers process records.
  • Where downstream data is stored.

13. Important Kafka Interview Concepts

Kafka vs Traditional Message Queues

Kafka is optimized for distributed, durable event streaming and high-throughput workloads.

Traditional queues often focus more on:

Message → Consumer → Message Removed

Kafka follows an append-only log model:

Producer

   ↓

Kafka Log

   ↓

Consumer A → Offset 100

Consumer B → Offset 75

Consumer C → Offset 20

Different consumers can independently maintain their positions.

Partition vs Consumer

Remember:

Partitions = Parallelism

Consumers = Processing Workers

If:

8 partitions

4 consumers

then consumers can process multiple partitions.

If:

4 partitions

8 consumers

only four consumers can actively process partitions at a time.

Kafka Topic vs Partition

Topic

Logical stream of related events.

Partition

Physical/logical subdivision of a topic that enables:

  • Parallelism
  • Scalability
  • Ordering within the partition

Kafka Offset vs Spark Checkpoint

These concepts should not be confused.

Kafka Offset

Tracks:

Which Kafka record has been consumed.

Example:

Partition 2 → Offset 1456

Spark Checkpoint

Tracks streaming query progress and state so Spark can recover after failures.

Kafka Offset

      ↓

Spark Streaming

      ↓

Checkpoint

      ↓

Delta Sink

14. Key Production Considerations

When designing Kafka + Spark Structured Streaming systems, consider:

1. Partition Count

Choose enough partitions to provide the required processing parallelism.

2. Partition Key

Choose a key that:

  • Preserves required ordering.
  • Avoids data hotspots.
  • Distributes traffic evenly.

3. Consumer Group Design

Separate applications requiring independent consumption should normally use separate consumer groups.

4. Checkpointing

Always use a persistent checkpoint location for production Spark streaming jobs.

5. Schema Management

For enterprise pipelines, establish schema governance and compatibility rules for evolving event payloads.

6. Security

Production Kafka deployments commonly require:

TLS / SSL

SASL authentication

ACL authorization

Secret management

7. Monitoring

Monitor:

  • Consumer lag
  • Broker health
  • Partition distribution
  • Throughput
  • Error rate
  • Failed records
  • Spark processing latency
  • Checkpoint health

  2. How would you avoid a hot partition?

Week 31: AWS Big Data Architecture, Compute Families & Serverless Analytics

1. AWS Cloud Ecosystem & Cross-Cloud Service Mapping

The AWS Big Data ecosystem provides services that map closely to the cloud analytics architecture established in Azure and GCP.

                 [ Cross-Cloud Service Equivalency Matrix ]

        AWS SERVICE                AZURE SERVICE             FUNCTIONAL ROLE

  +--------------------+      +--------------------+      +--------------------+

  | Amazon S3          | <--> | ADLS Gen2 / Blob   | <--> | Object Storage     |

  | Amazon EC2         | <--> | Azure VMs          | <--> | IaaS Compute       |

  | AWS Glue           | <--> | Azure Data Factory | <--> | ETL & Catalog      |

  | Amazon Athena      | <--> | Synapse Serverless | <--> | Pay-Per-Scan Query |

  | Amazon Redshift    | <--> | Synapse Dedicated  | <--> | Enterprise MPP DWH |

  | Amazon EMR         | <--> | Azure HDInsight    | <--> | Managed Hadoop/Spark|

  | AWS Lambda         | <--> | Azure Functions    | <--> | Serverless Compute |

  +--------------------+      +--------------------+      +--------------------+

Core AWS Data Architecture Components

  • Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service): Scalable cloud object storage that forms the foundation of many AWS data lake architectures.
  • AWS Glue & Glue Catalog: Managed serverless ETL service combined with a Hive-compatible metadata catalog.
  • Amazon Athena: Serverless interactive query engine that executes SQL directly against data stored in Amazon S3 without requiring the data to be moved into a separate database.
  • Amazon Redshift: Enterprise Data Warehouse using Massively Parallel Processing (MPP) for high-performance analytical and reporting workloads.
  • Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce): Managed cluster platform for running open-source Big Data frameworks such as Apache Spark, Hive, and Presto/Trino.

2. Amazon EC2 Compute Architecture & Provisioning Options

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) provides scalable Virtual Machines (VMs) running on physical infrastructure partitioned through virtualization.

                    [ Physical Server Virtualization ]

  Physical Server (e.g., 128 GB RAM / 32 CPU Cores / 4 TB Storage)

   ├── VM 1 (m4.large):  32 GB RAM / 8 Cores / Guest OS

   ├── VM 2 (m4.large):  32 GB RAM / 8 Cores / Guest OS

   ├── VM 3 (m4.large):  32 GB RAM / 8 Cores / Guest OS

   └── VM 4 (m4.large):  32 GB RAM / 8 Cores / Guest OS

EC2 Hardware Configuration Components

1. Amazon Machine Image (AMI)

An AMI is a pre-configured template containing the Guest Operating System, such as Linux or Windows, along with pre-installed application software and configuration.

It is used as the starting point when launching an EC2 instance.

2. Key Pair Authentication

EC2 uses public-key cryptography for secure SSH authentication.

  • The public key is stored on the EC2 instance.
  • The private key is retained by the client.
  • The private key is commonly provided as a .pem file.

3. Storage Types

Instance Store Volumes

  • Ephemeral storage physically attached to the host server.
  • Very high performance.
  • Data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated.

Amazon EBS

Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) provides persistent, network-attached block storage.

Unlike ephemeral instance storage, EBS volumes are designed to persist independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle.

EC2 Instance Families

AWS categorizes EC2 instances into families optimized for different resource requirements.

Instance Family

Prefix

Resource Profile

Example

Primary Use Case

General Purpose

M

Balanced compute, memory and networking

m4.large — 2 vCPUs / 8 GB RAM

Web servers, development, build servers

Compute Optimized

C

High compute-to-memory ratio

c5.xlarge — 4 vCPUs / 8 GB RAM

Batch processing, compute-heavy workloads

Memory Optimized

R

High memory-to-compute ratio

r5.xlarge — 2 vCPUs / 16 GB RAM

In-memory workloads, Spark drivers, distributed databases

Interview Shortcut

Think of the families as:

M → General Purpose → Balanced

C → Compute Optimized → CPU Heavy

R → Memory Optimized → RAM Heavy

EC2 Pricing Models

                        [ EC2 Cost Optimization Options ]

   ON-DEMAND INSTANCES            RESERVED INSTANCES              SPOT INSTANCES

  +---------------------+        +---------------------+        +---------------------+

  | Pay per second/hour |        | 1 or 3-year term    |        | Uses unused AWS     |

  | with zero long-term |        | commitment yielding |        | capacity at large   |

  | commitment.         |        | significant savings |        | potential savings.  |

  +---------------------+        +---------------------+        +---------------------+

On-Demand

  • Pay for compute without long-term commitment.
  • Useful for unpredictable workloads.
  • Highest flexibility.

Reserved Instances

  • Commitment-based purchasing model.
  • Suitable for predictable, continuously running workloads.
  • Provides significant discounts compared with On-Demand pricing.

Spot Instances

  • Uses spare AWS capacity.
  • Can provide substantial cost savings.
  • Instances can be interrupted when AWS needs the capacity.
  • Best suited to fault-tolerant workloads such as certain batch processing and distributed Spark workloads.

3. Amazon Athena Architecture & Analytics Engines

Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service used to analyze data directly from Amazon S3 using SQL.

                    [ Amazon Athena Decoupled Architecture ]

  ANALYTICS ENGINE

  +---------------------------+

  | Trino SQL / Spark Engine  |

  +-------------+-------------+

The key architectural idea is separation of storage and compute:

            Compute

Data remains in S3 rather than being loaded into Athena.

Supported Execution Engines

1. Trino SQL Engine

A distributed SQL engine designed for interactive analytical queries over large datasets.

For SQL queries, the source material describes pricing as being based on the volume of data scanned from S3.

2. Apache Spark Engine

Athena can also provide Spark-based analytics for workloads requiring Python/PySpark processing.

The source material describes Spark billing using Data Processing Units (DPUs).

Athena Billing Model

Trino SQL Engine

The provided study material uses the following pricing model:

  • Standard rate: $5 per TB scanned
  • Minimum billable amount: 10 MB
  • Failed queries: no charge
  • Cancelled queries: charged for the data scanned before cancellation

The learning formula is:

{Query Scan Cost}

{Data Scanned in TB} times $5

For example, if a query scans 0.25 TB:

[0.25 times $5 = $1.25]

Spark Engine — DPU Framework

According to the supplied material:

  • 1 DPU = 4 vCPUs + 16 GB RAM
  • DPU usage is charged based on execution resources consumed.
  • The notebook server itself is described as free.
  • Driver/coordinator resources consume DPU capacity while the session is active.
  • Worker DPUs are allocated during execution.

Example

Suppose:

  • Driver = 1 DPU for 1 hour
  • Workers = 20 DPUs
  • Six calculations each execute for 1 minute

Worker consumption:

[
6 \times 20 \times \frac{1}{60}
= 2\text{ DPU-Hours}
]

Total:

[
1 + 2 = 3\text{ DPU-Hours}
]

At the supplied rate of ₹/$0.35 per DPU-hour in the source:

[
3 \times 0.35 = 1.05
]

Interview takeaway: Athena SQL is primarily associated with data scanned, whereas Athena Spark is associated with compute resources / DPUs.

4. Query Optimization & Cost Reduction in S3/Athena

Athena costs can be reduced by minimizing the amount of physical data read from S3.

The three major techniques covered are:

                      [ Athena Scan Reduction Strategies ]

   1. Compression             2. Columnar Formats          3. Partition Pruning

  +------------------+       +----------------------+      +----------------------+

  | Reduce physical  |       | Read only required  |      | Skip irrelevant      |

  | file size        |       | columns             |      | partition folders    |

  +------------------+       +----------------------+      +----------------------+

1. Compression

Compression reduces the physical amount of data stored and scanned.

Examples:

  • Snappy
  • Gzip

Smaller files generally mean fewer bytes scanned.

2. Columnar Formats

Formats such as Parquet and ORC store data by columns rather than rows.

Suppose a dataset contains:

customer_id

name

city

salary

If the query only requires:

SELECT salary

FROM employees;

a columnar format can avoid reading unnecessary columns.

This is known as column pruning.

3. Partition Pruning

Partitioning organizes data into separate directory structures based on partition columns.

For example:

s3://data/orders/

    year=2025/

        month=01/

        month=02/

    year=2026/

        month=01/

        month=02/

A query such as:

SELECT *

FROM orders

WHERE year = 2026

  AND month = 7;

can avoid scanning irrelevant partitions.

Scan Cost Comparison

Consider a dataset containing 3 TB of raw data with four columns, where the query needs only one column.

Storage Strategy

Format

Approx. Stored Size

Approx. Data Read

Example Scan Cost

Raw uncompressed

CSV

3 TB

3 TB

₹/$15

Compressed

Gzip CSV

1 TB

1 TB

₹/$5

Compressed columnar

Parquet

0.25 TB

~0.0625 TB

₹/$1.25

Core principle:

Less data scanned → lower Athena query cost.

5. AWS Glue Catalog, Crawlers & Partition Management

AWS Glue Data Catalog serves as a centralized metadata repository containing information such as:

  • Table definitions
  • Column schemas
  • Data types
  • Partition metadata
  • S3 locations

                    [ AWS Glue Metadata Pipeline ]

  Amazon S3

      |

      v

  Glue Crawler

      | Schema / Partition Discovery

      v

  Glue Data Catalog

      |

      v

  Amazon Athena

      |

      v

  SQL Queries

AWS Glue Crawler

A Glue Crawler can:

  1. Scan S3 locations.
  2. Discover file formats.
  3. Infer schemas.
  4. Detect partitions.
  5. Register metadata in the Glue Data Catalog.

This avoids manually defining every schema and partition in many ingestion scenarios.

Manual Partition Registration

When partitioned data exists in S3 but the catalog does not yet contain the corresponding partition metadata, partitions can be registered using:

MSCK REPAIR TABLE table_name;

Example

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS trendytech_db.students_partitioned (

    student_id INT,

    exam_center_id INT,

    year INT,

    quarter INT,

    score INT,

    grade STRING

)

PARTITIONED BY (subject STRING)

STORED AS PARQUET

LOCATION 's3://trendytech-athena-demo/athena-input-parquet/';

Then:

MSCK REPAIR TABLE trendytech_db.students_partitioned;

What happens?

8. Key Interview Questions — Week 31

Q1. What is Amazon S3's role in a Big Data architecture?

Answer:
Amazon S3 provides highly scalable object storage and is commonly used as the foundation of AWS data lakes. Analytical services such as Athena and EMR can process data directly from S3, separating storage from compute.

Q2. What is the difference between EC2 and EMR?

EC2 provides virtual machines where you control the operating environment and installed software.

EMR is a managed Big Data platform designed to simplify running distributed frameworks such as Spark and Hadoop.

Interview line:

EC2 gives me infrastructure-level compute; EMR gives me managed Big Data cluster capabilities.

Q3. What is the difference between Athena and Redshift?

Athena:

  • Serverless
  • Queries data directly in S3
  • Excellent for ad-hoc analysis
  • Data-scan-oriented pricing model

Redshift:

  • Enterprise analytical warehouse
  • MPP architecture
  • Better suited to persistent, high-concurrency warehouse workloads

Q4. Why is Parquet preferred over CSV for Athena workloads?

Because Parquet is a columnar format.

If the query needs only a subset of columns, Athena can potentially read only those columns instead of scanning the entire row-based file.

It also works well with compression.

Q5. What is partition pruning?

Partition pruning allows the query engine to skip partitions that cannot satisfy the query predicate.

For example:

SELECT *

FROM orders

WHERE year = 2026

AND month = 7;

If the table is partitioned by year and month, Athena can avoid scanning unrelated partitions.

Q6. What is the AWS Glue Data Catalog?

It is a centralized metadata repository that stores information about datasets, including:

  • Tables
  • Columns
  • Data types
  • S3 locations
  • Partitions

Athena can use this metadata to query S3 data.

Q7. What does a Glue Crawler do?

A crawler scans data sources, detects schemas and partitions, and registers the resulting metadata in the Glue Data Catalog.

Q8. What does MSCK REPAIR TABLE do?

It discovers partition directories in the underlying storage location and registers those partitions in the metastore/catalog so that Athena can query them.

Q9. Explain EC2 M, C and R instance families.

M → General Purpose

    Balanced CPU + Memory

C → Compute Optimized

    CPU intensive

R → Memory Optimized

    Memory intensive

For example, a memory-heavy Spark workload may benefit from an R-family instance.

Q10. How can you reduce Athena costs?

The key techniques are:

  1. Store data in compressed formats.
  2. Prefer columnar formats such as Parquet.
  3. Partition data appropriately.
  4. Use partition filters in SQL queries.
  5. Select only the required columns.
  6. Avoid unnecessarily scanning large datasets.

Week 32: Enterprise Big Data Compute & Governance — Amazon EMR & AWS Glue

1. Amazon EMR Architecture & Node Types

Amazon EMR (Elastic MapReduce) is AWS's managed Big Data platform that simplifies provisioning and running distributed frameworks such as Apache Spark, Apache Hive, HBase, Presto, and Trino over EC2 infrastructure.

EMR Cluster Architecture

                    [ AWS EMR Cluster Node Architecture ]

                              PRIMARY NODE

                                (Master)

                                   |

                 +-----------------+-----------------+

                 |                                   |

          HDFS NameNode                    YARN ResourceManager

          (Metadata)                        (Orchestration)

                 |

        +--------+----------------------+

        |                               |

   CORE NODES                       TASK NODES

   (Workers)                        (Workers)

        |                               |

   Spark Tasks                     Spark Tasks

   YARN NodeManager                YARN NodeManager

        |                               |

   HDFS DataNodes                   NO HDFS Storage

   Stores Data                      Processing Only

EMR Node Types

1. Primary Node

The Primary Node is responsible for coordinating the EMR cluster.

It runs important cluster-management services such as:

  • HDFS NameNode — maintains HDFS metadata.
  • YARN ResourceManager — manages cluster resources and schedules applications.
  • Cluster coordination and management processes.

Think of the Primary Node as the control/coordination layer of the EMR cluster.

2. Core Nodes

Core Nodes are worker nodes responsible for both:

  • Computation
  • HDFS storage

They typically run:

  • Spark executors/tasks
  • YARN NodeManager
  • HDFS DataNode

Because Core Nodes contain HDFS data, removing them can result in data loss if the data has not been replicated elsewhere.

3. Task Nodes

Task Nodes are compute-only worker nodes.

They:

  • Execute Spark/YARN tasks.
  • Run YARN NodeManager.
  • Do not store HDFS data.

This makes Task Nodes ideal for:

  • Temporary workloads
  • Elastic scaling
  • Spot Instances
  • Cost optimization

Because they do not contain HDFS data, they can be added or removed more freely than Core Nodes.

Core vs Task Nodes

Feature

Core Node

Task Node

Compute

Yes

Yes

Spark tasks

Yes

Yes

YARN NodeManager

Yes

Yes

HDFS DataNode

Yes

No

Stores HDFS data

Yes

No

Safe to scale down aggressively

No

Yes

Good candidate for Spot

Possible

Excellent

Primary purpose

Compute + Storage

Compute only

Interview Question

Q: Why would you use Task Nodes in an EMR cluster?

Answer:
Task Nodes provide additional compute capacity without adding HDFS storage. They are particularly useful when Spark workloads require more processing power but do not require additional distributed storage. Since they are stateless from the HDFS perspective, they can also be scaled down or provisioned with Spot capacity for cost optimization.

2. EMR Provisioning — Instance Groups vs Instance Fleets

EMR provides two major approaches for configuring EC2 capacity.

             [ EMR Capacity Provisioning ]

        INSTANCE GROUPS                    INSTANCE FLEETS

        ---------------                    --------------

        Fixed configuration                Flexible configuration

              |                                  |

       Same instance type                 Multiple instance types

       per node group                     + purchasing options

              |                                  |

       Simple / predictable                Cost + availability

       capacity                            optimization

Instance Groups

Instance Groups provide a relatively simple and uniform configuration.

For example:

Core Group

 ├── m5.xlarge

 ├── m5.xlarge

 ├── m5.xlarge

 └── m5.xlarge

Instances in the same group use the configured instance type and purchasing model.

Advantages

  • Simple configuration
  • Predictable capacity
  • Easy to understand
  • Suitable for stable workloads

Disadvantage

Less flexibility when a particular EC2 instance type is unavailable or expensive.

Instance Fleets

Instance Fleets provide greater flexibility.

A fleet can use:

  • Multiple EC2 instance types
  • Multiple sizes
  • On-Demand capacity
  • Spot capacity

Example:

                CORE INSTANCE FLEET

                        |

          +-------------+-------------+

          |             |             |

       m5.xlarge     m5.2xlarge    r5.xlarge

          |             |             |

       On-Demand       Spot        Spot

EMR can use the available capacity options to satisfy the desired compute capacity.

Instance Groups vs Fleets

Feature

Instance Groups

Instance Fleets

Instance types

More uniform

Multiple types

Purchasing options

Simpler

Flexible

Configuration

Simple

More complex

Availability flexibility

Lower

Higher

Cost optimization

Moderate

Strong

Best use

Predictable workloads

Dynamic/cost-sensitive workloads

Interview Question

Q: Why would an enterprise choose Instance Fleets instead of Instance Groups?

Answer:
Instance Fleets allow the cluster to use multiple EC2 instance types and purchasing options, increasing the probability of obtaining capacity while also providing greater opportunities for Spot-based cost optimization.

3. EMR Cluster Resource Sizing

Consider a cluster with:

  • 1 Primary Node
  • 2 Core Nodes
  • 1 Task Node

Each instance is:

m4.large

2 vCPUs

8 GB RAM

32 GB EBS

The processing worker pool consists of:

2 Core + 1 Task = 3 Worker Nodes

Compute Capacity

If each worker provides 2 vCPUs:

Total vCPUs

= 2 vCPUs × 3 workers

= 6 vCPUs

The source material's example applies an additional multiplier and arrives at 12 vCPUs; retain that figure when following the source's specific calculation framework.

YARN Memory Allocation

Assuming 75% of memory is available to YARN:

Memory per worker

= 8 GB × 75%

= 6 GB

Total YARN memory

= 6 GB × 3 workers

= 18 GB

Therefore:

Usable YARN memory = 18 GB

Interview Tip: Always distinguish between the physical memory of an EC2 instance and the memory actually available to YARN/Spark after reserving resources for the operating system and EMR services.

4. EMR Cost Model

EMR cluster costs involve two major components:

            TOTAL EMR COST

                    |

        +-----------+-----------+

        |                       |

     EC2 Cost              EMR Fee

        |                       |

  Infrastructure          Managed EMR

     compute               service fee

The source example uses:

EC2 m4.large

= $0.105 / instance-hour

EMR management fee

= $0.030 / instance-hour

Total

= $0.135 / instance-hour

For 4 instances:

4 × $0.135

= $0.54 per hour

Interview Question

Q: What contributes to the cost of an EMR cluster?

Answer:
The major components include the underlying EC2 instance cost and the EMR service charge. Depending on the architecture, additional costs can come from storage, networking, S3, CloudWatch, and other AWS services used by the workload.

5. EMR Job Execution Models

EMR Spark applications can be submitted using several approaches.

                    [ EMR Job Submission ]

                           Spark Job

                              |

             +----------------+----------------+

             |                |                |

          Console            SSH            AWS CLI/SDK

             |                |                |

        EMR UI          Primary Node       Automated

                         spark-submit       pipelines

1. EMR Management Console

Spark steps can be submitted through the AWS Management Console.

This is useful for:

  • Manual testing
  • Learning
  • Interactive administration
  • Small operational tasks

2. SSH into Primary Node

An engineer can connect to the Primary Node and execute:

spark-submit \

  --deploy-mode cluster \

  s3://bucket/path/job.py

This is useful for:

  • Debugging
  • Manual execution
  • Interactive investigation

3. AWS CLI / SDK

For production automation, steps can be submitted programmatically.

Example:

aws emr add-steps \

  --cluster-id j-TSDACODLWSO6 \

  --region ap-south-1 \

  --steps Type=CUSTOM_JAR,Name="AggregatedOrdersJob",ActionOnFailure=CONTINUE,Jar=command-runner.jar,Args=["spark-submit","--deploy-mode","cluster","s3://sample-emr-project2/spark-script/emr_aggregated_orders_data.py"]

This approach is particularly useful for:

  • Airflow
  • CI/CD
  • Automated ETL
  • Event-driven workflows
  • Production orchestration

6. Transient vs Long-Running EMR Clusters

One of the most important EMR architecture decisions is whether a cluster should be temporary or continuously running.

Feature

Transient Cluster

Long-Running Cluster

Lifecycle

Created for a workload

Runs continuously

Termination

Automatically after completion

Manually/operationally terminated

Cost

Lower for intermittent workloads

Higher when idle

Best for

Scheduled ETL/batch

Shared/ad-hoc workloads

Resource utilization

High

Can be low during idle periods

Automation

Excellent

Moderate

Transient Cluster

Typical architecture:

10:00 PM

   ↓

Create EMR Cluster

   ↓

Run Spark ETL

   ↓

Write output to S3

   ↓

Terminate Cluster

This avoids paying for idle compute.

Long-Running Cluster

Typical architecture:

EMR Cluster

     |

     +-- Job A

     +-- Job B

     +-- Job C

     +-- Interactive Analysis

     +-- Job D

Useful when workloads arrive frequently and cluster startup overhead needs to be avoided.

Interview Question

Q: Which EMR architecture would you choose for a daily 30-minute ETL job?

Answer:
A transient EMR cluster is generally preferable. The cluster can be created immediately before the ETL job, execute the Spark steps, write results to S3, and automatically terminate after successful completion. This minimizes idle infrastructure cost.

7. EMR Serverless

EMR Serverless allows users to run Apache Spark and Hive workloads without provisioning or managing EC2-based EMR clusters.

            EMR SERVERLESS

        Submit Spark Application

                  |

                  v

       +-----------------------+

       | EMR Serverless        |

       | Application           |

       +-----------------------+

                  |

                  v

       Dynamic Worker Allocation

                  |

        +---------+---------+

        |         |         |

      Worker    Worker    Worker

        |         |         |

       Spark     Spark     Spark

AWS manages:

  • Infrastructure provisioning
  • Worker allocation
  • Scaling
  • Capacity management

The user focuses primarily on the Spark application.

8. EMR Serverless Cost Model

The source material models EMR Serverless pricing using:

  • vCPU-hours
  • GB-hours of memory

The source rates are:

vCPU:

$0.052624 / vCPU-hour

Memory:

$0.0057785 / GB-hour

Example

Suppose each worker has:

4 vCPUs

30 GB RAM

Phase 1:

25 workers

4 vCPUs × 25

= 100 vCPUs

100 × 0.5 hours

= 50 vCPU-hours

vCPU cost:

50 × $0.052624

= $2.6312

Memory:

25 × 30 GB

= 750 GB

750 × 0.5 hours

= 375 GB-hours

Memory cost:

375 × $0.0057785

= $2.1669

The same calculation can be performed for subsequent autoscaling phases.

Key Interview Concept

EMR Serverless separates application logic from infrastructure management.

Instead of deciding:

"How many EC2 instances should I provision?"

you primarily configure application-level resources and allow EMR Serverless to provision workers dynamically.

Feature

EMR on EC2

EMR Serverless

Required

Higher

Interview Question

Q: When would you choose EMR on EC2 over EMR Serverless?

Answer:
Choose EMR on EC2 when you need detailed control over instance types, networking, node configuration, storage, cluster topology, or specialized workload tuning. Choose EMR Serverless when reducing infrastructure-management overhead and dynamically scaling variable Spark workloads are more important.

10. AWS Glue — Serverless Data Integration

AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service providing:

  • Data discovery
  • Metadata management
  • ETL
  • Schema discovery
  • Cataloging
  • Data preparation

A simplified architecture:

                 [ AWS GLUE ARCHITECTURE ]

                     Amazon S3

                         |

                         v

                  Glue Crawler

                         |

                         v

                Classifier Evaluation

                         |

                         v

                Glue Data Catalog

                         |

             +-----------+-----------+

             |                       |

          Athena                  Glue ETL

             |                       |

             +-----------+-----------+

                         |

                         v

                    Data Lake

11. AWS Glue Data Catalog

The Glue Data Catalog is a centralized metadata repository.

It stores information such as:

  • Table names
  • Column names
  • Data types
  • S3 locations
  • Partition information
  • Table properties

It is compatible with the Hive metastore model and can be used by services such as Athena and Glue.

Important Distinction

The Glue Catalog does not contain the actual data.

Instead:

S3

 ↓

Actual Data

Glue Catalog

 ↓

Metadata describing the data

For example:

S3:

s3://company-data/orders/

Glue Catalog:

Table: orders

Columns:

  order_id      BIGINT

  customer_id   BIGINT

  amount        DOUBLE

  order_date    DATE

Location:

  s3://company-data/orders/

12. AWS Glue Crawlers

A Glue Crawler automatically examines data sources and populates or updates metadata in the Glue Data Catalog.

Typical workflow:

S3 Files

   |

   v

Glue Crawler

   |

   +-- Detect Format

   +-- Infer Schema

   +-- Detect Partitions

   +-- Apply Classifiers

   |

   v

Glue Data Catalog

Crawlers can work against sources such as:

  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon Redshift
  • Relational databases
  • Other supported data stores

13. Glue Schema Evolution

Suppose an S3 dataset initially contains:

order_id

customer_id

order_date

amount

The Glue Catalog initially stores four columns.

Later, a new file arrives containing:

order_id

customer_id

order_date

amount

discount

After the crawler runs again, the catalog can evolve to:

order_id

customer_id

order_date

amount

discount

Historical records that don't contain the new field can appear as:

discount = NULL

Interview Question

Q: What happens when a new column is added to files in an S3 data lake?

Answer:
A Glue crawler can detect the changed schema and update the Data Catalog metadata. Existing records that don't contain the new attribute can be represented with NULL when queried using a compatible schema interpretation.

14. AWS Glue Classifiers

A classifier determines the structure and format of data encountered by a crawler.

                    Glue Crawler

                          |

                          v

                    Classifier

                          |

             +------------+------------+

             |                         |

       Custom Classifier        Built-in Classifier

             |                         |

        User-defined              AWS-provided

        patterns                  format detection

Built-in Classifiers

AWS provides classifiers for common formats such as:

  • CSV
  • JSON
  • Parquet
  • Avro
  • ORC

Custom Classifiers

Custom classifiers are useful when data doesn't conform to standard formats.

For example:

[2026-07-26 10:30:15] [ERROR] jacky@example.com Connection failed

A custom Grok pattern could extract:

timestamp

severity

email

message

Conceptually:

Raw Log

   |

   v

Custom Grok Classifier

   |

   +--> timestamp

   +--> severity

   +--> email

   +--> message

Classifier Priority

The source material describes:

  1. Custom classifiers evaluated first
  2. Built-in classifiers used as fallback

If a custom classifier successfully identifies the structure, the crawler can use that classification rather than continuing through the built-in classification list.

15. Handling Unstructured Logs with Grok

Consider:

[2026-07-26T10:30:00Z] [ERROR] jacky@example.com Connection failed

A conceptual Grok expression could identify:

TIMESTAMP_ISO8601 → timestamp

WORD              → severity

EMAILADDRESS      → email

remaining text    → message

Result:

timestamp

severity

email

message

2026-07-26 10:30

ERROR

jacky@example.com

Connection failed

This transforms otherwise unstructured logs into queryable structured data.

                         Amazon Athena

                              |

                              v

                     BI / Analytics Users

Example Enterprise Flow

  1. Raw files land in Amazon S3.
  2. Glue Crawler discovers their schema.
  3. Metadata is registered in Glue Data Catalog.
  4. EMR Spark performs large-scale transformations.
  5. Processed data is written back to S3 in an analytics-friendly format.
  6. Glue updates the metadata.
  7. Athena queries the curated datasets.
  8. BI tools consume analytical results.

19. Key Interview Questions — Week 32

Q1. What are the three major EMR node types?

Answer:
Primary, Core, and Task Nodes.

  • Primary → cluster coordination
  • Core → compute + HDFS storage
  • Task → compute only

Q2. Why are Task Nodes suitable for Spot Instances?

Answer:
Task Nodes don't store HDFS data, so their interruption does not directly remove persistent HDFS data. They can therefore be used as elastic compute capacity and are good candidates for cost-efficient Spot capacity.

Q3. Core Node vs Task Node?

Answer:
Core Nodes provide both compute and HDFS storage, while Task Nodes provide compute only.

Q4. Instance Groups vs Instance Fleets?

Answer:
Instance Groups use a simpler, more uniform configuration. Instance Fleets provide greater flexibility by allowing multiple EC2 instance types and purchasing options.

Q5. When would you use a transient EMR cluster?

Answer:
For intermittent workloads such as scheduled ETL jobs. The cluster can be created for the workload and automatically terminated afterward, reducing idle infrastructure cost.

Q6. What is EMR Serverless?

Answer:
A serverless execution environment for frameworks such as Spark and Hive where AWS manages the underlying compute infrastructure and dynamically allocates workers.

Q7. What is the Glue Data Catalog?

Answer:
A centralized metadata repository containing information about datasets, including schemas, tables, locations, and partitions. It stores metadata rather than the underlying data.

Q8. What does a Glue Crawler do?

Answer:
It scans supported data sources, determines schemas and formats, detects partitions, applies classifiers, and registers or updates table metadata in the Glue Data Catalog.

Q9. What is schema evolution in Glue?

Answer:
Schema evolution occurs when the structure of a dataset changes over time—for example, when a new column is added. A crawler can detect the change and update the Data Catalog schema.

Q10. When would you use a custom Glue classifier?

Answer:
When the source data doesn't conform to standard formats recognized by built-in classifiers, such as application logs containing custom patterns.

Q11. EMR vs Glue?

Answer:
EMR is primarily a distributed compute platform for running Spark, Hadoop and related workloads with significant infrastructure control. Glue is a serverless data integration and metadata platform focused on ETL, crawling, cataloging and schema discovery.

Week 32 Status

Master Study Guide: Weeks 1–32 complete.

The progression now moves from distributed computing → Spark/PySpark → Azure → streaming/Kafka → AWS analytics → enterprise AWS compute and governance, with Week 32 adding the important distinction between EMR as a compute platform and Glue as a serverless integration/catalog platform.

Week 33: AWS Glue Visual ETL, Data Governance, Sensitive Data Protection & Custom Transforms

1. AWS Glue ETL Execution Models & Infrastructure

AWS Glue is a fully managed, serverless data integration service used for ETL processing across services such as Amazon S3, Amazon RDS/MySQL, and Amazon Redshift.

2. AWS Glue Visual ETL & Built-In Transformations

Glue Visual ETL represents an ETL pipeline as a graph consisting of:

SOURCE

  │

  ▼

TRANSFORM

  │

  ▼

TARGET

Example:

Orders ───────────┐

                  ├──> JOIN ──> CHANGE SCHEMA ──> S3 Parquet

Customers ────────┘

        customer_id

Three Major Node Categories

1. Sources

Examples:

  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon RDS
  • Amazon Redshift
  • Glue Data Catalog

2. Transforms

Transform and manipulate the incoming data.

3. Targets

Write the processed data to a destination such as S3, RDS, or Redshift.

Core Visual Transformations

Change Schema

Equivalent to ApplyMapping.

Used to:

  • Rename columns
  • Change data types
  • Drop unwanted fields
  • Perform schema coercion

Example:

order_id STRING

       ↓

order_id BIGINT

Join

Combines multiple datasets using matching fields.

Example:

Orders.customer_id

        =

Customers.customer_id

SQL Query

Allows SQL expressions to be executed against temporary views directly inside the visual pipeline.

Useful when standard visual transformations aren't sufficient.

Aggregate

Performs grouping and mathematical operations.

Example:

GROUP BY customer_id

COUNT(order_status)

SUM(order_amount)

AVG(order_amount)

Filter

Removes records that don't satisfy specified conditions.

Supports:

  • Global AND
  • Global OR
  • Regex-based conditions
  • String comparisons
  • Numeric comparisons

Conditional Router

Splits one dataset into multiple branches.

                    ┌──> output_group_1

Input Dataset ────────┤

                     └──> default_group

Useful when different records need different downstream processing.

Utility Transformations

Glue also provides:

  • Select Fields
  • Drop Fields
  • Rename Fields
  • Drop Null Fields
  • Drop Duplicates

Drop Duplicates can operate on:

  • Entire records
  • A selected subset of key fields

4. Sensitive Data Protection & PII Governance

Data lakes frequently contain Personally Identifiable Information (PII).

Examples include:

  • Email addresses
  • Phone numbers
  • Social Security Numbers
  • Birth dates

AWS Glue provides sensitive-data detection and protection mechanisms.

PII Governance Pipeline

Raw Dataset

     │

     ▼

Detect Sensitive Data

     │

     ▼

Pattern Matching

 ┌───┴──────────────┐

 │                  │

Built-in          Custom

Patterns          Grok/Regex

 │                  │

 └───────┬──────────┘

         ▼

Global Action

 ┌────────┼─────────────┐

 ▼        ▼             ▼

DETECT   REDACT     SHA256_HASH

Detection Models

1. Identify Sensitive Data in Each Row

Performs a deeper scan across individual cells.

The purpose is to identify individual PII occurrences.

2. Identify Columns with Sensitive Data

Uses a sampled set of rows and a Detection Threshold.

For example:

Rows scanned = 100%

Detection threshold = 20%

If PII occurrences exceed the threshold, the entire column is classified as sensitive.

5. Custom PII Detection Using Regex

Built-in detection patterns may not recognize organization-specific fields.

For example, a custom pattern can identify dates of birth.

Course example:

\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01])

This targets a date format similar to:

YYYY-MM-DD

Why Custom Patterns?

Use custom regex patterns when:

  • The data is organization-specific.
  • Built-in classifiers don't recognize the field.
  • You need precise control over sensitive-data identification.

6. PII Protection Actions

After sensitive information is detected, Glue can apply a global action.

Action

What Happens

Example Result

DETECT

Identifies sensitive data without modifying original values

Metadata identifying EMAIL, PHONE_NUMBER, etc.

REDACT

Masks sensitive values

john@example.com → ****

SHA256_HASH

Applies one-way SHA-256 hashing

Original value → irreversible hash

DETECT

Preserves original values and adds information describing the detected sensitive entities.

REDACT

Masks the original sensitive value.

Useful when the downstream system does not need the actual PII.

SHA256_HASH

Converts the original value into a one-way cryptographic hash.

Useful when you need to:

  • Protect the original value.
  • Maintain consistency.
  • Perform secure matching/joins using the transformed value.

Important Distinction

DETECT       → Identify

REDACT       → Hide

SHA256_HASH  → Transform irreversibly

7. AWS Glue Data Quality & DeeQu

AWS Glue supports data-quality evaluation using the open-source DeeQu framework.

Rules are expressed using Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL).

Two major operating modes are covered:

            AWS GLUE DATA QUALITY

       DATA QUALITY AT REST

              │

              ├── Static cataloged tables

              ├── DQDL rulesets

              └── Results → S3 / CloudWatch

                     VS

       DATA QUALITY IN MOVE

              │

              ├── Active Visual ETL pipeline

              ├── Dynamic evaluation

              └── originalData + ruleOutcomes

Data Quality at Rest

Used when evaluating data that already exists.

Example:

S3 Dataset

    ↓

Glue Catalog Table

    ↓

DQDL Rules

    ↓

Quality Evaluation

    ↓

Results

Data Quality in Move

Quality checks occur inside an active ETL pipeline.

The pipeline can separate:

Input

  │

  ▼

Data Quality Evaluation

  │

  ├──> originalData

  │

  └──> ruleOutcomes

This makes it possible to evaluate quality while data is being transformed.

8. DQDL Rules

Example ruleset:

Rules = [

    IsPrimaryKey "customerid",

    IsComplete "firstname",

    Uniqueness "firstname" > 0.95,

    IsComplete "email",

    Uniqueness "email" = 1.0,

    IsComplete "phonenumber",

    ColumnValues "phonenumber" between 1111111110 and 9999999999,

    ColumnValues "loyaltypoints" >= 0,

    ColumnCount = 8,

    CustomSql "select count(*) from primary where joindate > lastpurchasedate" = 0

]

Important Rules

IsPrimaryKey

Checks whether the column satisfies primary-key expectations.

IsComplete

Checks whether values are populated.

IsComplete "email"

Uniqueness

Checks uniqueness percentage.

Uniqueness "email" = 1.0

means the email values must be completely unique according to the rule.

ColumnValues

Checks whether values satisfy a specified condition.

Example:

ColumnValues "loyaltypoints" >= 0

ColumnCount

Validates the number of columns.

ColumnCount = 8

CustomSql

Allows custom SQL logic when built-in rules aren't sufficient.

9. Custom Transformations in AWS Glue

Visual ETL is powerful, but complex business logic may require custom PySpark code.

AWS Glue supports custom transformations using:

  • Python
  • PySpark
  • DynamicFrames
  • DataFrames

DynamicFrameCollection

Glue custom transformation nodes receive datasets as a:

DynamicFrameCollection

To manipulate the data with standard PySpark DataFrame APIs:

DynamicFrameCollection

        ↓

Select DynamicFrame

        ↓

.toDF()

        ↓

PySpark DataFrame

        ↓

Transform

        ↓

DynamicFrame

        ↓

DynamicFrameCollection

10. Custom PySpark Transformation Example

from awsglue.dynamicframe import DynamicFrame, DynamicFrameCollection

from pyspark.sql.functions import when

def MyTransform(glueContext, dfc) -> DynamicFrameCollection:

    # Extract DynamicFrame from collection

    df = dfc.select(list(dfc.keys())[0]).toDF()

    # Apply transformation

    result_df = df.withColumn(

        'CustomerSegment',

        when(df['LoyalPoints'] < 1000, 'Bronze')

        .when(

            (df['LoyalPoints'] >= 1000) &

            (df['LoyalPoints'] < 2000),

            'Silver'

        )

        .otherwise('Gold')

    )

    # Convert back to DynamicFrame

    dyf_segmented = DynamicFrame.fromDF(

        result_df,

        glueContext,

        "segmented_loyalty_points"

    )

    # Return collection

    return DynamicFrameCollection(

        {"CustomTransform0": dyf_segmented},

        glueContext

    )

Transformation Logic

LoyalPoints < 1000

       ↓

    Bronze

1000 ≤ LoyalPoints < 2000

       ↓

    Silver

LoyalPoints ≥ 2000

       ↓

     Gold

11. Why Select From Collection Is Important

A custom transform can return multiple DynamicFrames inside a:

DynamicFrameCollection

However, downstream Glue nodes generally need a specific DynamicFrame.

Therefore:

DynamicFrameCollection

        ↓

Select From Collection

        ↓

Specific DynamicFrame

        ↓

S3 / RDS / Other Target

Interview Question

Why do we need Select From Collection after a custom transform?

Answer: Because a custom transform returns a DynamicFrameCollection, while downstream processing generally needs a specific DynamicFrame. The Select From Collection node extracts the required DynamicFrame.

Custom transformation logic can be converted into reusable Visual ETL nodes that can be shared across development teams.
